This paper establishes a key result regarding the foundation of B-type Coxeter groups. Specifically, for any given foundation $T$, we explicitly characterize the elasticity and the set of left weakly $T$-flexible elements within the corresponding Coxeter group $W$. As a consequence, we provide a clear criterion to determine whether an element $w$ in $W$ belongs to the subgroup $\mathcal{W}_T$ associated with $T$. This approach relies on calculating the length of $w$ using the length function defined on $\mathcal{W}_T$. Furthermore, our methodology yields a new, constructive algorithm for computing $\mathrm{el}(w)$, which was previously only known to exist non-constructively. Finally, we explore various applications of these findings. In particular, we demonstrate that the elasticity of $W$ is invariably $1$, and we offer a constructive determination of the left $\mathcal{W}_T$-elasticity for any subset $S$ of the simple reflections of $W$. To achieve this, we explicitly describe the elasticity of $\mathcal{W}_T$ and identify its maximal $\mathcal{W}_T$-flexible elements. These results are derived by examining the structure of the quotient group $\mathcal{W}_T / T$. Additionally, we establish that the right $\mathcal{W}_T$-elasticity of $W$ also equals $1$. The primary motivation behind this research was to address an open question posed by J. Arun Kumar and S. Narasimhan in their work "On the structure of the space of foundations for a Coxeter group," which remains unresolved. Specifically, they asked for an explicit calculation of the elasticity of a foundation $T$ for $W$. Our findings effectively resolve this issue, as the elasticity of $T$ corresponds precisely to the elasticity of $\mathcal{W}_T / T$. To prove these results, we also explicitly computed the elasticity of specific foundational subgroups, including those related to the exceptional Lie groups $E_6$ and $E_7$. This calculation involved determining the elasticity of certain quotients, such as $S_5 / S_4$, $S_6 / S_4$, $S_7 / S_5$, $S_8 / S_5$, $S_9 / S_6$, and $S_{10} / S_6$. The Set-Union Knapsack (SKU) problem and the (Budgeted) Maximum Coverage (MC/MBC) problems are challenging combinatorial optimization tasks with significant real-world applications. In the SKU problem, the goal is to select a subset of items such that their union covers a predefined set of required elements, while maximizing the total value of the selected items. The (Budgeted) Maximum Coverage problem involves choosing $k$ items to maximize the number of covered elements, adhering to a budget constraint in the bounded variant. This study introduces a novel tabu search-based metaheuristic for addressing these challenges. The proposed method is proven to be both productive and efficacious, consistently generating high-quality solutions for SKU instances. Furthermore, it surpasses the best existing algorithms for both Maximum Coverage issues, achieving the optimal solution in every instance. Additionally, the method outperforms a recent state-of-the-art algorithm for the bounded budgeted maximum coverage problem. The approach is both simple and efficient, making it suitable for practical application. Experimental results confirm that the proposed method is robust and robust across all tested instances. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/ehsan-hosseini123/TabuSearch-for-SKU-MC-and-MBC. Future research will explore extensions of this method to tackle other related problems.

Our method accurately replicates the attrition rates observed in the original data. Furthermore, the model enables operators to calculate retained user volume under various hypothetical scenarios regarding the total amount of play. These results demonstrate that our approach effectively models attrition rates and facilitates the evaluation of new policies designed to encourage extended betting sessions. This capability supports the development of new retention strategies, thereby enhancing customer lifetime value. Finally, we outline how to extend this model to forecast operator revenue.

Accidents are the primary hazard confronting cyclists, yet the intricate nature of these events makes them difficult to model. This study introduces a novel descriptor for cycling accidents that integrates context and motion dynamics. The proposed descriptor is constructed using video streams from multiple cameras, which are processed to extract features describing the accident. It is designed to be adaptable to various contexts, including weather conditions, road surface types, and traffic volume. The research demonstrates that this new descriptor complements and enhances existing accident countermeasures by identifying effective interventions based on their corresponding video-derived risk profiles. Furthermore, it is shown to improve accident risk prediction by accurately anticipating potential risks and their specific contextual occurrences. Finally, the potential of this descriptor to facilitate accident management is highlighted through its application in risk-based decision-making. The method's efficacy is validated using a comprehensive dataset of cycling accidents from the Netherlands, spanning the years 2008 to 2018. Additionally, cross-validation is performed with the ACCIDENTS database, which contains accident records from the United States and Canada. The findings confirm that the new descriptor yields significant improvements in both risk classification and accident prediction. Specifically, the results indicate an enhancement in risk classification, and a further improvement in accident prediction when the new descriptor is employed. The new risk descriptor is anticipated to assist policymakers and practitioners in developing more effective and targeted safety countermeasures. Furthermore, it can be utilized to assess the efficacy of implemented countermeasures and to evaluate the accident risk of cycling infrastructure. To support these functions, an open-source software tool has been developed to compute the descriptor, and its source code is made available. This tool is intended to enable future research to leverage the advantages offered by the new descriptor. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/abdullahkaya1982/cycling-accident-risk-descriptor. The tool's functionality is demonstrated via two examples: (i) evaluating the effectiveness of proposed risk-based countermeasures, and (ii) assessing the accident risk of a newly proposed cycling infrastructure. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions and potential applications of the new descriptor. Furthermore, the new descriptor is expected to enhance the accuracy of accident simulation models, thereby aiding accident investigators in reconstructing incidents and determining root causes. Finally, the new descriptor is anticipated to assist practitioners in assessing the risk of new cycling infrastructure projects. Keywords: Cyclist Accident Risk, Risk Assessment, Risk Countermeasures, Accident Prediction, Accident Simulation, Accident Reconstruction.

The resilient security of Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) is a critical concern in the motion planning of ground robotics. This paper introduces a novel framework for UGV motion planning that employs Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to ensure both resilience and security against diverse network attacks, including jamming, malicious code, and logic attacks. Specifically, CBF constraints are applied to limit the robot's trajectory, thereby mitigating attack impacts and enabling a return to a safe zone. Beyond basic ground motion planning, the study also addresses secure and resilient 3D flight planning. To handle communication interruptions during attack responses, the proposed approach utilizes a distributed depth-first search algorithm. Additionally, to facilitate efficient planning under various attack scenarios, an attack graph is developed to visualize attack paths and their consequences. The method's efficacy is validated through simulations and experiments involving both ground and aerial UGVs. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully generates collision-free trajectories in complex environments, effectively enhancing the resilience of UGV motion planning. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits robustness against communication jamming, malicious code injection, and logic attacks. Finally, to support flexible and efficient motion planning, an attack-aware path planning algorithm is designed. This algorithm utilizes an improved distributed depth-first search to generate alternative trajectories, ensuring the UGV can evade attacks and reach its destination. The findings indicate that the system can achieve this despite experiencing up to 90% packet loss during attacks. Additionally, the attack-aware path planning completes its mission 1.5 times faster than conventional path planning methods. These outcomes confirm the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed security and resilience mechanisms for UGV motion planning. The study's findings also hold relevance for other dynamic robotics domains, such as autonomous driving. Ultimately, this research offers a resilient and security-aware motion planning solution for UGVs, which is essential for the widespread adoption of dynamic robotics. Furthermore, the security and resilience strategies developed here can serve as a foundation for securing future robotic systems. Classical Segal-Bargmann theory extends into new territories within Clifford algebras. By introducing a novel Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transformation alongside a corresponding weighted $L^2$ inner product, we establish a unitary mapping between squared $L^2$ spaces. This mapping connects $L^2$ spaces weighted by $\lambda^n$ and $\mu^n$ (where $\mu = -\lambda < 0 < \lambda$) with unitarily equivalent Hilbert spaces of Clifford algebra-valued functions defined on $\mathbb{C}^N$—the standard Clifford algebra Segal-Bargmann space. This space supports an algebra isomorphism between symmetric polynomials of degree $n$ and Clifford algebra-valued homogeneous polynomials of degree $n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Taylor isomorphism, which links the space of tempered distributions $\mathcal{S}'$ to the space of holomorphic functions on the entire complex space $\mathbb{C}^N$, is isometric under the established weighted $L^2$ inner product. The composition of these individual isometries yields a unified Segal-Bargmann transformation. This paper concentrates on the algebraic aspects of Clifford algebra isomorphisms, with future research to address the corresponding quantum field theory implications. The foundational work for these developments is documented in [1]. Additional related developments can be found in [2].

This thesis introduces a framework for formally defining the advanced value-of (VO) meaning within ontologies and for enhancing Valuation Objects (VOOs) through their integration with Ontology Value Components (OVCs). Both the superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation serve as techniques for reducing the dimensionality of integrals involving Grassmann variables. The superbosonization equation reduces a Grassmann integral to a set of Grassmann-valued integrals, whereas the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation converts it into an integral involving both Grassmann and complex variables. We demonstrate that both methods yield identical results when at least one Grassmann field possesses a finite number of components. Furthermore, we establish a condition ensuring their equivalence in scenarios where at least one Grassmann field has an infinite number of components. These findings are applicable to various contexts, including field theories, random matrix models, and disordered systems. Specifically, we analyze the one-dimensional disordered Hubbard model with two types of local quenched disorder: random chemical potential and random non-chiral potential. We determine the conditions under which both techniques produce equivalent results in this context. Notably, these equivalence conditions differ from those of a recently proposed generalized superbosonization method, which employs a distinct approach to Grassular integration. Consequently, the validity and equivalence of both methods require careful examination when dealing with complex Grassmann fields possessing a finite number of components. Finally, we note that both methods remain valid and equivalent when every Grassmann field possesses a finite number of components. In this specific scenario, the superbosonization equation simplifies to the standard superbosonization method. However, this standard method is not applicable when at least one Grassmann field has an infinite number of components. Thus, this study clarifies the conditions under which both the superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation can be effectively utilized in such cases. We investigate the production of light neutrinoless double-beta decay via high-energy collider processes involving longitudinal $Z$ bosons. This scenario offers a unique opportunity to probe the interference effect between heavy $Z$ states, which can be observed as a shift in the overall cross-section relative to the production of massless states. In the minimal $\mathrm{SU}(2)_L\times \mathrm{U}(1)_Y$ extension featuring $N$ additional $SU(2)_L$ doublet neutrinos, this phenomenon is highly sensitive to the $Z$ states' quantum numbers, specifically the relative magnitudes of their charges under the new abelian generator within the doublet neutrino multiplets. We establish the necessary conditions for such interference and propose a strategy to constrain the relevant quantum numbers using the nonobservation of neutrinoless double-beta decay at colliders. These findings provide valuable insights for interpreting experimental results and guide future searches for light neutrinoless decay in collider environments. Notably, we have identified a simple three-neutrino extension that exhibits this effect, a model that is also highly testable at colliders. Finally, we outline the necessary experimental sensitivities to constrain the $Z$ states' quantum numbers, thereby clarifying the physical implications of the nonobservation of neutrinoless double-beta decay in colliders. This study complements our recent work on the double-beta decay of heavy neutrinos produced in colliders. In both instances, we assume that neutrino oscillation data have confirmed the light neutrino mass matrix's off-diagonal block structure, indicating that the light neutrino mass matrix is effectively quasi-degenerate. Our findings demonstrate that this assumption is physically well-motivated, as it enables the interference effect in neutrinoless double-beta decay within colliders. Furthermore, the quasi-degeneracy of the light neutrino mass matrix is a necessary condition for the large mixing between active and heavy $Z$ states, which is essential for the decay of heavy $Z$ states in colliders. This condition also explains the unexpectedly large mixing between active and sterile neutrinos inferred from the anomalous disappearance of electron neutrinos in the MINERvA experiment. Additionally, the large mixing between active and heavy $Z$ states in colliders can account for the anomalous excess of low-energy events observed in the COHERENT experiment. Consequently, the high-energy production of light and heavy neutrinoless double-beta decay is a generic feature of the heavy $Z$ states' properties, which are determined by the quantum numbers

This article introduces a method for approximating the combined PSF, which is essential for photometric applications. The approach is grounded in a polynomial approximation of the individual PSFs, utilizing Legendre polynomials. We estimate the approximation order required to maintain a specific photometric precision. Although this technique is currently limited to PSFs that are positive and radially symmetric, it remains generally applicable. For the specific case of the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3, an approximation order of 7 is sufficient to achieve a flux error below 0.01%. Additionally, we provide a PSF model for the combined images, with code available at https://github.com/tpereira/psf_combiner. This model is particularly relevant for photometry involving small sources, such as supernovae. Finally, we outline an extension to handle non-symmetric PSFs. The proposed algorithm is implemented in Python and is freely accessible. The PSF model for combined images can be calculated using our tool, https://github.com/tpereira/psf_combiner, which offers a Python interface and a REST API. This model is especially valuable for photometry of small sources. A demonstration of the model is presented, showing its application to the PSF of the James Webb Space Telescope. The results indicate that for the primary mirror, an approximation order of 10 yields a flux error less than 0.01%. For the secondary and tertiary mirrors, higher orders are needed to achieve the same level of accuracy. We develop a theoretical framework to investigate the theoretical limits of fracture resilience in crystalline materials. Our analysis centers on resilience, defined as the fraction of absorbed energy that contributes to damage tolerance. The framework examines elastic wave propagation during material failure, emphasizing the connection between energy dissipation mechanisms and the evolution of microstructural damage. We demonstrate that the theoretical upper bound for resilience is governed by the competition between elastic wave speeds in a damaged versus undamaged state. Furthermore, we derive quantitative predictions for these theoretical limits, which are particularly pertinent to materials failing through ductile tearing. We argue that these findings offer valuable insights for guiding the design of resilient materials and can inform the interpretation of experimental data. Specifically, we examine data from steel fracture toughness tests, revealing a strong alignment with our theoretical predictions. This suggests that the undamaged wave speed acts as a fundamental parameter in ductile fracture, a concept that may prove useful in resolving discrepancies in the steel industry's recent empirical observations. Finally, we explore the implications of our theory for crystalline materials that are resilient to initial failure but experience reduced resilience as they progress through the failure process. We conclude that such a reduction in resilience is an intrinsic characteristic of the elastic-plastic fracture process. This insight is crucial for the development of advanced engineering materials, such as metallic glasses, which are currently under investigation for their ability to maintain high resilience even at advanced stages of failure. Our theory indicates that the resilience of metallic glasses may decline during the fracture process due to a reduction in the acoustic wave speed of the associated amorphous shear transformation zone. Additionally, we show that this reduction in wave speed is linked to an increase in fracture toughness, a phenomenon observed in some but not all metallic glasses. We contend that this variation in resilience is a key factor in the diverse behaviors exhibited by different metallic glasses during fracture. Finally, we outline how our theory can be integrated into computational models of material failure, providing a pathway for simulating the resilience of materials failing via ductile tearing. This enables a more accurate representation of energy partitioning and energy release rates in numerical failure simulations. Overall, we believe that our theory will enhance our understanding of the fracture resilience of crystalline materials and facilitate the more effective utilization of materials in critical engineering applications. This study establishes new bounds for the $L_\infty$-norm solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations under periodic initial conditions. These findings are derived from novel estimates regarding the norms of Riesz potentials and the heart-shaped convolution kernel. The resulting bounds refine previous $L_\infty$-norm resolutions of the Navier-Stokes equations. Additionally, we offer new insights into the regularity of Navier-Stokes equations by proposing a method to determine the critical space exponent $p$ where $\|u_0\|_p < \infty$ ensures the existence of weak solutions with energy conservation. Our work also provides a resolution for periodic initial conditions, demonstrating that for any $p$ with $p_0 \leq p < 6/5$, a solution exists for all time provided the initial velocity is sufficiently small. This confirms that the critical dimension-dependent exponent $p_0$ is not the threshold for the existence of small weak solutions in the periodic setting. We introduce a system designed to generate realistic models of cell shapes. By utilizing an implicit representation based on neural networks, the system can create realistic cell forms that are both editable and capable of random generation. A practical application, namely cell shape morphing, is presented to demonstrate the system's utility. Accessing legal documents is essential for ensuring a fair judicial process, a right secured for all citizens by Article 12 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. However, despite being a fundamental right, many individuals struggle to comprehend these documents due to poor readability, a problem that is especially acute for those with print impairments. This paper introduces a novel approach to assessing the accessibility of written text in documents, which is critical for people who cannot read printed material. We present a dataset comprising 1,000 text documents sourced from the Web, annotated with accessibility labels. Our data analysis reveals that access necessity and text length are the primary determinants of a document's accessibility. Furthermore, we propose a mixture model to predict document accessibility and demonstrate its effectiveness on the retrieved dataset. Finally, we explore the application of large language models, specifically GPT-3, as an alternative method for accessibility prediction. Our findings indicate that LLMs can serve as effective tools for estimating the accessibility of legal documents. Overall, this study aims to heighten awareness of document accessibility among researchers and practitioners, offering novel methods for analysis and prediction that can guide future efforts in creating accessible legal resources. Additionally, the accompanying dataset is made publicly available to support further research in this domain. Our code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/ashishkumar1234567890/docacc. Our results are accessible at: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ashishkumar1234567890/docacc. Exoplanet atmospheres are typically investigated through transit spectroscopy, a method inherently susceptible to stellar activity-induced noise. This study examines the mitigation potential of high-resolution spectroscopy, leveraging its ability to distinguish between stellar and planetary signals, in contrast to the more conventional low-resolution approach. We developed a simulation framework incorporating both active stars and exoplanets, utilizing synthetic spectra to model observations across a wide wavelength range. Our findings indicate that employing high-resolution spectroscopy can reduce effective noise by a factor of 100 compared to low-resolution techniques. Consequently, this shift may enable the detection of low-abundance species and facilitate the confirmation of previously reported molecular findings. Furthermore, our results suggest that high-resolution spectroscopy could potentially allow for the recovery of signals from an active M-dwarf that would otherwise be obscured by activity-related contamination. Ultimately, these outcomes underscore the critical necessity of high-resolution spectroscopy for the upcoming generation of space-based observatories. Finally, we provide a Python-based pipeline to generate synthetic active star spectra, which can be freely accessed at https://github.com/afg1999/synactspec.

The presence of anomalies in a theory governed by constant curvature metrics on a Riemann surface results in $U(1)$ fields with non-trivial cohomology classes. We investigate how to construct these metrics when anomalies are present. We define a method for constant curvature metrics to remain anisotropic due to anomalies and demonstrate that such metrics can exist even if anomalies impose strict constraints on the possible cohomology classes. Furthermore, we observe that the curvature tensor remains skew-symmetric despite anomalies, maintaining the equivalence between the Fubini-Study metric and Hilbert's metric. However, anomalies cause the geodesic distance between two points to differ from the distance between their corresponding holomorphic sections in the moduli space. Additionally, the existence of global holomorphic sections in the moduli space is significantly hindered by anomalies. Finally, we note that theories with constant curvature metrics and anomalies possess fermion zero modes. The number of these zero modes is determined by the topological invariants of the constant curvature metric and the specific characteristics of the anomalies. The magnitude of this number can be substantially increased by the contribution from anomalies. Consequently, this suggests that the mechanism for zero mode generation via anomalies is distinct from the Atiyah-Singer index theorem. The index theorem relies on the skew-symmetry of the curvature tensor and the Chern-Weil theory to establish the topological nature of the index; however, since anomalies allow the skew-symmetry of the curvature tensor to be relaxed, the index is no longer a topological invariant, thereby invalidating the application of the Chern-Weil method. Therefore, anomalies provide an alternative mechanism for zero mode generation that is independent of the Atiyah-Singer index theorem. This implies that fermion zero modes can arise solely from anomalies, even in the absence of non-trivial topological invariants. We also examine how to eliminate the contribution of anomalies to the zero modes. To achieve this, we demonstrate that the zero mode contribution from anomalies can be canceled by the topological charge density of magnetic monopoles. This finding suggests that the generation of zero modes via anomalies may be linked to the existence of magnetic monopoles. We also explore the relationship between fermion zero modes and fermion condensation within constant curvature metrics and anomalies. We show that the zero modes generated by anomalies can be interpreted as a form of fermion condensation. The successful return of centipedes to terrestrial environments depended on a flexible body plan that allowed for efficient locomotion on solid ground. This study presents the first experimental realization of a water surface locomotor for soft robots that utilizes a centipede-inspired body plan. The device was engineered to replicate key features of centipede biomechanics, specifically the alternating kinematics of dorsal and ventral segments and the use of adhesion for propulsion. By applying a slender body theory to the interface deformation generated by the locomotor, we identified the optimal ventral segment speed required for efficient movement. Furthermore, we examined the role of centripetal forces in body shape optimization and the impact of adhesion on the efficiency of the alternating gait. These findings offer a theoretical basis for creating bio-inspired robots capable of locomoting on both solid surfaces and fluid interfaces. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that centipede-like body plans are highly versatile for terrestrial movement and can be effectively adapted for water surface locomotion. The soft-robotic body, combined with bio-inspired locomotion strategies, holds significant promise for diverse applications, including search and rescue operations, environmental monitoring, and the transportation of goods. Additionally, these bio-inspired robots may serve as valuable tools for investigating centipede biomechanics and for delivering interventions that benefit centipedes. Finally, the versatility of these bio-inspired robots is highlighted by demonstrating their ability to climb vertical surfaces. This study presents and evaluates a methodology for modeling local-to-global asteroid impact scenarios involving large oceanic regions. The approach employs nested grids featuring significantly refined resolutions in specific zones to capture fine-scale phenomena, such as the dispersion-driven deceleration of waves in shallow coastal areas. This technique is applied to a 100 km impact event on an ocean-covered Mars-like planet, utilizing an octree-based grid system with nested regions of varying resolutions. The investigation systematically analyzes several parameters, including the trigger grid size, the location of highly refined zones, and the number of nested grids. Results indicate that the nested grid method enables the creation of highly resolved impact and run-up models. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that impact models utilizing between 5 and 15 nested grids produce comparable results when these nested models are mapped onto the same total number of octree grids. Consequently, the nested simulations are subsequently compared against direct simulations generated on an equivalent OCTAVE grid framework. This research is the initial phase of a broader investigation into the tsunami generation and propagation resulting from multi-kilometer asteroid impacts. The primary objective is to develop a general methodology capable of accurately simulating such large-scale events. Future work will extend this analysis to impacts of varying sizes and locations, as well as to events on planets with diverse topographies. Additionally, the study will explore the feasibility of utilizing high-resolution impact simulations to trigger secondary phenomena, such as weather systems, within global simulations. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate the study of large-scale asteroid impacts and their associated tsunami generation across a range of planetary bodies. Specifically, the methodology will be applied to assess the potential for large impacts to generate life-threatening tsunamis on Earth, Mars, and exoplanets. This represents a first step toward understanding the likelihood of such large-scale events generating dangerous waves. Furthermore, the methodology will be employed to investigate the probability of large-scale events capable of producing human-threatening tsunamis on Earth. This serves as a preliminary step in understanding the potential for human civilization to be wiped out by such catastrophic occurrences. Finally, the approach will be used to assess the potential for large-scale events to generate life-threatening tsunamis on exoplanets. This represents a first step toward understanding the potential for such large-scale events to produce dangerous waves on other planets. The clogged disk method is widely recognized for deriving lower bounds on the space required to sort objects based on their dimension and the specific constraints of the system. This study investigates a novel variant where objects with alternating dimensions $d_1, d_2, d_1, d_2, \dots$ must be sorted within a channel of unit width. We introduce a new algorithm capable of sorting these objects in the channel using $d_1d_2 + d_1 + d_2$ area. This storage requirement is optimal, as it matches the sum of the objects' individual widths and aligns with the upper bound established by the original clogged disk algorithm for sorting mass objects with uniform dimension $d_1, d_2, d_1, d_2, \dots$. Furthermore, we extend this approach to mass objects with alternating dimensions $d_1, d_2, d_1, d_2, \dots$, demonstrating that they can be sorted in a channel of unit width using $d_1d_2+\frac{d_1}{\rho} +\frac{d_2}{\rho}$ area, where $\rho$ represents density. For disks, this quantity equals the area, whereas for slabs, it corresponds to area multiplied by total length. Additionally, we explore methods to adapt the original clogged disk algorithm to sort mass objects in a channel with minimal time complexity. Finally, we examine a variant featuring arbitrarily varying dimensions $d_1, d_2, d_3, d_4, \dots$ and establish a lower bound for the space needed to sort such objects in a channel of unit width. This lower bound equals the sum of the objects' widths when $d_1 \ge d_2 \ge d_3 \ge \dots$, and when this condition does not hold, a specific subset of objects determines the lower bound for the required space. Our findings are supported by a computer search that validates the necessity of the proposed lower bound for disks with up to 12 items and mass objects with up to 8 items. We also present a formal proof for the case of six disks. These results have practical applications in designing parallel computing systems, manufacturing processes, and assembly lines. The computer search was conducted using a SAT solver, a technique increasingly utilized in algorithm design. Specifically, we map the geographic distribution of areas experiencing very low precipitation ($P<0.01$) and those with elevated precipitation ($P>99$) across all longitudes and calendar seasons from 1980 to 2018. Non-affine deformation, a phenomenon often observed in jammed systems, refers to the nonlinear relationship between macroscopic strain and the local displacement of individual particles. This study, conducted on 2D granular assemblies, employs X-ray scattering to measure local displacements. The resulting method is concise and efficient, capable of distinguishing between purely affine and non-affine deformed states. Furthermore, it demonstrates that granular materials exhibit greater non-affine deformations than both molecular dynamics simulations of frictionless systems and theoretical predictions. Finally, the study explores the connection between calculated storage modulus values and the observed non-affine deformations. These findings will facilitate future investigations into non-affine deformations and their influence on the mechanical characteristics of granular materials. This study examines S66, a benchmark dataset for non-covalent interactions between molecular pairs, within external electric fields. The dataset comprises 110 molecules and 3,580 molecular pairs, including both parallel and antiparallel configurations subjected to electric fields ranging from 0 to ±0.05 a.u. The analysis focuses on the electric field-induced enhancement of van der Waals and charge-transfer interactions. To achieve this, the study employs the Coupled-Pair Natural Orbital-Coupled-Cluster (CPNO-CC) method, which offers high computational efficiency. The findings indicate that van der Waals interactions are significantly amplified by external electric fields, with the most substantial increases occurring in pairs featuring weaker van der Waals forces in the absence of the field. Furthermore, the dependence of the interaction energy on the external electric field is observed to be non-linear. Additionally, the research confirms that the CPNO-CC method is sufficiently accurate for investigating the effects of external electric fields on non-covalent interactions. The study also explores the relationship between the magnitude of the first-order perturbation of the intermolecular potential and the energy gain resulting from the external electric field. Finally, the CPNO-CC method is evaluated against the CCSD(T) method using a subset of 100 pairs, including 20 pairs selected to represent the full range of energy changes observed across all pairs under the applied electric fields. This comparison demonstrates that the CPNO-CC method achieves an accuracy comparable to that of the CCSD(T) method. This study introduces a novel ambiguity model designed to handle non-deterministic data within industrial contexts. Unlike traditional models that assume independence, this approach incorporates dependence to better reflect real-world conditions, thereby enhancing the accuracy of scheduling plans. The formulation utilizes binary representations of ambiguity and supports both symmetric and asymmetric relationships between events. A mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) method is developed to efficiently compute optimal schedules based on the new model. Additionally, a heuristic algorithm is proposed to generate high-quality solutions for large-scale problems in reasonable timeframes. The effectiveness of these approaches is validated through a real-world case study and extensive numerical experiments. Results from the case study confirm the method's practicality for real applications, while the numerical experiments demonstrate the advantages of the proposed MILP approach over existing methods. Furthermore, the comparison between the new model and the traditional independent model reveals significant performance improvements achieved by accounting for dependence. Finally, the computational efficiency of the proposed heuristic is analyzed and compared against a comparison algorithm. Ultimately, the computational results indicate that the proposed heuristic algorithm performs more efficiently than the comparison algorithm. This paper introduces an STL-driven robustness formulation for cyber-physical systems. Specification languages based on temporal logic offer precise descriptions of desired system behaviors. Recently, there has been a shift toward using signal temporal logic (STL) rather than classical temporal logic, as STL can define properties over system trajectories by incorporating time-stamp constraints and comparisons with time-varying signals. We propose measuring robustness as the extent to which a trajectory satisfies a property, distinguishing between quantitative (time-based) and qualitative (margin-based) approaches. Subsequently, we formulate robustness optimization problems for both quantitative and qualitative STL, providing complexity analysis and establishing the relationship between these problems and model checking. Finally, the paper demonstrates the practical utility of this STL-driven robustness framework through a case study. Our model assumes the system is exposed to an adversary that manipulates system parameters, aiming to minimize the qualitative robustness margin for STL specifications. Model checking serves as a verification tool to determine if robustness goals are met, while robust optimization identifies parameter values that maximize robustness. We illustrate how to utilize both model checking and robust optimization within this context. Additionally, we provide complexity analysis for the proposed formulation and its connection to model checking. We validate the model and algorithms using a case study involving a wheeled robot navigating a cluttered environment. Trajectories are evaluated against STL specifications to assess both qualitative and quantitative robustness. To achieve maximum robustness, we apply model checking and robust optimization to the STL formulas, thereby determining the optimal parameters for the robot's controller. Trajectories generated by these optimized parameters exhibit an improved robustness margin. The proposed methods are implemented using PySTL, a Python library for signal temporal logic. This implementation integrates with other toolboxes, such as MPM, which solves the mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulation of robustness optimization. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing the maximum qualitative robustness margin achieved via the optimization method against margins obtained from the SMT-based model checker. Furthermore, to address scalability challenges, we introduce a novel constraint generation algorithm for STL robustness optimization. This new approach outperforms the model checker in terms of both runtime and robustness margin. The paper concludes with a discussion of these findings. Our results indicate that optimization methods are better suited for STL-driven robustness formulation in cyber-physical systems, whereas model checking remains a valuable tool for analyzing robustness in smaller systems. The origin of compact radio sources remains a significant unresolved issue in astronomy. This study investigates the angular dimensions of various source categories by stacking radio images of single-epoch compact sources with distinct angular sizes. Specifically, we created three image stacks based on standard sources ranging from 0.05 to 0.2, 0.2 to 0.4, and 0.4 to 0.8 arcseconds. Our results indicate that compact starburst galaxies, low-excitation radio galaxies, and radio galaxies of other types are generally larger than 0.2 arcseconds. In contrast, radio galaxies exhibiting jet-blob structures or radio jets are typically smaller than 0.2 arcseconds. Furthermore, we observed that the fraction of sources with sizes exceeding 0.2 arcseconds is higher among starburst galaxies than among radio galaxies. These findings suggest that the radio structures of starburst galaxies and low-excitation radio galaxies are typically larger than 0.2 arcseconds, whereas most other radio galaxies are usually smaller than this threshold. These conclusions are supported by the observation that the majority of known radio galaxies with prominent jet structures exhibit angular sizes less than 0.2 arcseconds. Ultimately, we conclude that the radio sources identified in this study possess characteristic sizes exceeding 0.2 arcseconds. These results are consistent with the notion that such sources are primarily starburst galaxies, as our analysis reveals that the fraction of large sources is greater in starburst galaxies than in radio galaxies. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the angular size distribution of single-epoch compact sources can be effectively examined through image stacking. Future research should utilize higher-resolution radio telescopes to investigate the angular sizes of compact starburst galaxies and low-excitation radio galaxies. This approach will help clarify the source of the radio emission and potentially uncover new classes of large, compact sources. Ultimately, these efforts aim to shed light on the nature of single-epoch compact radio sources. The data utilized in this study are accessible at https://doi.org/10.1145/1234567. Information leakage from program executions can be modeled using probabilistic or Markov models. This paper introduces a monadic framework for quantitative information flow based on concealed Markov models. This approach unifies probability theory and computational effects into a unified framework for information flow analysis. The monad explicitly represents probability distributions and the non-determinism inherent in programs. We illustrate this methodology using a leakage model of exception-based exception handling. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's utility by deriving a generic upper-bound analysis for information flow and proposing a numerical algorithm for computing exact information flow.

Information is typically revealed to an observer via exceptions, which are generated non-deterministically during program execution. This monadic approach enables the construction of an observer model that captures both the probability space and the exception-based execution non-determinism. We introduce concealed Markov models as the foundation for describing such observer models. These models are defined as tuples consisting of a hidden Markov model and a concealed probability distribution. We provide two equivalent characterizations of this model: one using a concealed probability distribution over Markov models, and another using a probability distribution over hidden states within a Markov model. Additionally, we define exception-based programs using a specialized variant of the generalized exception monad. This monad represents execution outcomes as functions mapping possible exceptions to underlying computations. Using this framework, we demonstrate how to construct exception-based concealed Markov models from exception-based programs.

Our analysis employs upper entropy as the quantitative metric for information flow. Upper entropy represents the maximum entropy an observer can deduce about a program's initial hidden state after observing a computation, assuming the prior probability distribution is unknown to the observer. We present an upper-bound analysis for exception-based information flow that relies solely on the program's transition matrix and the observer model's emission matrix, while remaining independent of the specific concealed Markov model or the specific program implementation. This analysis is derived from generic properties of upper entropy. Furthermore, we propose a numerical algorithm for calculating exact information flow by utilizing exception-based concealed Markov models. This method utilizes dynamic programming to compute the entropy of observations, thereby enabling the determination of upper entropy.

The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews background concepts, including information flow, exception-based programs, probabilistic computation, Markov models, and Markov models with emissions. Section 3 provides a concise overview of monads and their utility in modeling computational effects. Section 4 defines exception-based computation within the generalized exception monad. Section 5 introduces the concept of an exception-based concealed Markov model

We present a framework to analyze the statistical nonlocality of dynamical fields arising from spatio-temporally extended systems, utilizing the external coherent oscillator model (SCM) as a case study. By applying the dynamic factorization method (DFM), we derive a compact set of asymptotic field equations from the full model equations, which are parameterized by the SCM. Employing the time-scale separation method, we demonstrate that these asymptotic equations accurately capture the main dynamical features of the original system across all spatial and temporal domains. Furthermore, we establish that dynamic factorization preserves the asymptotic statistical nonlocality inherent in the system. Finally, numerical simulations of a finite-size system validate our analytical findings. These results provide a foundation for developing reduced-order models that maintain the full statistical nonlocality of the original system. Additionally, our approach enables the construction of simplified models that accurately represent the statistical properties of the original system without requiring the assumption of spatially localized interactions. This work serves as a precursor to our subsequent research on applying dynamic factorization to various extended systems. Specifically, in future studies, we will extend the application of dynamic factorization to the stochastic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, which exhibits spatially nonlocal correlations. This will facilitate the development of reduced-order models that retain the full statistical nonlocality of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. Furthermore, we plan to apply dynamic factorization to the Navier-Stokes equation to derive simplified models that accurately capture the statistical features of turbulent flows. In this context, dynamic factorization will enable the construction of simplified models that preserve the spatially nonlocal correlations present in Navier-Stokes turbulence. Finally, dynamic factorization will be utilized to derive simplified models for other extended systems, such as the Burgers equation, the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and the reaction-diffusion equation. In these instances, dynamic factorization will allow for the creation of simplified models that retain the spatially nonlocal correlations present in the respective original systems. The spatially nonlocal correlations within these simplified models will be derived from the dynamic factorization method. This work serves as a precursor to our subsequent research on applying dynamic factorization to various extended systems. Specifically, in future studies, we will apply the dynamic factorization method to the stochastic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, the Burgers equation, the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and the reaction-diffusion equation. By employing dynamic factorization, we can derive simplified models for these systems that accurately capture their statistical features.

We provide a phenomenological analysis of the flexible scattering amplitudes for $2\to2$ and $4\to4$ processes within the massless limit, incorporating constraints from analyticity, unitarity, and unitary irreducible representations of the Poincaré group. Our findings reveal that in the high-energy, large-momentum transfer regime, these amplitudes exhibit nontrivial angular dependencies. Furthermore, we establish that all such amplitudes adhere to generalized soft-winding asymptotics, thereby extending this behavior to a broader class of processes. Additionally, we derive explicit expressions for the imaginary components of these amplitudes, demonstrating their alignment with the optical theorem for the $2\to4$ process and the Mandelstam double-commutator theorem for $4\to4$ processes. Finally, we examine the implications of these amplitudes regarding differential cross sections, BSM search strategies, and the testing of causality in high-energy colliders. These amplitudes may become accessible through multi-particle final states in the future, such as those observed in $pp\to Z_{(1,2,3)}Z_{(1,2,3)}$ and $pp\to ZZtt$ events at the HL-LHC and FCC-ee. Our findings suggest that incorporating angular information into flexible scattering observables could significantly enhance the sensitivity of searches for new physics. This approach offers a comprehensive framework for final-state analysis, capable of fully utilizing experimental data and maximizing the potential for discovering physics beyond the Standard Model. Consequently, this methodology is expected to be applicable to various flexible scattering processes in the near future. This research addresses the challenge of designing a beacon transmission strategy that minimizes location estimator error while ensuring the generated outcomes are computationally difficult to distinguish from a uniform prior, thereby maintaining privacy. We introduce the concept of conditional priors—specific distributions of event outcomes—and establish that achieving the best possible trade-off between estimation accuracy and privacy is NP-hard when utilizing this conditional privacy framework. Furthermore, we present a randomized algorithm that achieves an approximation of this optimal conditional privacy trade-off within polynomial time. Additionally, we explore event-based privacy, a variant where event parameters are randomly selected from a conditional prior, and demonstrate that our algorithm achieves a similar level of performance in this context. Numerical evaluations utilizing an elliptical geometric model for both estimation error and estimator indistinguishability metrics illustrate the achievable approximations of the conditional privacy optimum provided by our algorithm. We also present an approximation algorithm for a related problem aimed at maximizing event-based privacy, showing that a constant-factor approximation can be achieved in polynomial time. Finally, we examine the relationship between conditional privacy and prior-independent privacy, demonstrating that the former subsumes the latter. Our computational results indicate that the constant-factor approximation for event-based privacy yields a constant-factor approximation for conditional privacy, though the reverse does not hold. We conclude by discussing extensions of this work, such as addressing probabilistic constraints on estimator error and introducing a novel privacy metric for conditional privacy. Ultimately, this paper establishes the fundamental trade-offs between privacy and estimation error in location tracking systems. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to analyze location tracking privacy through the lens of conditional priors, offering a foundation for future research in the field. The Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) has long been a preferred method for solving the 3D global localization problem for mobile robots, offering a robust balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. However, NDT's performance degrades when applied to modern, high-fidelity LiDAR sensors, primarily because its efficiency relies on approximating the posterior probability density function (PDF) as a Gaussian, an assumption that fails with detailed data. To address this, we introduce the Normal Distribution Transform-Transformer (NDT-Transformer), a novel approach that utilizes a Transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture to model the high-fidelity NDT posterior. This paper first analyzes the limitations of NDT in the context of high-resolution LiDAR and then presents the NDT-Transformer to effectively leverage detailed point cloud data. We retrained NDT-Transformer on a large-scale dataset and assessed its performance against NDT and other state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that NDT-Transformer significantly outperforms NDT and achieves a comparable level of accuracy to other leading solutions. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity is extensively employed in neuroscience to investigate brain organization and investigate links with behavioral traits. However, the reproducibility of connectivity metrics derived from rs-fMRI remains a significant concern. This study assesses the precision of connectivity measurements and the precision of prediction models utilizing these metrics. We conducted 100 sessions of fMRI scanning on a single subject, utilizing a multivariate approach to assess the reproducibility of functional network topologies and their capacity to forecast functional magnetic resonance imaging data. Our results indicate that while reproducibility is highly variable across different brain regions, it is consistently low for long-range connections. Furthermore, we evaluated the precision of a predictive model that uses rs-fMRI connectivity metrics to forecast individual differences in intelligence. Although the prediction model demonstrated moderate accuracy, it exhibited low reproducibility across repeated scans. These findings suggest that the inherent noise in resting-state fMRI is substantial, which may hinder both the detection of subtle neural mechanisms and the validation of hypotheses. Consequently, rs-fMRI should be utilized with extreme care when investigating mechanisms that are either weak or highly variable. To enhance the precision of connectivity metrics and the interpretability of prediction models, we propose that researchers either employ larger sample sizes or utilize more robust estimation techniques. Finally, we provide an R package that calculates and visualizes the reproducibility of connectivity metrics and prediction models, facilitating a more rigorous and interpretable analysis of rs-fMRI connectivity. We examine a beeping network where each of $n$ nodes operates with an independent, unknown battery duration. Communication occurs via "beeping," meaning nodes only transmit when listening; a transmission fails if a node is beeping and another signal interferes. Each node executes a randomized algorithm to complete specific distributed tasks. The primary objective is minimizing power consumption, defined as the maximum beeping time across all nodes required to solve the task. This study focuses on two problems: leader election and distributed routing. We introduce novel algorithms and establish corresponding lower bounds for both scenarios. Specifically, for leader election, we demonstrate that $O(\log\log\log n)$-time algorithms exist with a failure probability of $2^{-\Omega(\log\log\log n)}$, and we prove this bound is tight. Regarding routing, we present an $O(1)$-time algorithm that achieves $O(\log n)$ success probability, again showing that $O(\log\log\log n)$ is the optimal failure probability. Finally, we discuss extensions of these findings to broader network models. To our knowledge, this work represents the first analysis of leader election and routing in beeping networks. Additionally, the network assumptions align with those of the recently proposed beeping model in distributed computing. Our results are expected to advance the understanding of energy-efficient network algorithms. Furthermore, the techniques developed here are applicable to other distributed computing problems. Code-mixed languages represent a significant yet largely unexplored domain, primarily because standard NLP techniques fail to generalize to them. This mixture occurs when speakers combine two distinct languages, blurring the distinction between them. This paper examines the challenge of identifying codeswitching points, or "transition points," within such texts. We introduce PESTO, a transformer-based system that integrates custom positional encodings to detect these points. This study employs first-principles calculations to analyze the phonon spectrum and superconducting properties of CS hydride across a pressure range of 200 to 300 GPa. The results indicate that, unlike other high-temperature superconductors, the isotope effect on the critical temperature ($T_c$) in CS is negative and pressure-dependent within this interval. Furthermore, the ratio $\gamma = \alpha T_c / T_c$ (where $\alpha$ represents the isotope exponent) shifts from 0.5 to greater than 1 as pressure increases from 200 to 300 GPa. These variations are attributed to the van Hove singularity (VHS) in the CS vibrational density of states, which occurs at the R point in the Brillouin zone and is phonon-mode-specific. Notably, the frequency of the singularity-driven transverse acoustic (TA) mode is pressure-dependent, causing the TA branch to cross the VHS at progressively higher pressures. This shift moves the peak of the TA phonon mode self-energy to higher frequencies, thereby reducing the superconducting coupling constant and the critical temperature. Additionally, the TA mode dispersion is flattened near the R point due to VHS, resulting in an anomalous isotope effect on the mode frequency. Consequently, the TA mode exhibits a softening at the R point when hydrogen is substituted with deuterium. These findings underscore the unique nature of the VHS-driven coupling mechanism in high-temperature superconductors and suggest that similar phenomena may occur in other materials. Ultimately, this research provides a theoretical basis for exploring the phase diagram of high-temperature superconductors and developing new superconducting materials. Additionally, the computational framework employed is expected to be valuable for investigating the phase diagram of other advanced materials. This study addresses the challenge of navigating a self-propelled agent through a sequence of time-varying, dynamically populated regions of interest (ROIs) within a 2D environment. The primary innovation lies in spatially and temporally constraining the agent's navigation by partitioning the environment into ROIs, each governed by a specific agent policy. The objective is to reach a target ROI while minimizing travel time and energy usage, and resisting disturbances from other agents. To achieve this, we developed a method that employs model predictive control (MPC) for navigation, utilizing an extended version of the Rapidly-exploring Randomized Trees (RRT*) algorithm to generate time-dependent navigation plans. We validated this approach via Monte Carlo simulations on a simplified agent model in a 2D setting, demonstrating that the method outperforms standard MPC-based NMPCC approaches in terms of time and energy efficiency. Furthermore, we illustrate how the proposed method can be adapted to various agent models and settings by examining potential extensions to self-propelled particles and mobile robots. Finally, we outline potential real-world applications, including the navigation of self-propelled particles in social contexts and robots in dynamic industrial facilities. This paper introduces a novel, low-complexity algorithm utilizing the Group LASSO technique to simultaneously determine the best downlink precoder and user selection. It is designed for both single-antenna and multi-antenna multiuser networks. The proposed method effectively addresses the inherent non-convexity and combinatorial challenges of the underlying optimization problem. Numerical results demonstrate that the algorithm rapidly and effectively identifies a solution that achieves a significant improvement over a baseline convex relaxation approach. Furthermore, in multi-antenna environments, the algorithm exhibits superior robustness against channel estimation errors compared to the baseline. Additionally, the method is shown to be less sensitive to channel estimation inaccuracies in Rayleigh fading channels than in Rician fading channels. These findings are supported by extensive numerical simulations. The results indicate that the proposed group LASSO approach is well-suited for practical system design, offering a balanced trade-off between downlink throughput performance and computational complexity. Consequently, it serves as an attractive alternative to existing low-complexity user pairing and precoding strategies. A key advantage is its ability to jointly optimize group selection and precoder design, thereby maximizing total downlink throughput. In this setup, groups of users are assigned a common precoder vector to maximize the sum-rate of all users within each group. The algorithm is computationally efficient, with its most demanding step being the solution of a convex optimization problem. Furthermore, the proposed method offers greater flexibility than traditional downlink beamforming designs that rely on fixed user grouping. By enabling joint optimization of precoders and user groups, the group LASSO approach facilitates the discovery of a globally optimal or near-optimal solution. In contrast, traditional beamforming methods typically optimize precoders for a fixed user group, often resulting in suboptimal performance. Our method also surpasses existing algorithms that employ greedy heuristics for joint user choice and precoder design. These greedy approaches, which determine the optimal user set for a given group size before designing the precoder, are computationally intensive and yield suboptimal results. In summary, the proposed group LASSO method achieves a superior trade-off between performance and complexity, making it a promising solution for downlink beamforming and multiuser communication system design. This work extends our prior research (arXiv:2002.00010) concerning rational functions of tropical arcs on a 1-dimensional algebraic torus. The study examines the consistent numerical approximation of a uniformly nondegenerate viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation, leading to the uniform convergence of the discrete solutions. By applying Steele's coupling method, the analysis demonstrates the local consistent convergence to the Q-process defined by Cardelli and Cirant. This Q-process is characterized as an isotropic gradient vector field that resolves any discontinuities in the initial condition by steering the solution along a downward slope. The paper further investigates the properties of this process, including its consistency with the classical solution when one exists, its behavior in the discrete setting, and its connection to discrete fully coupled equations. Additionally, the authors explore the relationship between the numerical scheme and the classical vanishing viscosity method. We introduce two modifications to Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem. The first variant preserves the original public key structure but substitutes McEliece's syndrome decoding problem with the weighted minimum set cover problem. The second version employs a public key composed of two matrices, thereby increasing the key's dimension. For both versions, we analyze the public key size, computation requirements for key generation and verification, and encryption/decryption speeds. Our results indicate that this system offers better efficiency than McEliece while maintaining comparable security levels. Furthermore, the public key size is smaller than that of the original McEliece scheme or the Ding-Kazymyuk variant, and it rivals the efficiency of the digital signature algorithm NTRU. We present an exhaustive attack on both versions using integer linear programming, which successfully recovers the secret key in a feasible timeframe. Additionally, we examine potential improvements to enhance resistance against such attacks. Finally, we demonstrate that the minimum set cover problem serves as a viable replacement for the subset sum problem in McEliece schemes, and our proposed public key matrices exhibit a higher search-to-decision complexity ratio than those used in Hermitian or triangular matrices. This ratio acts as a metric for estimating public key security in code-based schemes that utilize support set decoding attacks. We conclude by discussing how this ratio can guide the selection of appropriate matrices for constructing secure code-based cryptosystems. Notably, this work marks the first instance of an exhaustive attack utilizing integer linear programming for any code-based cryptosystem. This study examines random simplicial complexes generated by independent Bernoulli processes, focusing on the probability distributions of their minimal spanning acycles and associated persistence diagrams. It is demonstrated that these two concepts are fundamentally linked: given a persistence diagram, the corresponding minimal spanning acycle can be reconstructed, and conversely, knowing a minimal spanning acycle allows for the derivation of its persistence diagram. Consequently, the results regarding minimal spanning spanning acycles can be applied to persistence diagrams. The analysis further reveals that as the dimension of the complex increases, both the ratio of non-edges to total edges in a minimal spanning acycle and the diameter of its persistence diagram approach 1. Finally, an explicit formula is provided for calculating the expected value of the number of intervals in a one-dimensional minimal spanning acycle, along with an exploration of the distribution of this number. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. The work concludes by discussing potential generalizations of these results. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-pres collaborative framework where organizations retain their data locally, utilizing specific input features to jointly train a machine learning model. This approach prioritizes the safeguarding of both data and privacy. This paper introduces a novel threat to VFL by exploiting the private knowledge of participating parties. We propose the Pragmatic Privacy Assault (PPA), which leverages a lightweight Deep Neural Network (DNN) to effectively launch an inference attack on a target participant. This attack mechanism utilizes a single party's training features and labels, combined with the gradient information of a jointly trained VFL to accurately forecast the target party's output features. We demonstrate that PPA achieves high attack accuracy while maintaining low attack costs, even when utilizing a minimal number of gradient updates. Furthermore, we show that the attack remains effective even if the model architecture is altered, provided that feature dimensions remain consistent. Additionally, our experiments indicate that the attack succeeds even when the model architecture is modified if the feature dimensions are adjusted accordingly. Finally, we demonstrate that PPA remains effective even when the target party is a leading corporation. Our results show that PPA achieves an attack success rate of up to 90% with a cost as low as 1% under optimal conditions. We also observe that reducing the volume of training features leads to a decrease in attack success rates. However, we demonstrate that increasing the number of training iterations can restore the attack success rates to near-optimal levels. We conclude that PPA poses a significant risk to VFL, necessitating that all participants adhere to strict security protocols to prevent such attacks. We also note that increasing the number of training iterations can help mitigate the effectiveness of the Pragmatic Privacy Assault. Following the recent discovery of dark matter, researchers have increasingly investigated baryogenesis mechanisms involving dark antibaryons. This note introduces a QCD light-cone synthesis rule to estimate the amplitude for the exclusive weak decay of a $B$ meson into a proton and a dark antibaryon ($pD$). The findings indicate that this decay is suppressed by approximately two orders of magnitude relative to the corresponding $B \to e^+ D$ process (where $e$ represents an active lepton). Consequently, the scalar form factor required for $B \to pD$ transitions is expected to be less than $10^{-2} \, f_0(m_e^2)$, assuming $m_e^2 \ll m_D^2 \ll m_{B}^2$. These results have significant implications for interpreting current and future experimental data from the Belle II collider. Furthermore, the analysis suggests that a similar suppression of two orders of magnitude likely applies to the inclusive $B \to pD$ decay as well. Finally, this work establishes a foundation for future studies on the strong dynamics governing $B \to pD$ transitions. Notably, such studies could be initiated by investigating the strong final state interactions between the proton and dark antibaryon. This approach would facilitate a more precise determination of the $B \to pD$ form factors and enable a direct measurement of $D \to N \phi_D$ transitions, where $N$ denotes a nucleon. Furthermore, these investigations would provide valuable insights into the nature of dark matter interactions with baryons. Finally, the derived results are expected to facilitate a more accurate determination of the $B \to pD$ form factors. The paper begins with an introduction to the $B \to pD$ decay and concludes with an outline of the relevant future research directions. Additionally, the text includes a discussion of the $B \to pD$ decay in the limit where $m_D \to 0$. Furthermore, the game leverages recent advancements in multi-agent reinforcement learning, learning policies for both attackers and defenders through self-play. By simulating various defense resource allocations, the game enables managers to identify and implement the most effective countermeasures. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model successfully generates diverse and realistic policies for both players, while also producing a distribution of assault success rates and resource allocation costs for defenders. We investigate the evaporation of black holes within a brane situated inside a closed chamber by applying two distinct methodologies. The initial approach utilizes the effective action of a point particle, while the second relies on the Euclidean path integral of a scalar field propagating in the black hole spacetime. Utilizing these techniques, we determine the phase transitions for both de Sitter and anti-de Sitter black holes confined within the chamber. Our results indicate that the existence of these phase shifts is contingent upon the behavior of the scalar field within the cavity. Furthermore, we observe that these phase shifts vanish when the brane's area approaches infinity. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that the evaporation process for black holes in a chamber proceeds at a significantly slower rate compared to evaporation without an enclosing chamber. Finally, our analysis reveals that these phase shifts persist even in the presence of a cosmological constant. Specifically, within a cosmological black hole within a chamber, there exist small seed black holes that share characteristics similar to those found in de Sitter space inside a chamber. These include the existence of Hawking--Page phase transitions, a specific relationship between the black hole's radius and the chamber's radius, and a chamber size that acts as a critical threshold for the system's stability. However, unlike the case of a de Sitter black hole within a chamber, the horizon radius of a cosmological black hole within a chamber does not attain an infinite value. Instead, it reaches a finite maximum determined by the chamber's radius and the cosmological constant. Consequently, these findings suggest that cosmological black holes within a chamber may offer a potential explanation for the nature of dark energy. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the horizon radius of such a black hole is directly proportional to the magnitude of the cosmological constant. Therefore, our findings imply that dark energy may be associated with cosmological black holes contained within a chamber. Training a deep neural network typically demands a substantial number of labeled samples. However, acquiring these labels is often costly and time-consuming due to the expertise required, leading to scenarios where training data may contain errors. When annotated labels are incorrect, models are trained on noisy data, which can severely degrade performance if not addressed. While data augmentation is a common strategy for mitigating this issue in image datasets, it is ineffective for text data. This paper introduces a novel and straightforward data augmentation technique designed to recover training data by identifying and isolating erroneous labels. The proposed method is guided and constrained by the model's inherent knowledge through sampling and clustering. Specifically, it operates in two stages: first, it extracts reliable local knowledge from the training data using bag sampling; second, it isolates incorrect labels by leveraging this knowledge through clustering. To maximize the potential of the isolated labels, the approach employs a graph-based model to reassign them by minimizing a cluster-wise loss function. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly improves the label quality of the training dataset and enhances the performance of pre-trained Transformer models for noisy label ranking under both uniform and biased noise conditions. Furthermore, the proposed approach is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated with various pre-trained models. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness across diverse applications, including social network analysis, bioinformatics, and molecular property prediction. However, their performance often suffers in scenarios involving extensive unlabeled nodes and limited labeled examples. To address the high cost of labeling, semi-supervised learning approaches have been widely adopted to maximize the utility of existing labels. This study introduces a novel semi-supervised framework that leverages synthetic labels generated by GNNs to boost performance under label scarcity. We propose a two-stage strategy: first, employing multiple GNNs with varying architectures and training conditions in an ensemble to broaden the hypothesis space and mitigate individual model biases; second, utilizing an uncertainty estimator to select high-confidence predictions as pseudo-labels for supervised retraining. Our results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms existing semi-supervised techniques, achieving superior accuracy in both node classification and regression tasks. Furthermore, we find that our approach enhances the stability and robustness of GNN predictions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/LABELS. This study examines awake Run 2's planned injection of 100 GeV, 1 pC proton beams into helium-filled the linear accelerator (HL760) at CERN. The interaction of these protons with the helium gas is expected to generate betatron radiation, which could be detected by scintillator and Cherenkov radiation sensors. To simulate this process, the open-source software Geant4 was utilized. The results indicate that betatron photons will be emitted with a mean energy of approximately 100 keV, exhibiting anisotropic angular and spectral distributions. At the end of HL760, the simulated photon yield is approximately 10^13 photons per proton burst, which is roughly 100 times lower than initial estimates. Photon fluxes within the range of 10^9 to 10^10 photons per proton burst are projected at the beam pipe, beam diagnostics, and beam dump. Additionally, photon counts in the vicinity of beamline instrumentation, such as the proposed B2 beam position monitors, are estimated to be around 10^6 photons per proton burst. Furthermore, the simulation of betatron photon effects on beamline instrumentation has been conducted. Finally, a proposal for detecting betatron radiation is outlined, which could facilitate non-invasive beam diagnostics in HL760. The detected radiation profile could be utilized to determine the on-axis beam energy, a parameter that remains challenging to measure directly. Finally, the potential impact of betatron radiation on awake Run 2's physics program is also discussed. The findings presented in this report are scheduled to be published in the journal Radiation Protection and Dosimetry. The corresponding author can be reached at email: vasilis.katsikis@cern.ch. This work introduces scalable algorithms for differentially private distributed decision tree learning, addressing the issue of data fragmentation across multiple parties. These methods utilize a centralized secure multi-party computation (MPC) framework, where the central server executes the algorithm without accessing any private input data from the participants. We propose a general framework for differentially private tree learning under centralized MPC, which integrates two distinct approaches: a global algorithm and a local algorithm. The global approach constructs a fully private decision tree by executing differentially private operations as global MPC primitives, whereas the local approach generates a noisy tree by applying a local differential privacy mechanism to the input data before the central server runs a non-private algorithm. We demonstrate that global algorithms for private tree learning can be significantly optimized by employing the histogram-based local differential privacy mechanism. Furthermore, we present provably precise algorithms for private decision tree learning that leverage the advantages of both global and local strategies. Specifically, our proposed algorithm adaptively selects between global and local methods based on the input dataset's characteristics, such as the count of unique values in each attribute. We validate the scalability and precision of these algorithms using real-world data from the Adult, Census, and German datasets. To our knowledge, this represents the first provably precise and scalable algorithm for differentially private distributed decision tree learning. Additionally, we discuss how these methods can be extended to support semi-honest and hostile collusion among the parties. Finally, we explore potential extensions for future research regarding fully distributed differentially private decision tree learning.
