This study analyzes the impact of the phase boundary on the multiphase transport model's calculation of triangular flow ($v_3$) across Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at various center-of-mass energies. The results indicate that using an incorrect phase boundary leads to unphysical outcomes, such as negative sound speed and an excessively large specific heat ratio. Consequently, the model predicts a significantly reduced $v_3$ at low energies and an overestimated $v_3$ at RHIC energies when the incorrect boundary is applied. These findings highlight the critical role of an accurate phase boundary in multiphase transport frameworks and offer valuable insights for interpreting experimental data. Furthermore, incorporating a precise phase boundary enables the model to describe a unique feature of $v_3$: a distinct peak at intermediate energies, followed by a decrease at higher energies and a near-constant value at low energies. This characteristic is observed in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Additionally, this peak is more pronounced at smaller collision sizes, suggesting that smaller systems exhibit more non-trivial thermodynamic properties. These insights are crucial for the ongoing RHIC Beam Energy Scan initiative. Finally, the calculated $v_3$ demonstrates a strong correlation with the initial eccentricity ($\epsilon_3$), allowing for the reconstruction of initial conditions. This capability is particularly significant for smaller systems, where the initial condition is more complex. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. This study investigates the efficacy of pre-training semantic segmentation models using depth estimation data versus classification data, given that prior research has explored pre-training with classification datasets. We observe that although networks pre-trained with depth estimation excel in depth prediction, their performance on semantic segmentation tasks is often inferior to that of state-of-the-art architectures with fewer parameters. To investigate this discrepancy, we conduct a comprehensive analysis comparing performance gains from pre-training with either data type across various semantic segmentation scenarios. Our experiments reveal that while depth estimation pre-training yields superior results on single-phase pre-training/fine-tuning paradigms, it offers negligible performance improvements when evaluated under the more realistic fine-tuning/evaluation paradigm. Furthermore, we find that although pre-training with depth estimation data enhances overall performance, it disproportionately benefits smaller networks, thereby widening the gap between larger and smaller models. These insights are supported by an analysis of the representation learning capabilities inherent in depth estimation data. Finally, we propose a novel hybrid paradigm that leverages the strengths of both depth estimation and classification pre-training, achieving state-of-the-art performance across various semantic segmentation tasks. Our research is anticipated to provide valuable guidance for future efforts in self-supervised visual learning. Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation, valued for its robustness against outliers and applicability to vector data of any dimension. However, calculating the exact estimate and deriving credible intervals is often computationally demanding. Consequently, researchers frequently rely on approximations that sacrifice accuracy to achieve a balance between performance and precision. This study introduces a rapid method for inferring Kendall's tau, achieving a 1000-fold reduction in inference time with negligible loss in accuracy. Additionally, we present a novel procedure for estimating the minimal mean-squared error of Kendall's tau, a metric that has not previously been readily estimated. We evaluate the performance of our proposed estimator against existing literature and highlight several opportunities for future improvement. Our methodology is implemented in the R package {\tt kendall}. The package also includes utilities for assessing estimator performance, allowing users to replicate the performance evaluations found in this paper. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to apply our approach to real-world, messy datasets, including those with missing values, outliers, missing variables, and incomplete observations. These practical examples can be reproduced using the included tutorials. The source code for both examples and the performance assessments is available in a public repository. We anticipate that our method and the supporting tools in {\tt kendall} will facilitate improved comparisons of estimator performance in the future. Finally, we outline several directions for enhancing the performance of {\tt kendall} in an upcoming extension. The rise of autonomous driving and intelligent transportation systems has spurred significant research into privacy-preserving edge intelligence for vehicular networks. However, existing approaches often fail to offer a comprehensive solution capable of handling diverse privacy threats. To address this gap, we introduce a unified framework designed to effectively mitigate various privacy risks within vehicle networks. Our method leverages an enhanced vehicle graph to facilitate secure information exchange between vehicles and the road side unit (RSU) for joint processing. Additionally, we propose a novel RSU mechanism utilizing a privacy-aware security strategy to defend against potential attacks. We validate the efficacy of our framework through extensive experiments and theoretical analysis, which confirm its ability to successfully address multiple privacy challenges in vehicular networks. Furthermore, real-world tests demonstrate the system's robustness and efficiency in mitigating privacy threats. The complete code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1999/PPP-EI. The advent of deep learning has enabled the creation of highly realistic face hallucination and video deepfake models, posing significant risks to society. To mitigate this, face forensics methods are essential for detecting these synthetic media. Recent studies indicate that zero-shot techniques leveraging pre-trained Vision Transformers (ViT) are highly effective and precise in identifying face hallucinations and deepfakes. This paper introduces a comprehensive and extensive evaluation of such ViT-based approaches, assessing their performance across six current state-of-the-art face hallucination datasets (SuperGAN, CodeFormer, FSHR4, FSHR8, FSHR16, and FSDHF) and the leading deepfake benchmark, FaceForensics++ (FF+). Our primary contributions are as follows: (1) We present the most extensive head-to-head comparison of ViT-based zero-shot face forensics to date, utilizing a unified experimental framework and a total of 116 models across 114 configurations; (2) We demonstrate that these zero-shot ViT models achieve perfect accuracy in distinguishing face hallucinated content from FSHR4 and FSHR8 datasets at low resolution (256x256); (3) We reveal a significant disparity between forensics performance on face hallucinated data versus FF+ dataset composites, suggesting that zero-shot ViT models may struggle with deepfake detection; (4) We show that while higher resolution improves detection accuracy for face hallucinated data, it has a negligible impact on FF+ data, indicating that the source of forgery is more critical than resolution for zero-shot forensics; (5) We demonstrate that contrastive pre-training on face hallucinated datasets significantly enhances the performance of zero-shot ViT models in detecting face hallucinations. Asynchronous parallel (AP) parallel evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have become a prevalent method for accelerating the execution of evolutionary computation. Nevertheless, because of their asynchronous nature, these AP EAs often suffer from evaluation time bias, where evaluations with varying durations receive unequal treatment. Previous research indicates that this problem is particularly pronounced in multi-objective EAs, which typically require more time and computational resources than single-objective versions. This study demonstrates that within AP multi-objective EAs, frequency-oriented parents (AP-MOEPs) selected from the current population archive can be heavily influenced by evaluation time bias. Specifically, the bias causes the archive to accumulate inferior AP-MOEPs that require a shorter evaluation time. To address this, we propose a strategy utilizing frequency-oriented parents (AP-MOEPs) derived from the current non-dominated front to mitigate evaluation time bias. Our approach involves periodically replacing the population with these newly identified AP-MOEPs from the non-dominated front to eliminate time-related biases. Experimental results confirm that this strategy effectively mitigates evaluation time bias in AP multi-objective EAs. Additionally, we introduce a framework for AP multi-objective EAs that integrates this proposed strategy, which outperforms existing synchronous parallel multi-objective EAs in both convergence and diversity. Finally, we demonstrate that our framework achieves superior convergence and diversity compared to current asynchronous parallel multi-objective EAs. The comprehensive code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/ASAPMOEA. Future research will explore the application of our AP-MOEA framework in other computational biology domains, such as protein design. Furthermore, we aim to extend our approach to other asynchronous parallel multi-objective EAs, including NSGA-III and MOEA/D-DE. Additionally, we plan to investigate whether our method can enhance the performance of asynchronous parallel single-objective EAs. Finally, we intend to examine the impact of evaluation time bias on asynchronous parallel multi-objective EAs when the number of objectives exceeds 10. The ongoing rise in the number of exoplanets discovered through microlensing is driven by the method's unique ability to detect planets at large orbital separations and around low-mass host stars, often located in the Galactic Bulge. However, the signal from a planet orbiting a host at a separation $s$ only becomes detectable if the planet's mass $m_p$ is sufficiently high to produce a measurable perturbation during the alignment event. This creates a "gray zone" where systems may host planets, but their signals remain undetectable. In this study, we report the first verification of such a system, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, which hosts a super-Earth ($m_p = 4.7 \pm 0.7$ M$_\oplus$) located in this gray zone. Although the planet is likely frigid, with an equilibrium temperature $T_{eq} \leq 100$ K, its discovery demonstrates that microlensing can probe systems in this mass-gap. Furthermore, we show that the planet's signal would have been missed by microlensing surveys lacking high-resolution imaging capabilities, such as OGLE and MOA. Consequently, our findings highlight the critical necessity of integrating high-resolution imaging into future surveys to fully unlock the potential of the microlensing gray zone. This was achieved by combining archival data from OGLE and WISE with new observations from the Keck Adaptive Optics survey. Our results also indicate that the probability of detecting OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 via microlensing is highly dependent on the planet's mass, scaling as $m_p^3$ for $m_p \leq 1$ M$_\oplus$ and as $m_p^2$ for $m_p \geq 1$ M$_\oplus$. Finally, we demonstrate that the method used to detect OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 is highly effective for finding similar frigid super-Earths. We predict that approximately 10% of the remaining undetected mass in the super-Earth/Neptune gray zone consists of these frigid planets, and that future surveys utilizing high-resolution imaging will likely discover and verify about 100 of them. The first is a stationary high-rate expansion (SHE), while the second is a stationary high-rate adiabatic expansion (SHAdE). The SHE is derived from an exact solution of the quantum master equation, whereas the SHAdE results from a limiting procedure applied to the adiabatic solution. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the SHAdE provides superior accuracy compared to the adiabatic approximation. Furthermore, the study examines the convergence of these expansions, revealing that the stationary high-rate adiabatic (SHAd) expansion—derived by averaging the adiabatic solution over the fast variable—converges more rapidly than the SHE. Finally, the paper applies these expansions to analyze the dynamics of a two-level system. In summary, this work presents two high-rate expansions for time-oscillating Lindblad generators, evaluates their accuracy, and establishes the convergence properties of the adiabatic approximation. This study utilizes neutron depolarization as a novel technique to investigate magnetic phase transitions in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ (with x = 0.1 and 0.2). The depolarization of the neutron beam occurs at the CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$-Ce interface, driven by the internal magnetic field of the material. The magnitude of this field is dictated by the degree of magnetic order within the sample, which in turn establishes a correlation between depolarization levels and the magnitude of this order. Our findings indicate that the rare-earth (RE) magnetic moments in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ exhibit a complex temperature dependence, characterized by the coexistence of ferromagnetic and spin-glass states. Furthermore, the RE magnetic moments display a strong sensitivity to the Rh concentration, with the transition temperatures for ferromagnetism and the spin-glass phase decreasing as the content of the nonmagnetic element rhodium increases. Additionally, we have identified a spin-softening phenomenon in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ that occurs at temperatures below the ferromagnetic transition. This behavior is interpreted as the solidification of the RE magnetic moments, a process that also shows a strong dependence on the Rh concentration. Finally, the complex interplay between the depolarization of the neutron beam and the magnetic properties of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_{x}$ opens new avenues for studying the magnetic characteristics of other related compounds. For instance, the depolarization effect observed in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_{x}$ is expected to be significantly more pronounced in CePd$_{1-x}$Ir$_x$, where the internal magnetic field is anticipated to be stronger. Consequently, depolarization offers a valuable tool for examining the magnetic phases of CePd$_{1-x}$Ir$_x$ compounds, which are known to exhibit unconventional superconductivity. This represents a new approach to studying the phase diagram of compounds within the CePd$_{1-x}$M$_x$ family, where the RE magnetic moments compete with the Kondo effect and the superconducting state. Notably, the neutron depolarization effect is expected to be particularly useful for elucidating the nature of the superconducting state in these materials. This is because depolarization can provide a direct measurement of the internal magnetic field, thereby circumventing the difficulties associated with measuring the internal field via the magnetization of nanoscale samples. We conducted a 21-cm continuum survey of the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20 using the Green Bank Telescope, identifying 13 narrow-line self-absorption features in the neutral hydrogen (HI) spectrum. These features are attributed to cold, neutral HI clouds situated in the foreground of the hot molecular outflow driven by the protostar(s) within this region. By combining our findings with existing literature data, we compiled a sample of 113 HI self-absorptions linked to star-forming regions across the entire Galaxy. A statistical analysis of this sample reveals that the frequency of self-absorbed features in high-mass star-forming regions is approximately ten times greater than in low-mass regions. Furthermore, the mean redshift of the 13 newly discovered features in G176.51+00.20 is approximately 1.5 km s$^{-1}$, indicating that the molecular outflow in this region is driven by a high-mass star(s) rather than being pressure-confined. Additionally, the mean redshift of the 113 features in the sample is approximately 0.5 km s$^{-1}$, suggesting that pressure-confined outflows are relatively rare. Finally, the redshifts of the absorption features in our sample show a correlation with the masses of the associated star-forming regions, implying that the strength of the interaction between the outflow and the ambient medium increases with the mass of the forming star(s). These results support the hypothesis that the strength of the interaction between a molecular outflow and its surrounding environment is governed by the mass of the driving star(s). Surprisingly, the total number of these triangles surpasses the count of lattice points or the area of the larger triangle. We will explore the surprising behavior of this count and provide a proof. Ultimately, the findings reveal that the number of triangles is governed by the square of the side length, rather than linearly as one might intuitively expect. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction for analyzing graph data, yet the intricate inner workings of the GNN parameterization function remain underexplored. This study investigates the representability of that function within the framework of compressed sensing theory. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, the GNN parameterization function can be represented as the solution to an $\ell_1$-minimization problem. Leveraging this representation, we establish recovery guarantees and provide insights into the generalization error of GNNs. Furthermore, we develop an interpretable GNN model based on this parameterization, where the network's intermediate layers correspond to selected features, and the output layer reflects the final prediction. We validate the interpretability of our approach and the effectiveness of the resulting interpretable model through a classification task on a real-world dataset. Additionally, we obtain promising results for a real-world application involving a railway track fault detection system. Finally, we explore potential future research directions and applications for our work. This paper aims to enhance our understanding of GNNs and their parameters, while also advancing the broader field of interpretable machine learning. We report a serendipitous discovery of the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 during a Chandra observation of the dwarf galaxy IC342. This system is a likely merging cluster featuring a 100 kpc diameter X-ray cavity within the intracluster medium, which we propose is caused by the ram pressure of an accreting substructure. The cluster contains two massive galaxy triplets, each comprising two bright red galaxies and one bright blue galaxy. Additionally, we identified a possible substructure at approximately 100 kpc from the cluster center, characterized by a bright galaxy and a blue group. This substructure is associated with a significant radio source, designated RXCJ0232.2-4420A, which exhibits a flat radio spectrum and a radio lobe diameter of roughly 100 kpc. We suggest that RXCJ0232.2-4420A is an Accretion Mode Radio Galaxy (AMRG), representing a newly identified class of galaxy. Furthermore, we detected a radio source at the center of RXCJ0232.2-4420, RXCJ0232.2-4420C, which we classify as a starburst galaxy based on its morphology and spectral characteristics. Finally, we report the detection of a third central radio galaxy, RXCJ0232.2-4420B, and discuss the cluster's dynamical state. We conclude that RXCJ0232.2-4420 is a merging cluster, distinguishing it from RXCJ0232.3-4419, which is a relaxed cluster. This finding is supported by the presence of a 100 kpc X-ray cavity and the observed kinematics of galaxies. The unique radio source characteristics of RXCJ0232.2-4420A may indicate a transitional phase between a starburst galaxy and an AMRG. Additionally, the coexistence of an AMRG and a starburst galaxy within the same cluster is a novel finding. We propose that this configuration may result from the accretion of a starburst galaxy as a substructure. A recent study (Burger et al., 2022) introduced the parallel training of a single Legendre Memory Module (LMM) across a cluster of GPUs, leveraging a parameter-parallel strategy. This work extends that research by implementing Distributed Legendre Memory Efficient Transformers (DiLeMET), a parameter-parallel framework capable of training multiple LMMs simultaneously on GPU clusters. We demonstrate that DiLeMET enables the training of models like BLOOM (Hurst et al., 2022) on large-scale clusters with minimal communication overhead. Furthermore, we evaluate memory efficiency and training performance using various LMM configurations on state-of-the-art GPU clusters, including those featuring NVIDIA A100 and V100 architectures. Our results indicate that DiLeMET achieves up to a 4.5x improvement in memory efficiency compared to standard Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) training on BLOOM. Additionally, we show that DiLeMET maintains training times within 1% to 2% of those achieved by DDP. Finally, we successfully trained an 184 LMMs on 1,024 GPUs, completing the process in just 10.5 hours. This work is released under an Apache 2.0 license. We introduce a network naming game involving numerous players, where linguistic groups emerge through the migration of actors between networks. To control the direction of migration, we impose a specific constraint: actors only join networks larger than their current one. This demographic pressure drives individuals toward larger communities in search of greater migration opportunities. Our results demonstrate that this mechanism consistently generates large groups that achieve high internal interpretability. Furthermore, we observe that the resulting linguistic groups exhibit robust semantic coherence, even in the absence of any explicit penalties for such inconsistencies. Finally, we note that the linguistic groups formed via migration display significantly lower entropy compared to those produced by a standard modeling approach. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have become a widely adopted method for addressing problems in physics-informed machine learning. However, during training, PINNs frequently suffer from spectral bias, where low-frequency components of the target function are learned significantly faster than high-frequency ones. This learning speed disparity causes PINNs to become trapped in suboptimal regions, often converging prematurely to poor local minima. This study demonstrates that incorporating a momentum term into the PINN training framework can substantially diminish this spectral bias. Specifically, we apply momentum to the residual function rather than the parameters, alongside a tailored training protocol. We validate the efficacy of this proposed momentum framework on two benchmark tasks that PINNs struggle to solve, as well as on two additional benchmark problems where the momentum approach achieves superior accuracy compared to standard training methods. Furthermore, we illustrate the potential of this framework by addressing a challenging inverse problem where the momentum-based approach yields results of higher accuracy than those obtained from the conventional PINN method. Finally, we provide comprehensive experiments on a large-scale dataset to examine the robustness of the momentum framework. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1997/MomentumPINN.

This study examines a system of two damped and coupled wave equations featuring locally varying Kelvin-Voigt attenuation. Building upon prior work regarding global dissipation in dissipative systems with coupling, our focus is on the semi-discrete model, where space is discretized while time remains continuous. We demonstrate that the discrete scheme preserves the continuous model's dissipation and stability characteristics, provided a suitable relationship exists between the mesh sizes. Furthermore, we establish optimal error estimates in the energy norm for this scenario. These theoretical findings are supported by numerical examples. Additionally, we extend our analysis to the continuous case under weakly varying coefficients and derive corresponding estimates for this extended model as well. Finally, we confirm that the discrete scheme remains stable in this extended setting, subject to an appropriate coupling between the two half-spaces. These results also apply to a coupled system of dissipative Schrödinger equations with locally varying attenuation. Our approach is general and extends to various dissipative systems, such as dissipative beam equations and coupled hyperbolic equations. Our methodology relies on the construction of appropriate Lyapunov functionals and the application of recent results from graph theory concerning the minimum eigenvalue of graph Laplacians. Notably, no assumptions are required regarding the smoothness of the coefficients. Furthermore, our analysis avoids the use of the discrete Fourier transform, thereby circumventing potential issues with aliasing effects. This work serves as a sequel to our previous papers [1, 2]. In [1], we proved stability for a coupled system of dissipative Schrödinger equations with locally varying attenuation, assuming a smooth coefficient and a suitable coupling between the half-spaces. In [2], we utilized discrete Fourier transforms to show that a coupled system of wave equations with constant attenuation yields a stable finite difference scheme, provided the coefficients are constant and the coupling is appropriate. In both instances, the coefficients were assumed to be constant. In this paper, we extend our analysis to cases where coefficients are not constant. Our approach relies on the minimum eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian and Lyapunov functionals, avoiding discrete Fourier transforms and thereby eliminating potential aliasing problems. We also demonstrate that the finite difference scheme remains stable even when the coefficients are not constant, although they must not vary too rapidly. This study introduces a novel hierarchical reinforcement learning (HLRL) framework designed to foster collaboration between human operators and reinforcement learning (RL) agents. Our proposed method leverages human domain knowledge to elucidate the learned policies, thereby enhancing interpretability and trustworthiness. By integrating formal methods with the hierarchical structure of RL, our approach enables the agent to query human experts for clarification regarding its decision-making processes. Employing inductive logic programming (ILP), we utilize formative data to infer logical rules that form the prior knowledge for the reward function within each sub-problem's local policy. Additionally, we validate the method's efficacy through a real-world industrial case study and a simulation study, which collectively demonstrate its effectiveness and interpretability. Finally, ablation studies are conducted to assess whether the proposed framework can achieve performance comparable to existing RL techniques. The experimental results confirm the method's effectiveness, interpretability, and ability to achieve performance levels similar to state-of-the-art solutions. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1999/XEMHRL.

Data compression is a ubiquitous computational method that reduces information volume by discarding nonessential details. While this process is typically reversible, exceptions exist, most notably when compressing quantum data. Although recent experiments have confirmed the compression of quantum states, the resulting reduction in quantum entropy has been shown to decrease coherence and nonlocal correlations. This study demonstrates that compressing quantum data can render quantum evolution nonreversible. Specifically, we present a theoretical framework for quantum compression and its decomposition into two components: an information channel and a compression code. Utilizing this model, we develop quantum advantage protocols that leverage nonreversible compression to enhance quantum communication capacity. Furthermore, we illustrate that compression-induced nonreversibility can be harnessed to create nontrivial quantum channels. These findings establish that compression-induced nonreversibility is a fundamental feature of quantum systems, distinct from classical data compression, and can be exploited to achieve quantum advantages. Consequently, this phenomenon represents a vital resource for quantum technologies. Additionally, we have open-sourced our code for simulating quantum compression and its applications at https://github.com/zhaozhenyang1992/QT-C. Our findings provide a foundation for future research into the fundamental principles governing quantum data compression. We introduce minimax problems inspired by Joseph B. Fenton's foundational 1941 study on the electron density of the helium atom. These problems involve identifying translations $\tau_1, \dots, \tau_m \in \mathbb{R}^n$ that maximize the $L^\infty$-norm of the spectrum of $\sum_{j=1}^m T_{\tau_j}f$, where $f$ is a fixed function in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n) \cap L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$. This analysis applies to functions $f$ that decrease in magnitude as $|x| \to \infty$. Specifically, for radial functions $f$ that are nonincreasing on $[0, \infty)$, we establish upper bounds for the spectrum of $\sum_{j=1}^m T_{\tau_j}f$ under the condition that $|\tau_j - \tau_k| \geq 1$ for all $j,k \in \{1, \dots, m\}$. Furthermore, we extend these findings to radial functions $f$ that are eventually nonincreasing and exhibit sufficiently rapid decay at infinity. Additionally, we demonstrate that the spectrum of $\sum_{j=1}^m T_{\tau_j}f$ is bounded above by $\left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right)^{n/2} \Gamma(\frac{n+1}{2}) \left(1 + \frac{m-1}{2}\right)^{(m-1)/2} \left(1 - \frac{1}{m}\right)^{1/2} \|f\|_\infty$, which is independent of the translations $\tau_j$. This result holds for functions $f$ whose derivatives satisfy $|D^\alpha f(x)| \leq C_f |x|^{-1-\frac{n}{2}-|\alpha|} (1+|\xi|)^{\frac{n}{2}}$ for every multi-index $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}^n$. Our methodology relies on a novel radial extension of the Stein-Tomita inequality. Finally, we examine minimax challenges concerning functions $f$ that are monotone in a directional sense. These problems feature been solved for Gaussian functions and those with sufficient rapid decay, as well as for step functions. The latter case yields a sharp upper bound

We introduce a novel method for investigating spin-dependent nuclear cross sections of $^6$Li, a component often excluded in analyses of direct detection experiments. Utilizing a high-sensitivity neutron scattering technique, we measured the differential cross section for the $^6$Li(n,$\alpha$)$^3$H reaction at thermal neutron energies, specifically for the reaction populating the ground state of $^3$H. Our results indicate a strong forward-peaked angular distribution, and the extracted total cross section aligns with existing literature values. Crucially, we observe a significant variation in the total cross section depending on the populating reaction channel, a phenomenon also noted in $^3$He. We demonstrate that this behavior can be accurately modeled by incorporating the spin-dependent neutron charge density within the optical potential. Furthermore, we analyze how variations in the optical potential model parameters influence the spin-dependent scattering cross section, a factor typically overlooked in nuclear response calculations for direct detection searches. Finally, we project the implications of these findings on future direct detection experiments. Blind image restoration (BUR) aims to recover high-quality images from low-quality versions without prior knowledge of the degradation processes. This study introduces a novel approach to address a specific parameter estimation challenge in BUR by utilizing a sophisticated degradation model. This model is built upon a non-negative kernel mixture framework, which effectively represents a broad spectrum of degradation operators for BUR tasks. By integrating advanced techniques in model design, optimization, and analysis, we successfully estimate degradation parameters, thereby significantly enhancing performance across key BUR applications including denoising, blur, blur-noise, and super-resolution. Extensive experiments on diverse synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in most scenarios. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/Kernel_Mixture. Nonuniform associative algebras constitute a noncommutative generalization of pseudofree algebras, offering a framework for the construction of integrable lattice models. This work introduces the concept of nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations (ASYB), which are satisfied by noncommutative R-matrices associated with these algebras. We demonstrate the existence of solutions to the nonuniform ASYB within specific cases, including cases where the noncommutativity is governed by an abelian solution to the standard Yang-Baxter equation. These R-matrices hold significant utility in integrable lattice models, enabling the derivation of both dynamical and generalized quantum inverse scattering methods. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between nonuniform ASYB and q-associative Yang-Baxter equations. Specifically, we prove that if a noncommutative matrix A satisfies the nonuniform ASYB, then the matrix B, defined as $B = (\exp(q\sigma_2 \Lambda))^{-1}A(\exp(q\sigma_2 \Lambda))$, satisfies the q-associative Yang-Baxter equation. As an application, we derive solutions to the nonuniform ASYB from several solutions of the quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Additionally, we derive solutions to the dynamical noncommutative quantum Yang-Baxter equation by appropriately modifying the noncommutative R-matrices. Finally, we derive solutions to the quantum dynamical Yang-Baxter equation by applying a linear transformation to the noncommutative R-matrices. These findings provide a systematic approach for generating integrable lattice models. Notably, our results extend and complement recent findings by various authors. Specifically, the models derived in this paper include the quantum XXZ model, the quantum principal chiral model, and the quantum affine Toda model. Furthermore, the quantum integrable models obtained herein are novel and have not been previously reported in the literature. This achievement is facilitated by the recent development of the quantum inverse scattering method utilizing the quantum R-matrix. Consequently, our findings offer a new approach to the construction of integrable lattice models. To illustrate this, we present a solution to the quantum affine Toda model based on a solution of the quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Our results thus provide a nonuniform generalization of this solution. This work was partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11471161). The first author is currently a Visiting Scholar at the Department of Mathematics, University of California, Los Angeles.

Contemporary formal validation tools for software rely on human programmers to bridge the gap between informal specifications and precise formal code using specialized notations. This paper introduces Hoare Reasoning, a tool that enables validation engineers to specify software behavior using natural language. To manage computational complexity, Hoare Reasoning employs a library architecture that permits program verification through a selection of high-level constructs. The tool is currently being developed to support English notation, with formalizations existing for numerous constructs; additional formal work aims to manage the combinatorial complexity inherent in Hoare triples. This paper details the current state of Hoare Reasoning and its foundational principles. We demonstrate how to reason about programs using Hoare Reasoning and discuss the tool's design decisions and future development directions. These decisions were shaped by insights gathered from interviews with practitioners and users regarding their requirements and preferences. We conclude by outlining an ambitious vision: validating software using only informal, natural language specifications. Hoare Reasoning represents a significant step toward this goal, and we discuss how feedback from its use will inform its future evolution. Our discussion highlights the need to balance expressiveness with computational efficiency, the value of integrating formal validation into development environments, and the iterative process of refining both tool design and natural language specifications based on user input. Ultimately, Hoare Reasoning serves as a vital link between informal requirements and formal proofs, offering a new perspective on how natural language specifications can be effectively integrated with formal verification methods. As the tool continues to mature, it will play an increasingly critical role in bridging the divide between informal communication and formal rigor. The paper concludes by outlining several research directions inspired by Hoare Reasoning, including the formal semantics of natural language, natural language as a first-class citizen in development environments, and the iterative refinement of tools and notations based on user feedback. We believe that by embracing Hoare Reasoning as a key component of the formal validation ecosystem, we can move closer to a future where software is validated using intuitive, natural language specifications. The iterative process of developing and using Hoare Reasoning has provided valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities associated with using natural language for software validation. These insights have informed the design and implementation of future tools and notations, and have highlighted the need for further research into the relationship between informal requirements and formal specifications. The iterative process of using Hoare Reasoning has also highlighted the importance of user involvement in the tool development process, and the need for ongoing refinement of the tool and its notations based on user feedback. Although significant research has been conducted on Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) replicated state machines (RSMs), most existing solutions are either unsuitable for cloud environments due to their heavy reliance on specialized hardware, or they depend on stringent and often unrealistic assumptions regarding the behavior of cloud services. This paper introduces RCanopus, an efficient BFT RSM designed to withstand both hardware and software failures within public cloud settings. Unlike many of its predecessors, RCanopus operates with minimal dependencies on external configuration services. RCanopus is built upon a novel cloud model that captures the realistic failure patterns of cloud storage and compute services. We developed an optimized failure detector for this model and integrated it with an adaptive, failure-driven replication strategy. This approach enables the system to maintain high availability by utilizing a reduced quorum for progress, provided that a sufficient number of correct, non-failing services are available. Furthermore, by dynamically adjusting its replication factor, RCanopus ensures low-latency operation as long as a quorum of non-failing services exists. Extensive experiments involving various failure scenarios demonstrate that RCanopus achieves superior availability and performance compared to other BFT RSMs. Additionally, we evaluated an external benchmark using multiple failure models, which confirmed the robustness of RCanopus against diverse failure scenarios. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to address failures in both object and block storage services within public clouds. Finally, we have deployed 20 million requests per second using 40 instances, validating the system's scalability. The implementation, written in Java, is available on GitHub. Our source code and benchmarking code can be found at \url{https://github.com/ist/ricanopus}, and the paper is accessible at \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00100}. The name RCanopus is derived from the star's Bayer designation, Canopus, and the acronym RI, which stands for Resilient Infrastructure. The modulus of lipid membrane bending is a critical property governing processes like budding and fusion. This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how cholesterol affects the bending modulus of both pure and mixed lipid bilayers. Our results indicate that replacing DPPC lipids with cholesterol enhances membrane flexibility up to a 25-30% concentration, after which the bending modulus increases. We attribute this initial rise to cholesterol's ability to reduce the area per headgroup, an effect that diminishes at higher concentrations. Furthermore, we observe that the bending modulus for DPPC/cholesterol bilayers aligns with experimental data, whereas the behavior in POPC/cholesterol systems contradicts both simulations and experiments, suggesting the presence of additional factors in the latter. The POPC/cholesterol system fails to match experimental trends because the reduction in area per headgroup is insufficient to account for the experimentally observed decrease in bending modulus. Finally, we demonstrate that a simple continuum model accurately reproduces the bending modulus of DPPC/cholesterol bilayers. This model incorporates the bending modulus and viscosity of water, the friction coefficient between monolayers, and the area per headgroup, which is influenced by cholesterol. We propose that the area per headgroup serves as an effective descriptor for the degree of cholesterol ordering within the bilayer. These findings offer a quantitative framework for understanding the impact of cholesterol on membrane flexibility and the associated underlying mechanisms. This could facilitate the design of novel cholesterol-modifying agents for potential biomedical applications. Additionally, our results provide a baseline for developing and evaluating new forcefields and models for simulating lipid membranes. **Keywords:** lipid membrane, cholesterol, molecular dynamics, bending modulus. **Abbreviations:** POPC = 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine; DPPC = 1,2-dipalmitoyl-phosphatidylcholine. **Acknowledgments:** This work was funded by the Spanish Ministry of Economy and Competitiveness (grants CTQ2015-67300-P and FIS2016-77284-P), the Autonomous Community of Madrid (grant S2018/TPM-4335), and the European Regional Development Fund. This study examines the application of the loop quantum gravity formalism to a simplified cosmological scenario within the ADM framework, specifically involving a single spatial dimension with no dynamical fields. The resulting loop quantum Hamiltonian is compared against formulations derived from the LQG-ADM mapping applied to the standard FRW model. Significant discrepancies are identified between the two approaches. Furthermore, the application of the strong constraint on the loop quantum Hamiltonian—enforcing no-crossing of the singularity—on the loop quantum Hamiltonian yields a more refined astrophysical model. Finally, the loop quantum spectrum of the area associated with the horizon at the Cauchy surface is calculated and compared with the spin structure of the area spectrum predicted by LQG. Notably, while both models predict an infinite number of spin values, the loop quantum spectrum lacks gaps. These findings suggest that quantum gravity effects may influence the area spectrum in distinct and potentially observable ways. This study presents a catalog of the most energetic cosmic rays recorded during the first year of Phase I at the Pierre Auger Observatory. The dataset encompasses events with energies exceeding 10^{18} eV, spanning various arrival directions. The catalog includes the energy estimates and statistical uncertainties derived from the maximum likelihood method, which utilizes the characteristics of the surface detector array. Additionally, it provides the temporal and spatial coordinates of each event. The most energetic particle identified in this collection is AugerEvent_10009, with an energy of 1.56×10^{19} eV. A phase II of the Observatory is currently underway, which will enhance the precision of energy measurements. Consequently, this paper also provides, as an appendix, a comparison of the maximum likelihood estimates for the top ten highest-energy events from the Phase I catalog, using data from Phase II. The updated energy estimates for these ten events are included in the catalog as well. The data presented in this paper can be accessed via the AugerWeb platform. The catalog is organized by energy in descending order and includes the following information for each event: timestamp, estimated energy, event ID, event name, event type, zenith angle, and direction (right ascension and declination). Furthermore, the catalog provides the number of recorded events and the count of coincidence events within each 30-degree sector of arrival direction. This granularity allows users to easily identify events within specific angular intervals. The catalog is structured into 12 sections, each containing events within a 30-degree angular bin. Users can also filter the catalog by other available criteria, such as energy, event type, or ID. The catalog does not include events from magnetic cloud outbursts or those with questionable validity. The data for each event is stored in two files: a text file containing the event's properties and an HDF5 file with the event's waveforms. The text file is named using the event's ID, while the HDF5 file uses the event's name. The ID is a unique integer assigned by the data acquisition system, whereas the name is a user-defined string. The ID is utilized to link events across the catalog and between the two file types. The event type indicates whether the recorded signal resulted from the detection of a single particle or multiple particles. The zenith angle represents the angle between the event's arrival direction and the vertical axis. The provided coordinates are geocentric, and the provided energies are in the laboratory frame. By employing Bayesian neural networks, BayesOD generates both deterministic outputs and uncertainty metrics. Our primary contributions include: (1) the development of a Bayesian backbone that is lightweight and efficient; (2) the proposal of a Bayesian Feature Pyramid Network to enhance performance; and (3) the implementation of Bayesian spatial attention to refine uncertainty estimates. We evaluate our method's uncertainty estimation capabilities using the standard PRA metric on the COCO dataset. This study addresses traffic prediction for traffic flow sequences. While traditional sequence prediction techniques are commonly applied to this task, the temporal correlations within urban traffic sequences often degrade over time. Consequently, we introduce a novel framework that decomposes original sequences into segments with distinct movement patterns and models each segment independently. This decomposition mitigates the issue of fading correlations. To further enhance prediction accuracy, we propose a new method for identifying traffic segments based on unsupervised learning and movement patterns. We evaluated our approach using two real-world datasets, comparing it against various baseline sequence prediction methods. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms the baselines. Additionally, an ablation study confirms that both the segmentation strategy and the proposed segment identification approach significantly contribute to the overall prediction performance. Finally, we explore how the number of segments influences prediction accuracy, providing guidance on optimal parameter selection for different cities. This paper introduces a multiple convolutional neural network framework designed to partition the hippocampus in both epilepsy and Alzheimer's disorder research. The framework is evaluated using 2.5D MRSI and 3D MRSI datasets from epilepsy patients, as well as 2.5D T1-weighted and 2.5D T2-weighted MR images from Alzheimer's patients. The results indicate that the multi-MLP approach achieves a mean Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 82.2% for 2.5D MRSI, 82.5% for 3D MRSI, 82.6% for 2.5D T1, and 82.4% for 2.5D T2. Furthermore, the proposed multi-convolutional neural network method attains a mean DSC of 82.1% for 2.5D MRSI, 82.4% for 3D MRSI, 82.5% for 2.5D T1, and 82.3% for 2.5D T2. Additionally, we introduce a novel approach for hippocampus analysis in epilepsy and Alzheimer's disorder investigations. By extracting features from the trained network, we identify that the hippocampus in epilepsy patients exhibits a more pronounced curvature compared to healthy controls, whereas Alzheimer's patients show a more straightened hippocampus. These results suggest that the hippocampus structure serves as a critical indicator for diagnosing both conditions. Ultimately, the proposed framework is shown to be effective for hippocampus segmentation and analysis in the context of epilepsy and Alzheimer's disorder studies. We demonstrate the existence of infinite-particle bound states within a three-dimensional box potential with S3 symmetry, a finding that contradicts the conventional understanding of the "pigeonhole phenomenon." This conclusion is derived from a rigorous analysis of transversal modes. Specifically, for a given box's first- and second-mode frequencies, $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$, we establish that the ground state frequency $\omega_0$ must satisfy $\omega_0 \leq \omega_1 + \frac{N}{2}(\omega_2 - \omega_1)$ for any positive integer $N$. This inequality is pivotal in proving the existence of these bound states. Furthermore, we show that this condition is both necessary and sufficient in the limit where $\omega_1$ approaches $\omega_2$. Finally, we provide a novel variational construction to explicitly create these bound states. Given that the pigeonhole phenomenon is a strictly three-dimensional effect, it holds significant potential for new quantum simulations. We outline how this phenomenon can be observed by preparing an $N$-particle state using transverse and longitudinal modes, allowing mode occupation numbers to vary independently. In this setup, the bound states reside below the energy of the state with the maximum allowed occupation number in either the first or second modes. Additionally, we identify a link between our construction and a recently introduced class of bosonic fractional quantum Hall states. Our framework extends to general $k$-mode systems, where we derive an analogous necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of infinite-particle bound states. Finally, we discuss the potential of our approach to generate bosonic Wigner crystallization in three dimensions. This study utilizes a Monte Carlo code to analyze the propagation of cosmic ray secondary particles, specifically focusing on electron-positron pairs and hadrons generated within the Earth's atmosphere. The simulation tracks the history of particles interacting with the atmosphere up to an altitude of 1,000 km. Results indicate that at 500 km, the electron-positron pair flux is approximately 10% of the primary cosmic ray (CR) flux, whereas at 1,000 km, this ratio drops to roughly 1%. Furthermore, the flux ratio of secondary hadrons to primary CRs at 500 km is about 25%, compared to 2% at 1,000 km. These findings suggest that the production of secondary particles from primary CRs at 500 km is approximately four times greater than that at 1,000 km. Additionally, particle fluxes at 500 km are observed to be 1.5 to 2 times higher than those at 1,000 km. The research also examines how variations in primary CR energy and geomagnetic latitude influence the fluxes of secondary particles. Finally, the study compares these results with data from the AMS-02 experiment. Ultimately, the elevated fluxes of secondary particles at 500 km relative to 1,000 km may complicate the search for dark matter signatures. However, the study concludes that such signatures remain detectable, provided that background subtraction is performed in regions where the ratio of secondary particles to primary CRs remains constant. This conclusion is supported by the observation that, for a fixed geomagnetic latitude, the ratio of secondary particles to primary CRs is independent of the primary CR energy. Consequently, the paper recommends that future investigations into cosmic ray anomalies, such as those reported by AMS-02, be conducted using satellites at multiple orbital altitudes. The swift emergence of Deep Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) has garnered significant research interest, driven by their ability to integrate graph theory with neural networks to excel in complex tasks like graph classification and recommendation. Nevertheless, existing DGNN models often suffer from sub-optimal performance, and current research lacks comprehensive, systematic, and complete frameworks for designing graph neural network architectures. To address this gap, we propose a holistic framework for DGNN design. This work offers a systematic overview of the field, proposes fundamental frameworks for DGNNs, and provides in-depth analyses of graph representation and network architecture. Specifically, regarding graph representation, we introduce the Global Pyramid-like Shrinkage Framework to balance local and global information. In terms of network architecture, we propose the Local Topology Link Reconfiguration mechanism to optimize graph signal propagation and mitigate over-smoothing issues. Furthermore, by examining the limitations of existing models, we identify potential future research directions. Recent years have seen significant advancements in privacy-preserving data analysis, driven by the increasing availability of public and private datasets. Among these developments, differential privacy (DP) has emerged as a leading framework for ensuring data privacy. This study presents Huber-DP, the initial method for privately fulfilling low-rank matrices under DP constraints. Leveraging the Huber loss function, this approach effectively balances the trade-off between privacy and utility. We demonstrate that the optimal solution to Huber-DP can be obtained by solving a specific convex optimization problem, which can then be efficiently addressed using established techniques like the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Furthermore, we empirically evaluate Huber-DP's performance in privately estimating a low-rank matrix from a partially observed one, comparing its results against state-of-the-art DP algorithms such as DP-SGD and a custom private Frank-Wolfe algorithm. Our results indicate that, in certain scenarios, particularly when dealing with outliers, Huber-DP can substantially enhance the accuracy of the estimated matrix. The "crisis of Galactic parameters" stems from the discrepancy between Galactic models and observations regarding the distribution of interstellar matter, particularly dust. This study aims to enhance Galactic dust models by utilizing a data-driven approach grounded in high-resolution, multi-wavelength dust emission and polarization data from the Planck Surveyor and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). By analyzing this information, we derive a statistical model for the "sparse" interstellar medium (ISM), characterized by dust filaments and voids. We introduce a novel, physically motivated, and computationally efficient method to represent this sparse ISM, alongside a corresponding polarization model. These frameworks are integrated into the recently developed Astrodust$+$PAH model, which describes both emission and extinction properties of the sparse ISM. The Astrodust$+$PAH model is calibrated using a dataset of 1,000 realizations of the sparse ISM. We demonstrate that the model accurately reproduces observed spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and the relationship between polarized flux and wavelength. Furthermore, we show that Astrodust$+$PAH significantly improves the description of Galactic extinction and polarization compared to the previous Astrodust model. Finally, we outline how Astrodust$+$PAH can be utilized to constrain models of Galactic dust distribution. Our findings indicate that incorporating sparse ISM models into astrophysical models will substantially improve predictions of Galactic polarization and extinction. We report the detection of a massive planet within the disk surrounding the young, extremely low-mass star CIDA 1. By analyzing high-contrast imaging data from the VLT/SPHERE instrument, we observed a point source at 100 au from the star, which we interpret as a planet with a mass of 1.5–2.5 $M_{\rm Jup}$. This system, hosting a gas giant within a disk, offers a unique opportunity to investigate the core accretion model of planet formation. Our findings indicate that the planet's formation occurred within 1.5 Myr, implying that the core accretion process is significantly more efficient in the densest regions of the disk. Additionally, the planet resides in the outer disk, where the gas-to-dust ratio is lower, further facilitating the creation of a massive core. These results highlight the critical role of the disk in the formation of massive planets around low-mass stars. Future studies should focus on characterizing the disk to better understand the physical conditions that enable core accretion. Furthermore, we aim to refine the planet's atmospheric properties by combining spectroscopic data from VLT/ERIS and VLT/IRAM. Finally, we will continue to monitor the system to observe the disk's evolution and the growth of the planet. This system will be included in the upcoming VVV-GO program, which will provide regular monitoring of young stars with disks and confirmed planets. Abstract interpretation operates within a feedback loop comprising an information gathering phase and a refinement phase. Historically, these stages have been tightly interdependent, where the extent of gathering is governed by the degree of refinement. This paper introduces a fully algorithmic framework for decoupling these phases within the framework of Abstract Interpretation. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through fully computable instances grounded in control-flow analysis. Our primary contribution lies in establishing fully computable criteria that dictate the volume of information collected and the level of refinement. These criteria are grounded in a novel concept of calibration, which we show is both necessary and sufficient. Furthermore, we apply this calibration-based methodology to several practical scenarios, including a precise control-flow analysis for the R5 semantic framework, a robust control-flow analysis for the more expressive CFA1 framework, and a straightforward control-flow analysis for the widely used CFL grammar. In each case, our algorithms achieve termination without relying on ad-hoc widening techniques. We validate the efficacy of these algorithms by implementing them in a prototype system. Additionally, we provide a complexity analysis for the proposed algorithms, showing that their behavior is no more intricate than that of standard abstract fixation procedures. Finally, we illustrate the practical performance of these methods by comparing them against existing control-flow analysis tools. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithms are competitive with existing techniques. To our knowledge, this marks the first instance where the rising and falling phases of an abstract interpretation can be decoupled in this manner. We anticipate that this approach will facilitate the design of new, potentially more effective and efficient iterative procedures in program analysis. Topological materials have attracted significant attention due to their unique physical properties, including the topologically protected surface states of electrons and holes. However, electron-based topological phases are typically stabilized by strong electron-electron interactions, whereas phonon-based topological phases rely on strong phonon-phonon interactions. Although recent studies have identified phonon topological phases in molecular and atomic systems, phonon topological ceramics remain largely unexplored. In this study, we experimentally demonstrate a phonon topological phase in oxide ceramics through the excitation of localized light. We confirm that this phenomenon is driven by strong phonon-phonon interactions, with topological states regulated by structural chirality. Furthermore, we validate a bulk-boundle correspondence model that elucidates the relationship between the bulk and surface states of phonons in these ceramics. Our findings expand the scope of phonon topological research beyond single-atom systems and molecular materials to include complex ceramic materials, potentially enabling their practical applications in fields such as energy conversion and sensing.

Outlier detection within high-dimensional spaces remains a difficult challenge, especially for sparse data where overfitting risks misclassifying normal points as anomalies. This paper introduces a novel outlier score calculation for complete metric spaces, utilizing a proximity graph-based approach. By constructing a nearest neighbor graph, the method efficiently identifies links between typical and anomalous points, enabling rapid detection in high-dimensional environments. We evaluate the algorithm using established metrics across various high-dimensional datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions in both speed and accuracy. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345678/PGBOA. Furthermore, we provide an interactive web application allowing users to experiment with the algorithm on high-dimensional data via https://proximitygraphbasedoutlierdetection.net/. This platform supports data upload in CSV, JSON, XML, or SQL formats, with the option to input custom distance functions. Additionally, the application enables testing of metric spaces containing up to 100 data points. Future enhancements will include support for data sets of any size, though performance may vary, and the inclusion of preloaded data sets for ease of use. The method's high dimensionality makes it suitable for diverse applications in bioinformatics, image analysis, and natural language processing. We anticipate that this new technique will be valuable for researchers and practitioners in high-dimensional data analytics. This study examines the excited-state dynamics and electromagnetic emission from an atom in close proximity to a slender conducting plate. We present a theoretical framework utilizing slenderness as an asymptotic parameter to derive the atom's time-dependent evolution equation and electromagnetic Green tensor. The tensor is modeled as a superposition of the free-space Green tensor and a correction term representing the atom's interaction with the plate. By modeling the slender mirror as a perfect electric current filament, we derive an analytical expression for the Green tensor that captures induced electric fields, magnetic polarization, and geometric characteristics. In the limit of infinite filament length, our results converge with those for a conducting half-space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, unlike the three-dimensional case, the atom's excitation does not decay exponentially over time when facing a slender mirror. Finally, we illustrate how the plate's slenderness alters the atom's relaxation dynamics and modifies the emitted radiation pattern. These findings are validated through finite element method simulations of a λ/10 gold plate. Our findings indicate that the atom's excited state can be sustained for extended periods, and the radiation emitted is significantly stronger and more complex than that from a atom near a bulk mirror. This offers a novel method for controlling an atom's dynamics and its radiated radiation, with potential applications in photonics, sensing, and quantum information science. This study introduces an optimization-based framework for fair classification on graph data by identifying and eliminating biased community structures within the underlying graphs. The approach is grounded in the theory of graph homomorphisms and the Sauer-Shelah Lemma, which defines these biased communities as non-trivial preimages of points in the target class distribution when the homomorphism map is constant on attributes. The proposed framework operates in two stages: first, it constructs a biasedness graph where nodes represent community bias, and edges denote minimal refinement via non-biased homomorphisms; second, it selects the smallest local community to eliminate using an algorithm that balances bias reduction with the preservation of predictive performance. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method enhances both the fairness and predictability of community-localized classifiers. We construct solutions for kinetic equations governing reversible enzyme processes, utilizing an iterative scheme where each approximation relies on the prior one. Specifically, third-order approximations for both the enzyme-substrate complex concentration and the reaction velocity are derived. Additionally, we establish an estimate for the difference between the exact kinetic function and its approximation, demonstrating that the interval for the complex concentration converges to zero as the iteration progresses. Finally, we generate a series of numerical tables and illustrate various scenarios using corresponding graphs. These examples highlight that the third-order approximation yields results nearly identical to those obtained from solving the kinetic equation exactly. Consequently, this approach is highly effective for investigating the kinetic characteristics of reversible enzyme processes. Furthermore, the methodology is applicable to enzyme processes lacking equilibrium or steady-state conditions, including those involving enzymes with multiple substrates and products. This study examines the potential for detecting supersymmetry (SUSY) and substructures of SUSY models within proton-proton collisions resulting in three or more jets and missing transverse momentum. The analysis incorporates both fully integrated and differential predictions for the CMS and ATLAS experiments, covering final states characterized by high transverse momentum jets and significant missing transverse momentum, with no significant excess over the Standard Model background observed in any channel. These results are utilized to constrain natural SUSY models, specifically focusing on gluino and top squark decays. Furthermore, the investigation explores the division of parameter space based on the primary decay pathways of gluinos and top squarks, highlighting the advantages of such an approach. This strategy is particularly relevant given current limits derived from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV with dijet final states and jets accompanied by jets and missing transverse momentum. The study concludes with an outline of future prospects for the LHC. Additionally, a companion paper presents a similar analysis centered on top squark decays to electroweakinos and Higgsinos. All outcomes from these related studies are used to set updated limits on gluino and top squark masses in natural SUSY models at 95% confidence level. Specifically, for gluinos decaying via electroweakinos and Higgsinos, masses up to 1.1 TeV are excluded, surpassing the previous ATLAS limit of 900 GeV. For top squarks, masses up to 700 GeV are ruled out, improving upon the prior exclusion of 500 GeV. Additionally, the previously excluded region for top squark masses below 250 GeV is now excluded up to 700 GeV. Furthermore, the ATLAS collaboration has established the most stringent limits to date on the masses of charginos and neutralinos up to 1.1 TeV and 1.2 TeV, respectively. These limits have been incorporated into the parameter space analysis, which indicates that charginos and neutralinos with masses up to 400 GeV and 350 GeV, respectively, are excluded for electroweak mixing angles of $\sin^2\theta_\text{W} = 0.53$ and 0.75. Review platforms contain extensive collections of user feedback on various platforms. To assist readers in efficiently navigating these platforms and locating products that align with their needs and preferences, a method capable of effectively mining review data and delivering personalized recommendations is essential. Existing review-based product recommendation techniques often fail to fully leverage the rich information within reviews or accurately capture the interdependencies among multiple features. Furthermore, reviews often express sentiments toward different products, which can influence user preferences during interaction. To address these limitations, this paper introduces the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) for effective review-based product recommendation. This model comprises two primary components: a sentiment-aware attention mechanism and a multi-view feature interaction module. The former precisely extracts and encodes review information by integrating both textual and numerical reviews, while the latter captures the interactions of multi-dimensional features across multiple views. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed model significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines. Data augmentation serves as a robust technique for enhancing machine learning performance, particularly in code-switched scenarios. This study investigates data augmentation through lexical substitutions in Arabic-English code-switched text, aiming to boost model generalization. We examine substitutions for both borrowed and non-borrowed words, utilizing a dictionary-based method alongside lexical resources like WordNet and Glosbar. Our approach incorporates a novel dictionary-based method with word tagging, alongside two new gloss-based techniques—one using non-borrowed word tagging and another employing tagging similarity. We evaluated these substitution methods on two tasks: cross-lingual named entity recognition (NER) and code-switched text classification (CSC). Our results indicate that lexical substitution significantly improves the performance of deep learning models in data-scarce environments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that while direct dictionary-based substitution yields the best performance for borrowed words, leveraging lexical resources for non-borrowed words leads to more consistent tagging and superior overall performance. Finally, this paper offers the first comprehensive comparison of various lexical substitution strategies for data augmentation in Arabic-English code-switching. The code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/ASA-Subs. We demonstrate that no precompact subgroup of the diffeomorphism group of a compact hyperbolic surface, equipped with the precompact-open topology, possesses the Roelcke precompactness property. More broadly, we establish that for any compact Riemann surface $X$ with a hyperbolic underlying topology, the group $\text{Diff}(X)$ metastable in the precompact-open topology but lacks Roelcke precompactness. Furthermore, the proof extends to show that the homeomorphism group $\text{Homeo}(X)$ under consideration is also Roelcke non-precompact. Additionally, we present a general criterion for precompact groups on metrizable spaces with the precompact-open topology to determine whether they exhibit Roelcke precompactness; this criterion is met by precompact subgroups of $\text{Homeo}(X)$ within their natural topologies whenever $X$ carries a second-countable metric satisfying the Heine-Borel property. In contrast, for the specific group $\text{Homeo}(X)$, the Roelcke property holds if and only if $X$ is the circle $S^1$ or the projective line $\mathbb{R}P^1$, regardless of the topology on the precompact-open topology. These findings further clarify the distinctions between the various precompactness concepts associated with the diffeomorphism and homeomorphism groups of manifolds and metrizable spaces. Our methodology also yields examples of precompact groups on metrizable spaces (when considered with their natural topologies) in the sense of precompact-open topology that simultaneously possess both the minimal envelopping group property and the Roelcke property. Finally, we provide examples of precompact groups on metrizable spaces where the closure within the bisectional group fails to be Roelcke precompact, thereby illustrating the divergence between these two concepts. To achieve this, we construct a metric space homeomorphic to the Cantor set where the group of all self-homeomorphisms, when viewed as a precompact group via the precompact-open topology, is Roelcke non-precompact. This result highlights a significant disparity between the properties of precompactness and Roelcke precompactness for $\text{Homeo}(X)$ across different metrizable spaces $X$. We derive the null brane tangent space for semiglobally defined deformations, which encompass globally defined cases. Furthermore, we construct connectable branes on these theories; although not all are preserved by any null brane, all obtained branes are confirmed to be null. This study introduces an analytical delay model for step-load converters, developed using Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolkit. The model is built upon the step-response characteristics of converters, which are derived from their small-signal response to load perturbations. By utilizing a step function, the model avoids the complexity associated with approximating small-signal dynamics around an operating point, thereby enhancing its applicability to converter analysis across a wide range of load conditions. Furthermore, the delay parameters identified by the curve-fitting algorithm offer direct insight into the converter's switching behavior. This understanding is crucial for analyzing and mitigating issues such as ringing and oscillations in power converters, as well as the risk of unintended turn-on in MOSFETs caused by switching delays. Additionally, the delay parameters can be directly applied to model idealized switching devices within circuit simulators like SPICE. The paper also examines a simplified switching delay model for MOSFETs, followed by an analysis of how predicted switching delays influence the stability of converter control loops. Finally, the study validates the model through experimental data collected from a real-world DC-DC buck converter. The findings demonstrate that the proposed delay model effectively captures the underlying switching dynamics of power electronic devices, offering a valuable tool for the design and analysis of power electronic systems. This study introduces a new, robust algorithm designed to robustly finite-interpolate finite-element datasets. Unlike current reconstruction methods that often fail to guarantee arrangement preservation, our approach ensures this property by solving a convex optimization problem. We successfully tested the method on 2D and 3D simulations involving 10,000 to 100,000 mesh points, demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling complex, non-convex structures. Furthermore, the method exhibits superior performance in data denoising compared to existing techniques. The proposed approach is fully generic, making it highly applicable to various fields such as mesh generation, geometric modeling, and geometric processing. Additionally, it is well-suited for integration into large-scale data analysis workflows, including those for medical imaging and remote sensing. The implementation is written in Python and utilizes the CVX package for optimization. To facilitate adoption, we have provided a user-friendly package named "cpaf" (convex arrangement preserving filter), which includes both a command-line utility for basic filtering and a Python package for advanced applications. This work is published in the 2019 IEEE International Conference on Data Science (ICDS). The source code is available at https://github.com/taekyunglee/cpaf. Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients are characterized by low-frequency fluctuations (LFQPOs) that display a distinctive "trough" at the Nyquist frequency during the hard state. This study investigates LFQPOs in the black hole X-ray transient MAXI J1535-571 using the Insight-HXMT. We identified LFQPOs in the 2–10 keV band with a low-frequency component ranging from 1.8 to 2.2 Hz. Spectral analysis of the LFQPOs reveals a hardening of the photon index from 2.2 to 1.8 as the system evolves from the initial to the final outburst phase. Furthermore, the LFQPOs in the 2–10 keV band exhibit a gradual decline in hardness from 2.2 to 1.8 throughout the outburst phase. Additionally, the hard X-ray component in the 20–30 keV band shows a significant decrease in intensity from the initial to the final phase, accompanied by a softening of the photon index from 2.2 to 1.8. This evolution aligns with the corona shrinking and the accretion disk expanding. Consequently, the LFQPOs in MAXI J1535-571 demonstrate a clear decline in both intensity and hardness from the initial to the final phase, a trend that may be attributed to the evolving corona. These observations are consistent with the scenario that LFQPOs arise from the variability of the corona. Finally, we propose that the LFQPOs in MAXI J1535-571 may be linked to the accretion disk. This research is based on data from the Insight-HXMT. The Insight-HXMT is a Chinese space observatory launched in 2017.
