This work investigates inference methods for multi-dimensional time series characterized by heavy tails and potential temporal dependence. The study establishes limit theorems for linear and non-linear time series, as well as autoregressive models, under conditions of general dependence. These theoretical findings are utilized to develop consistent estimators for the spectral measure and the linear/non-linear AR coefficients. Additionally, estimators for the spectral density of a linear process are derived, with their performance evaluated using various simulation methods. The authors demonstrate that the asymptotic properties of the linear component estimator remain valid even when temporal dependence exists. Furthermore, a new class of non-linear estimators is proposed, which is shown to be consistent for strictly linear processes, thereby expanding the range of models where non-linear components can be effectively identified. Finally, a cointegration model is analyzed, revealing that the proposed estimation approach yields a consistent estimator for the cointegrating relationship. This result is particularly significant because the traditional phrasing of cointegration, which relies on the concept of a unit root, is not applicable in this context. Furthermore, a test for linearity is introduced, and its performance is assessed through simulations. The paper concludes by applying these results to two datasets: simulated data and the daily closing prices of the S&P500 and S&P600 indices from 2007 to 2009. The empirical analysis demonstrates that the proposed methods are effective in characterizing non-linear and non-stable time series. Finally, the study addresses the challenge of estimating the tail index using the sample Hill estimator, showing that it performs well for i.i.d. samples but fails when applied to multi-dimensional time series with temporal dependence. To overcome this, a new tail index estimator is introduced, which remains consistent for linear autoregressive models and Gaussian error terms. Simulations confirm that this new estimator outperforms the Hill estimator. The work ends with a discussion of the empirical results. **Keywords:** Heavy tails, non-stable time series, temporal dependence, non-linear autoregressive models, linearity test, tail index estimation, cointegration. **Mathematics Subject Classification (2010):** 62M10, 62P35, 62G09, 62G20. **Bibliography:** 45 pages, 10 figures. **Acknowledgments:** The authors thank the editors and two anonymous referees for their constructive feedback, which greatly improved the quality of this manuscript. Leveraging linear-time classical LDPC decoders, we develop an $O(r)$-time algorithm capable of decoding any error pattern with a probability exceeding $1 - e^{-r}$. By utilizing random Clifford encoding, we further demonstrate that the family can correct bit and phase erasures with high probability. This study addresses the distributed $r$-dominating set problem, specifically focusing on its distance-$r$ covering variant. An $r$-dominating set is defined as a vertex subset where every node in the graph is within distance $r$ of at least one member of the set. Unlike standard dominating sets, $r$-dominating sets allow for greater flexibility in selecting nodes. We demonstrate a lower bound for the size of the smallest $r$-dominating set (at distance $r$) and utilize this finding to establish a bound on the distributed complexity required to identify an $r$-dominating set of minimal cardinality within high-girth sparse graphs. Specifically, we propose a distributed algorithm that computes a $1$-dominating set (equivalent to finding a vertex cover) in sparse graphs with high girth $g$. The algorithm operates in $O(\sqrt{n})$ rounds, where $n$ represents the total number of nodes. Furthermore, we prove that any distributed algorithm capable of finding a vertex cover in $k$-excluded graphs with girth $g$ must require at least $\Omega(\sqrt{g})$ rounds. This finding resolves an inquiry posed by Ghaffari et al. [PODC 2020] and indicates that the lower bound is tight. Additionally, our findings establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ on distributed vertex cover complexity, which is tight given the existence of a deterministic algorithm achieving an upper bound of $O(\sqrt{n})$. Finally, we examine a more general scenario involving "local" vertex covers, where edges within a distance-$r$ neighborhood of a node must be covered rather than just edges incident to it. For the case of $1$-local vertex covers, we present an algorithm with a runtime bound of $O(n^{1/3})$. Our results indicate that the lower bound is tight up to a constant factor, thereby answering another question raised by Ghaffari et al. [PODC 2020].

Recent studies on mass-boundary correspondences have primarily concentrated on systems featuring uniform masses. In this work, we extend these findings within the framework of disordered higher-order topological materials. Through the analysis of the non-Hermitian effective model, we demonstrate that the mass-boundary correspondence holds for disordered zero modes, revealing a connection between the symmetry-breaking strength of the mass term and the boundary-like character of these modes. Furthermore, we numerically characterize the scaling properties of the hypermode volume and explore the influence of different disorder types on the mass-boundary correspondence. Finally, we examine the symmetry-breaking effect on higher-order topological phases, revealing a novel phenomenon where the number of chiral edge modes increases as the system transitions from the trivial to the topological phase. Our results offer valuable insights for investigating symmetry-breaking-induced phase transitions in higher-order topological materials, with potential applications in the study of non-Hermitian systems. Additionally, the methodologies employed here can be applied to various other topological models. Our findings are applicable to the following models: Su-Schrieffer-Heeger, Kane-Mele, Samuelsen, Su-Schrieffer-Heeger with next-nearest neighbor hopping, and Su-Schrieffer-Heeger with bond disorder. In recent years, neural visualization has increasingly adopted machine learning techniques to overcome the labor-intensive nature of traditional hand-crafted methods. However, current neural radiance networks, which model light propagation in 3D scenes, typically rely on fixed base color assumptions that limit their flexibility. This paper introduces a novel rendering approach called Bright Field Neural Visualization, which renders 3D scenes of point clouds by explicitly estimating per-vertex base colors instead. We demonstrate that this technique enhances the trainability of neural network-based volumetric rendering for neural visualization. Our findings indicate that it significantly improves rendering quality, particularly for scenes featuring thin structures and complex geometries. We successfully applied this method to 3D point clouds of neurons and synapses to generate scientifically valuable and aesthetically superior renderings. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/3dvlab/BFNV. Furthermore, the 3D point cloud datasets utilized in this study can be downloaded from our repository at https://github.com/3dvlab/BFNV/tree/main/data. We also provide a user-friendly executable version of the code at https://github.com/3dvlab/BFNV/tree/main/NeuralViz. Additional source code and user documentation are available at https://github.com/3dvlab/BFNV/tree/main/docs. Finally, we have established a new neural visualization repository at https://github.com/3dvlab/NeuralViz. Our code supports the 3D point cloud data used in this research, located at https://github.com/3dvlab/BFNV/tree/main/data, as well as other publicly available point cloud datasets, including Sintel, Tanks and Temples, and the Stanford Bunny. The repository also features sample configurations for various scenes. We invite researchers to submit their 3D point cloud data for testing by creating a new repository and issuing an invitation to our team. Please note that our current workflow is optimized for 3D point clouds; we do not support RGB images or 3D volumes at this time. We intend to expand our capabilities to support these other input types in the future. We appreciate your understanding and look forward to your contributions. This study presents speckle interferometric data for 100 stars, observed using the SOAR telescope's speckle instrument during 2021. The dataset includes 57 binary systems, 35 tertiary systems, and 8 quaternary systems. The primary objective was to determine angular separations and position angles for these additional third and fourth components. For 20 of the observed stars, these newly derived separations and position angles will be incorporated into the speckle catalog of multiple stars within the Large Magellanic Cloud. The remaining 80 stars were selected from various sky regions, including the Galactic plane, the Carina Nebula, and the Large Magellanic Cloud. The 2021 observations consist of 118 individual nights, with each night typically involving the imaging of two stars. This paper reports the measurement results for all 100 stars, providing updated physical parameters for the 57 binary and 35 tertiary systems. For the 57 binary systems, we report new physical parameters for 21 systems, while the remaining 36 previously published parameters are utilized to calculate the physical evolution of these systems. For the 35 tertiary systems, we calculate the angular separations between the primary and third components, the position angles of the third component relative to the primary, and the orbital periods of the binary systems. Additionally, we provide the current separations and position angles for the 35 tertiary systems. For the 8 quaternary systems, we report the separations and position angles of the third and fourth components. Finally, we compare the 2021 Speckle Interferometry data with the 2009 and 2019 data to calculate the proper motions of the 35 tertiary and 8 quaternary stars. Furthermore, we compare the 2021 data with the 2019 and 2011 data to derive the proper motions for the 57 binary stars. Finally, we compare the 2021 data with the 2009 and 2019 data to calculate the proper motions for the 100 observed stars. The 2021 Speckle Interferometry data will be made available to the public. This dual representation is derived from the integrable structure governing these amplitudes, specifically the monodromy of the celestial scattering matrix. We demonstrate that heavenly space, which possesses this monododromy, adheres to colour-kinematics duality. Consequently, within the space of colour-kinematics dual objects, the equations of motion for both heavenly space and AKST take on a self-dual form. Furthermore, we elucidate how this dual object relates to conformal field theory. Our findings suggest that heavenly space serves as a valuable example for understanding colour-kinematics duality, with potential extensions to other spaces exhibiting monodromy or conformal symmetry. In this context, we propose that the self-dual nature of the colour-kinematics dual of gravitational equations of motion is linked to the integrability of the AKST amplitude. Solar jets are believed to originate from magnetic reconnection occurring above filament channels, yet their precise formation mechanisms remain unclear. This study presents LOFAR observations of a piston-driven shock wave accelerating along the side of a jet within the low solar corona. The persistent and superior sensitivity of LOFAR's wide-field imager (WFI) to plasma density fluctuations enables the detection of a dense jet core, which exhibits a width of approximately 1 arcsec and a length exceeding 0.5° in the low corona. The jet's leading edge is propelled by a shock wave traveling at roughly 150 km/s. By applying the small-angle approximation, we determined the low-coronal shock velocity to be approximately 300 km/s. This velocity is consistent with the front of the same shock wave detected by the Sun's radio emission at 1.4 GHz, indicating a direct link between jets and coronal piston surges. We investigate a scenario where new physics beyond the Standard Model manifests as flavour irregularities in meson decays and anomalies regarding the (g-2) of the muon. By employing the probability assessment function, we estimate the likelihood of coexistence between these two phenomena within the general Two Higgs Doublet Model. Our analysis indicates that the prob(coex) value is minimal when the new physics contributions to meson decays and (g-2)_mu share the same sign, a finding that aligns with previous research. Additionally, we determine the individual prob(new) associated with measuring prob(coex). The prob(new) values for the (g-2) and B_u decays are significantly lower than those for K decays, suggesting that the B_s \to f_0 a_0 decays serve as a promising avenue for discovering new physics. Furthermore, we observe that prob(new) for K decays remains relatively low compared to that of B decays, implying a potential new physics effect in the B_s \to K^* a_0 decay. Finally, we note that these results remain consistent with the B_s \to K^* \gamma decays. These findings can be further validated by the LHCb experiment through its upcoming measurements of B_s \to K^* f_0 decays. We anticipate that the prob assessment method will prove valuable in estimating the new physics effect of specific decay channels. Additionally, we have prepared a Mathematica package to facilitate future calculations using this prob assessment approach. We conclude that this prob assessment method offers a novel and effective tool for identifying new physics effects. A detailed description of this method will be provided in a forthcoming paper. Finally, we expect that this prob assessment technique will prove beneficial in searching for new physics effects. This study introduces a functional probabilistic differential equation (fube) designed to model random fluid dynamics, applying it specifically to a functional Schrödinger equation (fSe) within quantum mechanics. Utilizing a Liouville-type theorem, the authors establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the fube. The core innovation lies in the superposition principle, which provides a novel and practical method for resolving complex nonlinear equations by breaking them into simpler components. This approach offers a new perspective and framework for addressing random nonlinear phenomena in fluid dynamics, while also introducing fresh concepts and methodologies for solving nonlinear problems in functional quantum mechanics. Furthermore, the paper examines various scenarios regarding initial conditions and stochastic perturbations. It demonstrates that the proposed random fSe can yield exact or closed-form solutions by identifying appropriate potentials, thereby providing a comprehensive and unified framework for resolving functional probabilistic problems. Additionally, the study explores the application of the random fSe to the Schrödinger equation, revealing that its solutions differ from those of the quantum harmonic oscillator and the hydrogen atom. Finally, the paper discusses several applications of the random fSe within functional quantum mechanics. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to be difficult for classical computers to replicate. While the average entanglement within this framework has been the subject of prior study, this work examines its distribution across all possible output states. By calculating the expected value of entanglement measured by geometric entropy, we identify a phase transition occurring at a specific ratio of photons to modes. Furthermore, we explore implications for verifying the quantum advantage of boson sampling. In contrast to average entanglement, our findings indicate that the entire distribution of final-state entanglement is required to construct a meaningful verification metric. Additionally, we establish an upper bound for entanglement in arbitrary output states and empirically demonstrate that most of these states remain highly entangled. Finally, we empirically confirm that these highly entangled final states can be isolated without relying on post-selection. To support these findings, we have made all relevant code and data available online. Accessing this resource enables the computation of expected geometric entanglement for any given circuit configuration. To our knowledge, this represents the first time final-state entanglement in boson sampling is characterized without relying on post-selection. This approach is particularly advantageous for scaling up experiments, as it avoids the need for post-selection, which is necessary for analyzing average entanglement. Consequently, our results suggest that the entanglement distribution in boson sampling undergoes a phase transition driven by the ratio of photons to modes. This insight is expected to facilitate the design of new experiments capable of observing this critical phenomenon. Additionally, our findings may aid in the verification of quantum advantage in boson sampling, as current verification protocols rely on average entanglement, thereby obscuring the true entanglement distribution. To address this, we propose a method for constructing a verification metric based on the entanglement of individual output states. This metric is derived from the expected value of geometric entanglement and is expected to surpass the performance of the standard verification protocol. We have also made this metric code available for circuit design and verification purposes. We anticipate that researchers will utilize our findings to design new experiments that explicitly investigate the entanglement distribution in boson sampling. We also expect that future verification protocols will leverage our proposed metric to surpass the performance of the current protocol. Finally, we anticipate that our findings will inspire further research into the entanglement distributions of other quantum computational models. Our findings are also expected to encourage the development of new metrics for quantifying quantum advantage, which will enable the systematic study of how quantum advantage scales with system

High-dimensional time series are common in life sciences, yet their analysis remains difficult. While various models exist to learn from such data, we contend that sequential brief and high-dimensional temporal event chains offer a more practical approach for scientific learning. We demonstrate that this paradigm is both feasible and effective across diverse life science contexts, including protein folding, drug binding, and ribosome translation. To achieve this, we introduce guided sequential behavior clustering (GSBC), a method that identifies brief, high-dimensional temporal sequences within large datasets. We show that these sequences can be sequentially chained to form event chains that encapsulate the essential behaviors of the system. Furthermore, we prove that these GSBC-derived event chains serve as effective learning data for two prominent supervised learning models: Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Our evaluation on three protein folding, ribosome translation, and ligand binding examples indicates that GSBC-based event chains retain the essential scientific information of the original data while filtering out noise. Consequently, this framework enables learning from high-dimensional temporal sequences that are orders of magnitude more concise than the original datasets. Empirical results confirm that models trained on these derived event chains achieve accuracy comparable to or superior to those trained on full datasets, particularly for the two most critical assessment questions. This approach is especially advantageous for low-data regimes, where it facilitates the learning from hundreds of samples that were previously deemed insufficient. Overall, our findings suggest that GSBC can enhance the scientific utility of data-driven models in high-dimensional temporal domains. Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms frequently encounter challenges when operating within environments where not all relevant information is directly observable. In these partial observability scenarios, maintaining a belief state becomes essential. This study investigates whether recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can substitute for explicit belief states without compromising performance in such environments. Through experiments on two partially observable gridworlds, we demonstrate that RNNs achieve performance parity with methods that rely on computationally expensive belief state calculations. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence suggesting that the RNNs implicitly replicate the belief states required by optimal policies. Consequently, this finding offers a significant avenue for developing more efficient RL approaches in partially observable settings. Additionally, we present analysis of the internal dynamics of these agent policies, indicating that the learned representations align with established principles of optimal control. Finally, we explore the potential of this research avenue by proposing a new architecture that integrates the implicit efficiency of RNNs with the robustness of function approximation techniques. This proposed model matches the efficacy of current state-of-the-art methods while being substantially more concise. Overall, this work elucidates the internal operational mechanisms of policies within partially observable contexts and paves the way for future developments characterized by enhanced efficiency and robustness. In video-based action detection, identifying relevant contextual cues is crucial for achieving weakly-guided detection. While current state-of-the-art methods typically leverage global context, they often neglect other significant contextual factors. Furthermore, manually selecting the most pertinent contextual features remains a labor-intensive and unreliable process. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel weakly-guided action detection framework that integrates context selection with weakly-guided action detection. Specifically, we represent contextual features as a graph, where nodes correspond to individual features and edges denote their relationships. Subsequently, we develop a graph convolutional network to learn adaptive edge weights, thereby pinpointing the most informative context. Finally, weakly-guided action detection is implemented using these selected optimal features. Experimental results on the standard THUMOS14 dataset demonstrate that our proposed framework surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, an ablation study confirms that the weakly-guided action detection mechanism effectively selects the most relevant contextual features. The adaptive graph convolutional network functions as a feature selector to identify the most relevant context for weakly-guided action detection. This study examines the long-term dynamics of solutions to a class of parabolic equations, characterized by specific diffusion mechanisms and disturbances. These disturbance terms encompass both spatially and temporally dependent "classical" forcing and spatially fixed "switching" forcing, which evolve randomly over time based on a Markov chain. The equations under consideration allow for diffusion coefficients to vanish at boundary points, a property that introduces significant mathematical challenges. Specifically, these issues include a modified boundary value problem, metastability phenomena, and effective boundary conditions within a homogenization framework. The analysis addresses boundary conditions of Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin types, as well as nonlinear boundary mechanisms. Furthermore, the initial data are formulated as a random process, with its evolution also governed by the Markov chain. The primary methodologies employed include spectral analysis, the maximum principle, stochastic analysis, and a newly developed technique known as "quasi-stationary analysis." These tools are utilized to characterize asymptotic behavior, determine convergence rates, and investigate various effective boundary conditions. The work presents both rigorous theorems and a variety of examples illustrating diverse dynamics, including metastability, within this newly defined parabolic framework. Additionally, the discussion covers the interplay between metastability and effective boundary conditions during the homogenization process. The results are supported by numerical simulations. This research represents a synthesis of findings previously published in various journals and conference proceedings. The material draws upon works by the first author alongside researchers from the University of Duisburg-Essen, University of Duisburg, and University of Siegen. This study investigates the properties of nuclear substance at zero temperature under intense magnetic fields using the LOCV (Landau Orbit Covariant Expansion) framework. By solving the gap equations derived from the energy per particle, we determine the magnetic field-dependent energy and momentum. Our results indicate that the LOCV-based equation of state aligns with empirical data. Furthermore, we observe that the compressible equation of state remains valid even at extremely high densities, while the magnetic field's influence on the momentum is significant only at very high densities. Additionally, we find that the LOCV method successfully predicts the energy of nuclear matter without relying on the magnetic moment. Finally, the calculated energy and momentum exhibit reasonable sensitivity to the values of the coupling constants. These findings suggest that the LOCV approach is highly effective for analyzing nuclear substance in magnetic fields, particularly at very high densities. Future research will extend this work to finite temperatures. This study was conducted within the framework of the HEDP (High Energy Density Physics) laboratory at IIT Roorkee. The LOCV method is widely used in nuclear physics to model nuclear matter under extreme conditions, such as those found in neutron stars. This study introduces a new privacy-preserving federated learning algorithm called DP-REC, which employs a randomized feature selection technique to lower the noise variance added during the training phase. We analyze the privacy guarantees of this method using differential privacy theory and evaluate its performance against existing approaches in image classification tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that DP-REC surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior accuracy while demanding less communication bandwidth. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of the number of features on the algorithm's performance and privacy levels. The findings indicate a strong correlation between privacy and model accuracy, suggesting that reducing the feature selection probability enhances privacy but may compromise accuracy. These results provide valuable insights for optimizing hyperparameter configurations in practical deployments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Deepak-Prasad/DP-REC. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) imaging observations of the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga (TAP) region using the FUV Imaging Spectrograph (FIS) aboard the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE). These observations successfully identified 15 previously unknown FUV sources, designated FIS16 through FIS30, within Taurus. The sources range in FUV flux from $10^{-15}$ to $10^{-13}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ and possess estimated distances of 140 pc. Their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) are characterized by a lack of strong emission below 1500 \AA, a steep rise in flux between 1500 and 2200 \AA, and a flux decline at wavelengths exceeding 2200 \AA. These spectral characteristics indicate that the sources are likely young stellar objects (YSOs) with masses between 0.1 and 10 solar masses, along with substantial amounts of neutral hydrogen. Furthermore, FIS30 is likely a binary system composed of two YSOs. This study confirms that FUV sources are a significant component of the Taurus region, with a total population of at least 100. Their spectral characteristics align with those observed in other FUV sources in Taurus and across the entire TAP region. Additionally, we observed FUV emission from the reflection nebula surrounding the Herbig Ae/Be star HD 28298 (TWA 5) and the reflection nebula surrounding the Herbig Ae star HD 2910 (TWA 10). These observations demonstrate that FUV sources are not limited to YSOs but also include reflected FUV radiation. Finally, we present a newly created catalog of 105 FUV sources in Taurus, including 15 newly discovered ones, and compare their spectral characteristics with those of YSOs. The comparison reveals that the majority of FUV sources in Taurus are YSOs. However, further research is required to determine the nature of the remaining sources. This study significantly expands the existing catalog of FUV sources in Taurus, thereby enhancing our understanding of the spectral characteristics of the region. Ultimately, the spectral characteristics of FUV sources in Taurus can be used to investigate the nature of the sources and the physical properties of the region. Cognitive domains are frequently interdependent, prompting the need for sequential decision-making structures like games. However, existing literature has largely focused on single-domain games or sequential structures characterized by complete information and perfect rationality. In contrast, this study examines sequential decision-making environments where agents operate across multiple cognitive domains with imperfect information and limited computational capacity. We introduce a multi-phase game framework and assess four distinct levels of cognitive sophistication. Our analysis of this hierarchy reveals that the optimal strategy for each level can be derived from the solution to the next higher level. Furthermore, we investigate how the optimal strategies and resulting payoffs evolve as agents ascend through these cognitive levels. Finally, we apply this multi-level game model to a dynamic pricing scenario involving multiple products. By analyzing this application, we demonstrate that the level of cognitive sophistication significantly impacts both strategic choices and financial outcomes. Ultimately, this work offers a novel framework for analyzing the sequential cognitive processes inherent in complex decision-making environments.

Population and health surveys serve as the primary method for determining health indicators in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). These surveys, which rely on field enumerators to map and estimate the health status of all individuals within defined areas, are particularly vital for LMICs due to the absence of reliable census data. This study examines the sustainability of implementing such surveys in settings where specialized expertise is scarce. Through an action research project involving the Mozambique Ministry of Health, we developed a survey estimation system utilizing machine learning. The model was trained on geospatial data from two recent surveys conducted by the Ministry of Health, which included information on household characteristics and the presence of people. We assessed the model's performance on held-out data and compared its predictions against census figures. The results indicate that the estimator achieved a 95% accuracy rate in estimating population counts across various administrative levels. However, the practical application of this system within the Ministry of Health faces significant challenges, including a lack of technical skills, high costs, and substantial time requirements. These findings underscore the necessity for sustainable solutions in LMICs, emphasizing the critical role of stakeholder engagement throughout the entire project lifecycle. We conclude by offering several recommendations to enhance sustainability in LMIC machine learning initiatives. This paper introduces EMQ, a novel collection class designed to eliminate false positives while maintaining minimal overhead for inclusions. EMQ leverages the concept of membership queries, which determine if an element belongs to a collection without revealing the actual members. While exact membership queries are difficult to estimate due to the NP-hard complexity of the minimum set cover problem, the authors propose a new filter family called EMQ that can be automatically derived from any member generator. This design allows EMQ to avoid false positives by training on an infinite set of known non-members. The authors present an automatic construction algorithm for the filter and demonstrate EMQ's effectiveness across various applications, including code obfuscation, data structures, and IP blocking. The method achieves near-perfect precision and within 1% recall compared to the optimal solution, all while requiring only 10% more space than standard bitsets. Furthermore, the paper provides a theoretical analysis of EMQ's performance regarding time complexity, space complexity, and the distribution of non-zero entries. Finally, the authors discuss how EMQ can be extended to become a probabilistic member filter. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/256colors/EMQ. The molecule-atom dimerization concept, originally developed for electronic systems, is extended here to neutral atoms. This approach transforms two free atomic degrees of freedom into one molecular and one atomic degree of freedom through the creation of a molecular degree of freedom. In this study, we achieve dimerization in a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate using an anharmonic potential generated by a third atom within a three-body recombination process. This method offers a new avenue for exploring dynamics in interacting bosonic systems with an effective nonlocal dimerization Hamiltonian. Additionally, we analyze potential applications in spinor superfluids with extended s-wave interactions, which can be modeled using contact-plus-ramp potentials. These findings are particularly relevant for investigating the interplay between spin- and orbital-ordering transitions in such systems. Finally, we propose a novel technique for generating spin imbalances in spinor Bose-Einstein condensates by preparing non-equilibrium states with an imbalance in the population of different spin components. This technique is demonstrated via quantum simulations of spin-imbalance relaxation in a spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensate of $^{87}$Rb, where we observe a relaxation mechanism driven by spin-wave excitations. The resulting spin-imbalance relaxation dynamics are well-described by a Hamiltonian that includes spin-exchange interactions, density-dependent chemical potential, and an anisotropic interaction term. Furthermore, we show that preparing initial states with a finite imbalance in the $m_F=0$ spin component can be achieved by carefully selecting laser detunings and Rabi frequencies. This ability to control spin imbalances could offer a new method for investigating spin dynamics in spinor Bose-Einstein condensates. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these findings in quantum simulation research. Specifically, we demonstrate that this technique can be utilized to prepare initial states with a molecular degree of freedom, thereby enabling the investigation of bosonic-fermionic dimerization in fermionic systems. Additionally, the technique can be applied to study the interplay between spin- and orbital-ordering transitions in spinor Bose-Einstein condensates. Finally, the technique can be used to generate spin imbalances in spinor Bose-Einstein condensates, thereby opening up new avenues for research on spin dynamics in spinor Bose-Einstein condensates. In conclusion, the technique can be used to prepare initial states with a molecular degree of freedom, thereby enabling the investigation of bosonic-fermionic dimerization in fermionic systems. This paper introduces a new framework designed to investigate fluid-structure and fluid-fluid interactions within compressible flows. The approach integrates two distinct SPH variants: the Compressible SPH (CSPH) for fluid phases and the Projected-SPH (PSPH) for structural phases. To simulate fluid-fluid interactions, the method employs a unified kernel density function that allows both liquid and gaseous phases to utilize the same particle set while maintaining distinct thermodynamic states. The solid phase is modeled using a collection of rigid bodies. Validation against established benchmarks confirms the accuracy of the proposed model. The study presents three applications: a fluid-fluid interaction scenario where gas and liquid phases interact; a fluid-structure interaction involving a liquid column impacting a rigid wall; and a fluid-structure case featuring a liquid jet impacting a flexible plate. These results demonstrate the potential of the framework to enable complex multi-phase fluid-structure interactions. Furthermore, the method is applied to investigate the free-surface deformation of a liquid jet impacting a flexible plate, revealing dynamic behaviors such as jet deflection, splashing, and the formation of a liquid sheet. Finally, the jet deflection phenomenon is analyzed in detail, and the influence of the plate's initial configuration on the system's dynamics is examined. The findings indicate that the plate's initial deflection can be controlled by adjusting the nozzle-to-plate distance. Additionally, the results show that the plate's initial deflection is minimal when the plate is positioned far from the nozzle. However, the plate's deflection increases as the nozzle moves closer to the plate's centerline. The proposed framework is anticipated to facilitate the study of various complex fluid-structure interaction problems. Machine learning is rapidly expanding, yet it faces challenges from data heterogeneity and bias. Although quantum computing offers a potential alternative approach, it has not yet been fully explored in this domain. This study addresses data bias and heterogeneity through unmonitored and instructed quantum learning. Using superconducting quantum processors, we executed a quantum unmonitored learning protocol to detect whether input data represented cats or dogs. Subsequently, we implemented an instructed quantum learning protocol on the same processor, where cat images were input, and the system was trained to output data indicating dog characteristics. These experiments demonstrate that both unmonitored and instructed quantum learning are feasible on current superconducting processors. Furthermore, within the application scope, these methods offer a solution to issues such as data bias and heterogeneity. Future research will expand these approaches to more complex tasks, such as quantum natural language processing. Ultimately, quantum unmonitored and instructed learning on superconducting processors holds significant potential for addressing fundamental problems in machine learning. FastPitch is a neural sequence-to-sequence model designed for high-quality speech synthesis that maintains efficient inference by predicting speech directly from mel-spectrograms. It utilizes a pitch track as prior information during inference to control speech intonation. While Timbre-Preserving Pitch Augmentation (TPPA) is an effective method for enhancing pitch tracks, directly applying it as the pitch track input in FastPitch can result in degraded speech quality. This issue stems from the fact that FastPitch's encoder, which relies on quantized vocoded pitch tracks, is sensitive to pitch track accuracy. Consequently, this sensitivity causes the encoder to lose essential timbre information, thereby reducing the model's pitch controllability. To address this, we propose a novel fastpitch model featuring TPPA, termed FastPitch+TPPA, which separates timbre and pitch components to ensure the timbre is preserved within the generated output. This model employs an auxiliary loss to enhance timbre preservation and utilizes a timbre extractor to refine the quality of the pitch track. Experimental results demonstrate that FastPitch+TPPA achieves superior timbre preservation and pitch controllability compared to the baseline FastPitch, without compromising speech intelligibility. This study introduces Hopper, a general multi-hop framework designed for reasoning within image-based spatiotemporal contexts. By accepting a question in natural language, Hopper decomposes it into several intermediate tasks, including object detection, relation identification, and object re-detection. The framework constructs these tasks using state-of-the-art deep neural networks and addresses challenges related to object occlusion and dynamic movement through object tracking and object localization modules. Evaluated on two public datasets, Hopper demonstrates robust performance in handling multi-hop queries. Furthermore, the study explores intermediate task visualization to enhance interpretability and extends the framework to multi-hop reasoning based on this visualization. The CMS experiment at the LHC investigates the production of lepton pairs alongside $b\bar{b}$ pairs in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. This analysis utilizes data from 2016 and 2017, encompassing an integrated luminosity of 14 fb$^{-1}$, to probe potential new physics. Specifically, the mass of the $W$ boson is determined by examining the $m_{\mathrm{T2}}$ mass variable, which arises from the transverse masses of the two visible leptons. The resulting $m_{\mathrm{T2}}$ distribution is fitted using Monte Carlo simulations normalized to the observed total event count. The $W$ boson mass is extracted from the peak of this fit, yielding a value of $80.77\pm 0.51$ GeV. This measurement aligns with the Particle Data Group average of $80.385\pm 0.015$ GeV, with the dominant uncertainty arising from jet energy calibration. Additionally, the production cross section for $W$ bosos in association with $b$ quarks is measured at $\sigma(pp\rightarrow W+b\bar{b}X) = 13.2\pm 0.6$ pb. This result is consistent with predictions from the CTEQ6.6 and MMHT11 parton distribution functions but shows a 1.6$\sigma$ discrepancy from ASAT parton distributions. Furthermore, the study examines the production cross section for $t\bar{t}$ events decaying into the lepton+$b\bar{b}+X$ channel. The measured cross section of $326\pm 10$ pb agrees with ASAT, MMHT11, and CTEQ6.6 predictions within 1.5% but deviates from MiNNLOPP and Powheg-Pythia6 predictions by 1.6$\sigma$ and 2.1$\sigma$, respectively. Finally, a new search for supersymmetry is presented, focusing on the production of $W$ bosons in association with gluinos. No significant excess over the background-only hypothesis was observed, leading to lower limits on gluino masses of 1,000 GeV at 95% confidence level for all considered models. Telepresence robots (TPRs) serve as effective tools for remote human-agent interaction, yet their limited and constrained visual interfaces can degrade the experience for users seeking to control them. This study systematically investigates how specific TPR design elements—such as field-of-view (FOV) management, navigation speed, and motion smoothness—affect user productivity and quality of experience. By integrating subjective assessments from 18 participants with objective metrics from computer vision applied to 20 participants, we demonstrate that specific design parameters significantly influence performance outcomes. Our findings indicate that optimizing these control design aspects can substantially enhance both the efficiency of remote operations and the satisfaction of the user. Ultimately, the research demonstrates that evaluating design parameters through a multi-faceted approach yields a more comprehensive understanding of TPR performance than relying solely on subjective or objective measures. This knowledge is critical for developing and optimizing future TPR technologies. The experimental datasets will be made available to support further research and evaluation. This paper offers a gentle introduction to Bayesian hierarchical linear models (BMLM), a statistical method widely used in the social sciences for analyzing grouped data. The analysis examines whether high school attendance influences the probability of obtaining a university degree. Because students attend high schools in an aggregated manner, individual high school attendance rates exert a significant influence on degree outcomes. To account for this, a Bayesian hierarchical model is employed, which allows for the estimation of individual-level effects of high school attendance on university degrees while simultaneously accounting for the group-level influence of high school attendance rates. The study demonstrates how Bayesian modeling facilitates the calculation of the posterior distribution for model parameters and how hierarchical modeling enables the inference of group-specific parameter values. Furthermore, the paper illustrates how these models can be utilized to determine the probability that high school attendance positively impacts the likelihood of earning a university degree. The discussion begins with an overview of Bayesian modeling and its advantages within the social sciences, followed by an explanation of linear regression and grouped data. Finally, the hierarchical Bayesian linear model is applied to analyze the relationship between high school attendance and university degrees. The motivation for this work stems from my experience as a high school teacher, where I am deeply committed to the belief that attendance significantly boosts the likelihood of students achieving university degrees. Additionally, my interest lies in the application of Bayesian methods in education, where hierarchical modeling proves particularly valuable. This framework allows teachers to assess the impact of attendance on each student's degree prospects while also evaluating how individual attendance rates affect the success of every specific student. I hope this motivation inspires readers to explore these models in their own educational contexts. The first section of the paper provides a pedagogical introduction to Bayesian hierarchical linear models, while the second section applies this approach to the question of whether high school attendance increases the probability of securing a university degree. The analysis is supported by Jupyter Notebooks, which are available on my GitHub repository. Additionally, the Jupyter Notebooks can be accessed via Binder, allowing users to run the analysis directly in their browser without installing any software. Mafia is a well-known party game where participants act out roles such as Mafia members, villagers, and doctors. These roles vary in capabilities; for instance, doctors can prevent criminal killings, while seers can identify specific players. Groups then compete to achieve their objectives: the Mafia and its allies aim to eliminate all villagers, whereas villagers must discover and eliminate them. This paper introduces a numerical model of the game to simulate scenarios that are difficult to play or that reveal strategies and tactics used to deduce identities. Our model tracks individual and collective knowledge, allowing agents to act based on their perceptions. We observe that when mafia presence is low, the village can easily identify and destroy the mafia. Conversely, when the mafia is strong, the village struggles to distinguish between players, leading to self-inflicted damage. Additionally, we demonstrate that even a single seer can significantly aid the village in eliminating the mafia. Finally, we show that doctors can effectively protect the village by eliminating mafia members. These findings are supported by both theoretical analysis and experimental results. To our knowledge, this is the first time a Mafia game has been modeled in this manner. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/SepehrJavadi/numerical-model-of-Mafia. We conducted 2D hydrodynamical simulations to examine the gas accretion dynamics of two massive planets ($M_{\rm p} \simeq 100\,\mathrm{M_{\rm J}}$) located at approximately 1.5 and 2.5 au from their host star. These simulations modeled a phase where the initial gas disk was evolving toward the mid-plane, driven by the settling of dust grains. Our findings indicate that the system accumulated a total mass of $\simeq 1.5\,\mathrm{M_{\rm J}}$ of hydrogen and helium during a brief interval of roughly 1000 years. This short timescale corresponds to the phase where the two planets shared a common accretion disk, a configuration characterized by a pronounced density peak between them. We demonstrate that the presence of this density peak significantly enhanced gas accretion onto the planets by an order of magnitude. Furthermore, we show that the entire system's mass is partitioned as follows: the host star ($M_{\rm *}$) comprises 99.5%, the planets ($M_{\rm p}$) account for 0.4%, and the disk ($M_{\rm d}$) makes up the remaining 0.1%. These results suggest that the formation of multi-planet systems with masses around 100 $\mathrm{M_{\rm J}}$ requires a substantial gas disk mass, and that the presence of a density peak between the planets is crucial for the rapid accretion of a significant fraction of the disk material onto them. Finally, we conclude that our findings provide a viable explanation for the massive nature of the planets in the HD 106906 system. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the migration of the outer companion (HD 106966 c) from 400 au to its current position of 650 au requires a large amount of disk mass, which can be naturally explained by the accumulation of mass in the region between the planets. The electronic behavior of multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) is governed by two primary mechanisms: electron tunneling within and between the individual tubes of each wall, and electron tunneling between the different nested cylinders. This study presents the first experimental validation of a phonon-assisted pathway enabling electrons to traverse the gaps between the walls of a single solid MWCNT. This specific mechanism involves the simultaneous disruption of the quantum states of the nested cylinders through phonon activity, allowing electrons to move between the cylinders of an MWCNT. This phenomenon was identified by analyzing the temperature-dependent transport characteristics of a MWCNT-based device, where the transition between the phonon-assisted and direct electronic regimes was observed to shift as the contact with an MWCNT changed from a metallic to a semiconducting contact. The findings are consistent with an analytical model describing electron tunneling between armchair cylinders of a MWCNT. These results offer a novel perspective on the physics of MWCNTs and may facilitate the development of new phonon-assisted quantum devices. Furthermore, this research may provide insights into the electronic properties of other nanostructures involving carbon nanotubes. This study introduces a novel fuzzy clustering technique designed for high-dimensional data, termed the Weighted Fuzzy k-Means (WFKM) method. Drawing inspiration from Entropy Weighted k-Means (EWKM), WFKM assigns variable weights to features based on their information content, thereby enhancing the clustering process. The method is grounded in the Fuzzy k-Means (FKM) framework, which has been extended to allow for individual feature weighting. We have developed an optimization strategy utilizing the Majorization-Minimization (MM) approach, demonstrating its equivalence to the original FKM optimization method. Furthermore, an efficient initialization algorithm has been designed to significantly accelerate the WFKM method. Experimental results indicate that WFKM outperforms FKM in clustering high-dimensional data and shows promising potential for application in bioinformatics. Additionally, the method demonstrates robust performance across various datasets, including low-dimensional, high-dimensional, and sparse data. The WFKM method has been implemented in C++ and is available as open-source software at https://github.com/ChenYi1993/WFKM. Future research will explore extensions of WFKM for clustering complex data structures, such as network and graph data. Finally, the method's applicability in other fields, including image processing, will be investigated. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYi1993/WFKM. Keywords: Fuzzy Clustering, Feature Weighting, High-Dimensional Data.

The mixture-of-experts (MoE) framework is increasingly popular in machine learning, offering a way to integrate diverse expert models for robust predictions. However, determining the number of components in an MoE remains a difficult challenge. This paper addresses that issue by presenting a novel statistical dead-lock-breaking mechanism. We introduce two new algorithms, the Deadlock-Aware MoE (DA-MoE) and the Adaptive DA-MoE (ADA-MoE), which can be derived from hierarchical expert models. DA-MoE operates in an online setting, while ADA-MoE functions as a batch algorithm. Both methods achieve constant regret under relatively mild assumptions. Additionally, we propose a statistical consistency test to identify when an MoE model is necessary. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithms outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, we apply these methods to various real-world datasets to estimate the optimal number of MoE components and to cluster real-world data. The code is available at https://github.com/zhongtao2000/DA-MoE. Finally, we release the data used in this study at https://github.com/zhongtao2000/MoE-Data. This study examines the phenomenology of quantum gravity effects on photon polarization. We analyze data from the Planck satellite regarding the global disruption of spacetime symmetry, specifically addressing potential violations in quantum gravity frameworks. Our investigation focuses on parity-odd couplings between photons and a graviton within quantum field theory, utilizing a model where gravitons possess a small mass. We assess constraints on the disconnection and violation of global quantum spacetime symmetry based on the Planck polarization dataset. We estimate the binary rotation angle of polarized light generated by these parity-odd interactions and determine the resulting limits on the binary amplitude. Furthermore, we examine the sensitivity of the global disruption of quantum spacetime symmetry to the graviton mass. Finally, we outline future research directions concerning this symmetry violation, the mass of quantum spacetime symmetry, and the associated phenomenology. This research contributes to the broader effort of defining the phenomenology of quantum spacetime. This work examines the connections between three mathematical principles: a variant of Bourbaki's and Mumford's (pseudo-)effectivity criteria, a modified version of the $b$-principle, and the intersection theory of moduli spaces of curves. A key component of the proposed solution is the Mumford pseudo-Kodaira vanishing theorem, which can be viewed as a form of effectivity. The relationship between effectivity and vanishing constitutes one of the three primary relationships established. Additionally, the paper explores the link between effectivity and pseudo-Mumford effectivity, noting that this relationship is somewhat tenuous. The analysis begins with an examination of effectivity prior to delving into these intricate relationships. To provide context, the paper also examines related effectivity principles, including the Andreotti-Frankel principle, the $G$-effectivity of Gruson and Lazarsfeld, the $K$-effectivity of Eisenbud and Greene, and the $L$-effectivity of Ein. Furthermore, the role of semi-ampleness in these principles is examined. The structure of this paper was influenced by a question posed by David Mumford regarding the relationship between effectivity and vanishing. Although the authors do not claim to resolve this relationship, they outline the existing relationships and offer a partial answer. The paper concludes with a discussion of the interplay between vanishing and semi-ampleness. A deep learning model's transferability is fundamentally grounded in two principles: (1) task irrelevance, meaning transfer occurs regardless of the target task, and (2) knowledge transfer, where model knowledge is believed to be shared between source and target domains. However, we challenge the second principle, arguing that transferability stems from two distinct forms of knowledge transfer: cross-domain knowledge transfer (aligning source and target domains) and cross-task knowledge transfer (transfer between tasks without requiring domain alignment). We redefine transferability based on these two agreements and demonstrate empirically that cross-task transfer more effectively enhances performance than cross-domain transfer. Furthermore, we propose a unified transfer learning framework utilizing domain-adversarial training to simultaneously enable both cross-domain and cross-task transfer, which surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. The code and experimental results are available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYiLi97/UDL}. Our findings hold significant practical value, particularly in resource-constrained scenarios, as they allow independent deployment of tasks and domains, thereby eliminating the need for costly domain adaptation processes. The Standard Perturbation Model (SPM) within the time-domain S-parameter framework offers a method for analyzing nonlinear distortion in links, including memory effects. In unamplified links, these memory effects originate from the dispersion characteristics of the physical media. Previous research on the SPM in the time-domain focused exclusively on bandwidth-limited, non-memory-dependent scenarios. This paper extends the SPM precision analysis to unamplified links that exhibit memory effects. The proposed approach utilizes the autocorrelation function of the medium to define a precision metric, termed the precision bandwidth. This metric quantifies the extent of memory and serves as a practical tool for estimating the necessary length of the SPM impulse response. Furthermore, the impact of sampling jitter on distortion analysis is examined, and a memory-dependent precision metric for sampling is introduced. Simulation results validate the accuracy of this analysis. The study demonstrates that the medium's autocorrelation function is pivotal in precision analysis and reveals that memory effects can significantly degrade both precision bandwidth and sampling precision. Consequently, accounting for memory is essential when analyzing distortion in unamplified links. The developed methodology is applicable to various nonlinear distortion models in the time-domain, such as the Volterra series. Finally, an example application to chirp analysis in optical fiber links is provided. This case study illustrates how the proposed analysis can determine the optimal sampling rate for chirp analysis and estimate the memory depth of the equivalent SPM impulse response. The findings indicate that memory effects can substantially influence chirp analysis, thereby affecting the selection of the appropriate sampling rate. Additionally, the significant memory depth in optical fibers can be attributed to the fiber's group delay dispersion. The results also show that a group delay dispersion of $1 \text{ ps}^2/\text{km}$ can generate a memory depth of approximately $100 \text{ km}$ in a $10 \text{ Gbit/s}$ signal. This insight is valuable for designing optical fiber communication systems, particularly in the C-band where dispersion is minimal. Furthermore, this example highlights the critical role of the precision analysis metric in model precision evaluation. In contrast, choosing the sampling rate based on the proposed chirp precision metric ensures accurate peak-to-peak nonlinear distortion analysis. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the Issue-Space Evasion Assault (ISEA) within the Android operating system. Android's security architecture relies primarily on two mechanisms: the SandBoxing Defense (SBD), which restricts inter-process communication, and the Capability-Based Defense (CBD), which governs kernel access. However, existing research has predominantly concentrated on SBD, largely overlooking vulnerabilities in CBD. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Capability-Based Deception (CBD), which involves tricking the kernel into granting specific capabilities to malicious applications. We systematically categorize current capabilities and assaults targeting CBD, examine their limitations, and analyze the potential for SBD to be bypassed as a consequence of CBD strategies. Furthermore, we outline several novel ISEA categories that extend beyond prior work, supported by 10 newly discovered issues serving as proof-of-concept demonstrations. Finally, we propose future research directions aimed at enhancing Android's security posture. We anticipate that this study will deepen the understanding of ISEA and guide subsequent kernel-focused capabilities-based assaults. Additionally, we believe this work will encourage further investigation into Android's security architecture, thereby fostering a more resilient mobile ecosystem. To our knowledge, this represents the most thorough examination of CBD and ISEA to date. All code and data related to this study can be accessed at https://github.com/2022-CBD-Impact/Android-Impact. We introduce an incompressible phase diagram for the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall phase at the $\nu=2$ spin-polarized Landau level, derived from the second-order effective Hamiltonian of the pseudospin model proposed by Bernevig and Zhang. By adjusting the Landau-level-coupling strength, we demonstrate a reentrant phase where the reentrance point relies on the specific type of reentrant phase. Utilizing the exact diagonalization of a 36-site cluster, we confirm that the reentrant phase corresponds to a reentrant topological superconducting state. Furthermore, we establish that this topological superconductivity is driven by a real-space charge density wave. Finally, we calculate the entanglement spectrum, revealing that its structure aligns with that of the Moore-Read state. These findings indicate that the pseudospirituation, resulting from Landau-level mixing, is the fundamental origin of the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall phase. Additionally, the presence of reentrant topological superconductivity offers a viable explanation for the observed reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall phase in experimental Hall bar experiments. This study provides a theoretical basis for investigating the 5/2 quantum Hall phase using realistic experimental techniques. Specifically, measuring the entanglement spectrum in a quantum dot and detecting reentrant quantum Hall phases through mesoscopic devices can offer compelling evidence for the validity of the pseudospirituation model. These approaches are expected to be feasible with advancements in nanofabrication technology. We anticipate that these proposals will stimulate experimental efforts to verify the theoretical predictions regarding the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall phase. Finally, our results offer a promising avenue for developing new quantum computing technologies based on Majorana zero modes. In particular, the reentrant topological superconductivity could enable the creation of Majorana zero modes at the interface of two superconductors with opposite superconducting phases. This proposal can be tested using a Josephson junction, providing a straightforward method to detect Majorana zero modes and advance quantum computing research. We hope these theoretical suggestions will inspire experimental efforts to explore the reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall phase and to investigate Majorana zero modes, thereby advancing the field of quantum computing. Cosmological black holes, including those of a primordial nature, are frequently described in the literature using the Thakurta metric, which represents a spherically symmetric solution to Einstein's equations featuring a black hole at the origin and uniform mass density throughout space. However, this work demonstrates that such a description is invalid because the physical conditions required to generate this solution are inconsistent with the cosmological model. Specifically, the Thakurta solution requires a universe that is both homogeneous and isotropic outside the black hole, contradicting the singularity present at the center of this metric. Furthermore, we examine the constraints LIGO-Virgo imposes on the mass function of potential primordial black hole populations, demonstrating that these limits are independent of any cosmological description of individual black holes. Consequently, the recent LIGO-Virgo restrictions on primordial black hole mass functions remain applicable and unaffected. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the cosmological abundance of black holes. Our analysis indicates that, absent any additional properties, the abundance of black holes is constrained by the requirement that their total density not exceed the critical density of the universe. This yields an upper bound on the fraction of black holes, $\frac{f_{bh}}{M_{\odot}\rho_{cr}} \leq 1.2 \times 10^{50} M^{-1}$, which aligns with previous results derived from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and LIGO-Virgo data. Additionally, we note that the Thakurta metric implies a specific relationship between the black hole mass function and the critical density, suggesting that the fraction of the critical density contributed by black holes is approximately 1.2 times the ratio of the black hole mass function to that critical density. This leads to the conclusion that the total mass density of black holes in the universe is roughly equal to the critical density. However, this conclusion is only valid if the assumptions underlying the Thakurta metric solution are met. Therefore, we cannot definitively assert that the mass density of black holes equals the critical density, as this would imply a closed universe, whereas observational evidence strongly supports a flat universe. Instead, we can only state that the density of black holes is bounded by the critical density. We also examine the consequences of this conclusion for the Thakurta metric solution. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the primordial density fluctuations and the formation of primordial black holes. Accretion of dust and pebbles is widely regarded as the primary mechanism for forming planetesimals and planetary cores. Recent research indicates that planet formation via pebble accretion is closely tied to the radial migration of dust and pebble belts, which is governed by the gas's density fluctuations. These density perturbations generate radial pressure gradients that drive dust and pebble rings to move inwards or outwards. In this study, we numerically investigate how these density fluctuations influence planet formation through pebble accumulation. Our results demonstrate that dust and pebble belts exhibit significant radial fluctuations driven by density perturbations in the gas. These fluctuations create a self-regulating mechanism that stabilizes the peak radial width of pebble belts over time. Furthermore, we find that the maximum planetesimal mass formed is highly sensitive to the amplitude of density fluctuations, with a strong anti-correlation observed between the two. This suggests that planetesimal formation is inherently unstable with respect to density fluctuations, a factor that must be accounted for when interpreting exoplanet mass distributions. Additionally, we show that the migration speed of pebble belts is also affected by these density fluctuations, leading to a similar conclusion. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the evolution of exoplanetary systems. Specifically, we find that the peak radial width of pebble belts and the planetesimal mass formed are anti-correlated with the amplitude of density fluctuations, a relationship that can be used to interpret the current gas giant mass distributions. Overall, our findings indicate that gas density fluctuations play a critical role in planet formation. Future research should aim to incorporate the effects of these fluctuations into planet formation models. In this work, we have established a foundation for such future studies. Specifically, we have developed a pebble accretion model that incorporates the effects of dust and pebble density fluctuations, which is available for public use. This model will be utilized in future research to investigate the impact of density fluctuations on planet formation. We believe that accounting for density fluctuations in density fluctuation models will be essential for a more comprehensive understanding of planet formation. We hope that this work will inspire further research in this area. Our findings suggest that gas density fluctuations are crucial to planet formation, and we have provided a framework for this consideration. We believe that incorporating density fluctuations into models will lead to a more complete understanding of the planet formation process. We hope that our work will encourage future research to account for these fluctuations. Our results indicate that gas density fluctuations are important, and we have established a basis for considering them.

This work demonstrates that significant overparameterization also emerges from the inherent computational constraints of modeling and learning computable functions. Specifically, even when the target function is guaranteed to be simple, a learner may require an exponential number of samples to identify a simple equivalent function with high probability. Consequently, the learner is compelled to utilize a complex alternative that, although relying on a substantially larger hypothesis space, can be effectively trained with a polynomial sample complexity. We illustrate this phenomenon using finite automata, perceptrons, and circuits as hypothesis families, alongside decision trees and perceptrons as target families. Furthermore, our examples extend to more realistic scenarios involving input and output noise. We also present a positive result concerning concept classes that are easy to learn in the exact setting but necessitate complex hypotheses even under a relatively relaxed sample complexity requirement. Finally, we show that allowing the hypothesis space to be only approximately equivalent to the target space can mitigate the sample complexity issues described in this study. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical role of computational constraints in shaping the trade-offs between sample complexity and the complexity of the resulting learned representations. Additionally, our examples offer further insights into the relationships among exact learnability, statistical learnability, and sample-complexity-qualified learnability. From a purely statistical perspective, this research may also advance the understanding of representation complexity. In this work, we address the question of whether simple targets necessitate complex hypotheses. We present examples where the answer is negative, yet we conjecture that complexity is generally required. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the converse of this statement does not hold. Additionally, we suggest that the exact learning capacity of concept classes can be quantified by the computational resources needed to construct circuits that map inputs to the most probable output labels. This computational framework for learning offers a novel avenue for understanding the capabilities of concept classes. This paper introduces a Branch-and-Trim algorithm designed to address static dial-a-ride problems in large metropolitan areas, focusing on two core challenges: generating initial feasible solutions and enforcing driver and passenger constraints. Driver-related constraints are managed through a dynamic two-relaxation approach, whereas passenger constraints are addressed by transforming the problem into a variant of the Multi-Depot Open Vehicle Routing Problem (OVRP), which is subsequently solved using state-of-the-art heuristics. The algorithm was tested on both randomly generated instances and real-world data from the "Punto a Punto" service operated by the municipality of Rome, Italy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can solve instances involving hundreds of requests within minutes, yielding optimal solutions for small instances and high-quality results for large ones. Furthermore, the method achieves an average reduction of 15% in total driving time and 11% in cost compared to various existing heuristics. Finally, the computational performance of the algorithm was evaluated in a large-scale context. For the "Punto a a Punto" dataset comprising 1,000 requests, the method achieved an average cost reduction of 14.5% relative to a widely used heuristic. These findings underscore the algorithm's potential to facilitate the operational management of dial-a-ride services. Additionally, the paper provides a novel definition for the "dial-a-ride ratio," a key performance metric in this domain, and reports an average ratio of 1.75 achieved by the proposed algorithm. This represents a 10% improvement over the best available solution in the literature, highlighting the method's effectiveness. The authors have also developed a software tool to validate these results, which is made available to the research community. To the best of our knowledge, this tool represents the first software solution for dial-a-ride problems that integrates both driver and passenger constraints. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/AndreaCocchi/p2p_dial-a-ride. Finally, the study concludes by discussing potential extensions of the algorithm to handle dynamic dial-a-ride scenarios. Source code: https://github.com/AndreaCocchi/p2p_dial-a-ride. Keywords: Dial-a-Ride, Urban Mobility, Heuristics, Operational Management, Software Tool.

This paper introduces a new architecture for interpreting language semantics utilizing modern deep neural networks. Our model employs a two-layer recurrent neural network (RNN) where the initial layer processes input word embeddings to generate feature representations, which are subsequently fed into the second layer to derive semantic representations. We evaluate various preprocessing techniques for the first layer and explore diverse loss functions to optimize the second layer. Experimental results demonstrate that our Two-layer RNN (TRLN) model surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in multiple tasks, including Sentiment Analysis (SANTAN), Question-Answer Matching (QAM), and Question-Keyword Interpretation (KKI). Furthermore, TRLN exhibits robustness and stability across different datasets and preprocessing configurations. Finally, we illustrate how the TRLN model can be customized for specific applications by adapting its architecture and loss functions to meet task-specific requirements. Spin-orbit interaction (SOI) is a vital element in spintronics, a field that leverages this quantum mechanical phenomenon to manipulate electron spin for data processing. In spin-based logic circuits, strong SOI enables the conversion of spin polarization into a detectable voltage via the inverse spin Hall effect. Within the framework of the $t$-$J$-model, we demonstrate a significant enhancement of SOI in strongly correlated systems by analyzing the single-particle spectral function. This increase in SOI strength correlates directly with the formation of spin singlets. Our findings indicate that strongly correlated oxides, such as nickel oxide, are promising candidates for developing novel spintronic devices capable of achieving superior performance. The theoretical model utilized in this study can be realized experimentally through cold-atom systems. (Preprint submitted to Phys. Rev.
