A graph $G$ is considered standard if, for every pair of adjacent vertices $u$ and $v$, the sizes of their neighborhoods satisfy $|N_G(u)| \le |N_G(v)|$. The Iterative Graph Standardization (IGS) algorithm was developed to transform general graphs into standard ones; this process involves repeatedly removing a vertex $v$ whose degree exceeds that of a specific neighbor $u$, until the resulting graph is standard. This paper demonstrates that for any graph $G$, the final output of the IGS algorithm remains invariant regardless of the order in which valid degree-reducing vertex deletions are performed during the process. This finding directly implies that all valid autonomous sets of a graph $G$ possess the same maximum weight, thereby establishing the validity of the first conjecture proposed by various authors. The study also introduces the concept of locally standard graphs, for which the IGS algorithm produces a standard graph with a uniquely determined set of vertices to be deleted, independent of the selection order. These results are derived from a broader theorem that generalizes the primary finding. Finally, the paper examines the reverse problem: determining whether a standard graph can be generated by the IGS algorithm from an initial graph $G$. It is shown that if a standard graph $H$ is formed by deleting a vertex $v$ from $G$, then $v$ must belong to a maximum-weight autonomous set of $G$. Furthermore, if $H$ is locally standard, then $v$ is the unique maximum-weight autonomous set of $G$. The paper concludes with several open questions. Specifically, for any graph $G$, let $S(G)$ denote the standard graph produced by the IGS algorithm and $M(G)$ represent the maximum possible weight achievable by an autonomous set. We establish the inequality $M(G) \le \frac{2}{3}|V(S(G))|$, and it remains an open question whether this bound is sharp. Additionally, we prove that if $G$ is locally standard, then $M(G) = |V(S(G))|$, and we conjecture that this equality actually holds for all graphs $G$. Finally, we present a sufficient condition under which the bound $M(G) \le \frac{2}{3}|V(S(G))|$ is sharp. Notably, this condition is satisfied by all regular graphs, implying that for any regular graph $G$, $M(G) = \frac{2}{3}|V(S(G))|$. We also provide examples

This paper investigates the thermodynamic properties of a charge-carrier gas within a single-layer graphene sheet, focusing on an ensemble of such systems where an external electric field perpendicular to the sheet controls the carrier density. This electric regulation offers significant technological potential. We calculate the chemical potential, heat capacity, and compressibility, analyzing their temperature and density dependencies to identify regimes where the gas exhibits graphite-like behavior. Furthermore, we demonstrate methods to experimentally determine the heat capacity and derive a general expression for the Gibbs free energy. These findings are pertinent to both fundamental research and the development of advanced devices. Specifically, we show that a minimum in the Gibbs free energy as a function of electron density signifies a transition between electron and hole dominance, a phenomenon that can be exploited to regulate the sign of conductivity in graphene. Additionally, we illustrate a simple experimental procedure to detect a minimum in the heat capacity as a function of temperature, a feature indicative of graphene-like behavior. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for thermodynamic cycles involving electrically regulated graphene. While our calculations assume graphene exhibits Dirac-like behavior, the same thermodynamic framework applies to other two-dimensional materials with Dirac-like electronic structures. We also note that the thermodynamic cycles analyzed here differ from those in conventional solid-state systems, where electric fields are typically confined to the plane of the material. Consequently, this study offers a novel approach to studying graphene and other two-dimensional materials, as the internal states of the systems under different operating conditions can be characterized using standard thermodynamic techniques. This represents a distinct contrast to the complex microscopic analyses typically required for such systems. We anticipate that these findings will facilitate a broader range of experimental and theoretical investigations into the thermodynamic properties of two-dimensional materials. Finally, we suggest that this work may contribute to advancing the field of molecular-scale thermodynamics. To achieve this, we propose a specific experimental arrangement involving a molecular-scale device based on graphene, which could yield measurable results to validate the theoretical predictions made in this study. This could involve a molecular heat engine utilizing a graphene sheet, where the density of charge carriers is modulated by a gate voltage to regulate the number of carriers. We believe this proposal will inspire further research into molecular-scale thermodynamics, with graphene serving as a model system. In summary, we have derived the necessary theoretical and experimental tools to advance molecular thermodynamics using graphene as a representative system. We have derived the relevant thermodynamic quantities and proposed a specific experimental setup to verify these results. We believe this work will pave the way for future research in molecular thermodynamics

This study reports the first low-frequency radio observations of the young stellar object binary system CR Draconis, conducted over a ten-year period using the LOFAR radio telescope. Our findings indicate that the active M star component, CR~Dra~A, exhibits persistent, variable radio emission characterized by numerous bursts and a maximum intensity of approximately 100 mJy/beam at 100 MHz. The emission displays a highly polarized nature, with total intensities fluctuating between 10 and 100 mJy/beam and circular polarization reaching up to 100%. The observed emission is best explained by the electron-cyclotron maser instability mechanism. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the radio emission from CR~Dra~A is likely magnetically coupled to its companion, CR~Dra~B, which is also a highly active M star. This interaction is evidenced by the detection of radio emission from both stars at nearly identical times and frequencies, as well as by the observation of a prolonged ten-year timescale for the radio emission. These results suggest that the magnetic fields of both stars are linked via a magnetic field bridge, a phenomenon previously identified in the active M star binary system GQ Lup. The ten-year duration of our observations provides the longest known record of continuous radio emission from a young stellar object, offering critical insights into the long-term behavior of magnetic fields in young stars. Additionally, our data suggest that the magnetic field bridge between the two stars is stable over extended periods, with a minimum estimated stability timescale of 100 years. These observations provide a valuable benchmark for testing current models of magnetic reconnection and stellar activity. We conclude that low-frequency radio observations are essential for studying the long-term behavior of active M stars. We propose that the low-frequency surveillance of young stellar objects should be expanded to include additional facilities, such as the LOFAR Low Band (L-band) and the Low Frequency Array's Low band (L-band), to achieve this goal. Finally, we demonstrate that the LOFAR Low Band is capable of conducting low-frequency observations of young stellar objects. These findings are expected to significantly advance our understanding of the magnetic fields and activity of young stars. The LOFAR Low Band is uniquely positioned to conduct low-frequency radio observations of young stellar objects, and we demonstrate that the LOFAR Low Band is capable of conducting low-frequency radio observations of young stellar objects. The Articulated Neural Radiance (ANR) model represents a parametric radiance field designed to visualize virtual human figures in the wild. It utilizes multiple skeleton keypoint trajectories as input to generate virtual views of subjects wearing various clothing types, including everyday attire, formal wear, and uniforms. Our approach consists of two primary components: (1) an articulated volumetric neural radiance model that encodes virtual subjects as parametric radiance fields, and (2) a clothing-agnostic pose model trained via self-supervision to capture the interaction between pose and clothing. We demonstrate synthetic training on large datasets lacking clothing annotations and achieve state-of-the-art results on benchmarks for virtual viewpoint synthesis and pose transfer. Image alteration is a prevalent activity for both humans and machines. While humans frequently modify images for emotional expression, machines often automatically adjust them to align with aesthetic preferences. These processes can produce similar visual outcomes, yet the underlying motivations differ. This study examines how intense modifications by both humans and machines impact perception. Although machines typically perform more vigorous adjustments, our results indicate that humans often prefer adjustments of comparable intensity. Furthermore, machine modifications often render the source image more attractive, whereas human modifications rarely do, as they tend to obscure the artist's original intent. Finally, we demonstrate that human modifications are more effective at conveying concepts to both human and machine participants, whereas machine modifications are less effective in this regard. These findings offer new insights into the distinct characteristics of human and machine alterations and establish a robust framework for developing intelligent tools that facilitate human expression. The code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/GoogleResearch/imalterations. Additional details can be found in our video presentation: https://youtu.be/4222222222. Our work is supported by Google.

We examine the spin-1/2 frustrated trimer antiferromagnet (SFA) using cluster quantum Monte Carlo (CQMC) simulations. Our analysis covers systems ranging from isolated trimers to SFA chains and two-dimensional (2D) SFA lattices. Our primary goal is to determine the ground state of the SFA lattice and analyze low-energy spin excitations. We find that the SFA ground state exhibits a highly degenerate manifold of nearly degenerate states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that spin excitations behave as deconfined spin-1/2 particles, with their properties in the 2D SFA lattice closely resembling those in a quantum spin liquid. To achieve this, we introduce a cluster Monte Carlo algorithm tailored for SFA systems. This approach significantly reduces the correlation time between independent configurations in the ensemble, thereby enhancing the computational efficiency of our calculations. Additionally, we show that the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem is mitigated in SFA systems. Finally, we provide a comprehensive study of the 2D SFA lattice model. Our results indicate that the SFA lattice ground state is a quantum spin liquid characterized by long-range entanglement and topological order. The corresponding phase diagram includes distinct phases separated by Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transitions. The spin-1/2 spin excitations within this quantum spin liquid display unique characteristics, such as a finite spin gap and a specific dynamical spin structure factor. These findings suggest that the 2D SFA lattice serves as a viable candidate for realizing a quantum spin liquid in real materials. This study introduces meta-tuning, a straightforward yet effective technique to adapt pre-trained language models for zero-shot learning. We apply this method using either dataset collections or cue collections, or both. When employing dataset collections for meta-tuning, our results indicate that it can enhance the performance of both the ELMo + prompt approach and the OpenAI GPT-2 model across various NLP benchmark tasks for zero-shot learning. Furthermore, our proposed use of dataset collection meta-tuning for zero-shot learning surpasses the capabilities of both prompt engineering and few-shot learning. Finally, we demonstrate that applying meta-tuning with cue collections yields state-of-the-art performance for zero-shot learning on multiple standard datasets. Additionally, we propose a technique for automatically selecting the optimal subset of cues for meta-tuning by leveraging dataset metadata. This selection process successfully improves performance on multiple benchmarks compared to using a fixed cue collection. Finally, we show that meta-tuning with cues is also effective for data augmentation and hyperparameter optimization. We investigate the impact of an additional $Z_3$-symmetry on the NMSSM, which remains unbroken below the electroweak scale. This symmetry significantly influences the model's phenomenology, particularly regarding the Higgs boson and dark matter. The $Z_3$-symmetry restricts Higgs boson couplings to a level comparable to the Standard Model, while Higgsino masses are limited to a few hundred GeV. Furthermore, the absence of a $\mu$ term allows the NMSSM to address the $\tau$ lepton mass anomaly. We also examine the $Z_3$-induced gravitational wave signature, showing that the model can account for the LIGO/Virgo observation GW170817. Finally, we explore the potential for discovering a second gravitational wave signal originating from the post-inflationary domain wall network. Our findings suggest that the $Z_3$-symmetric NMSSM offers a viable framework for simultaneously resolving the $\tau$ lepton mass anomaly, the Higgs coupling anomaly, and the gravitational wave data from GW170817. Additionally, we propose that a gravitational wave signal from domain walls could provide a unique method for probing the Higgs sector and detecting new physics. We also discuss the feasibility of detecting these gravitational waves using pulsar timing arrays. In conclusion, we advocate for a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary approach to testing the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM, leveraging both the LIGO/Virgo and future pulsar timing array gravitational wave observatories. This complements the search for Higgs boson deviations from the Standard Model and the search for $\tau$ lepton masses in the few hundred GeV range. The $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM is thus a promising candidate for new physics, with the potential to be confirmed through the detection of gravitational waves. This would represent a groundbreaking discovery, marking the first instance of gravitational waves serving as a tool to explore Higgs sector physics. In this scenario, gravitational waves would function as a novel and highly effective means of investigating the Higgs sector. We also discuss the implications of this proposal for future research directions. We introduce a novel technique for the reliable recognition of (sub)millimeter source displacements in high-redshift galaxy studies, utilizing the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). By analyzing public HST and ALMA imaging data for 1,000 sources with redshifts greater than 3, we determined that our method achieves a 99.7% success rate in detecting reliable offsets, with a false positive rate of 0.3%. We demonstrate that this approach can distinguish genuine (sub)millimeter sources from spurious detections at a significance level of 3$\sigma$ or higher. Furthermore, we show that the method's performance remains stable across varying source brightnesses, source separations, and source redshifts. We provide a detailed description of our procedure, including specific examples of robust detections, and release a version of the code for public use. This approach represents a significant advancement in the reliable identification of (sub)millimeter source shifts, thereby substantially enhancing our ability to study the physical properties of high-redshift galaxies. Additionally, we illustrate how this method can facilitate the robust measurement of dust temperatures and star formation rates in high-redshift galaxies. Our findings suggest that HST and ALMA are now capable of reliably detecting and measuring the shifts of (sub)millimeter sources, marking a new era of precision in the field. These capabilities will significantly advance our understanding of the physical properties of high-redshift galaxies and their contributions to the cosmic star formation and dust emission history. We investigate the thermodynamic properties of the spin-$S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice using large-scale ($L=160$) quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our analysis of specific heat, magnetic susceptibility, and spin structure factor data reveals that the classical $120^\circ$-ordered ground state, which breaks $C_{3v}$ symmetry, undergoes a first-order transition to a spin liquid phase as quantum fluctuations increase with the strength of fourth-nearest neighbor interactions. Furthermore, we identify a novel phase characterized by a finite spin chirality, defined as the local scalar product of neighboring spins. This chiral phase exhibits a first-order boundary with the $120^\circ$ phase and a continuous boundary with the chiral spin liquid phase, distinguished by the emergence of a local topological Hall effect in the local spectral function. Finally, we discuss the potential connection between the phase diagram of this spin model and that of a frustrated quantum magnet on the kagome lattice. Additionally, we note that our study confirms a previously reported accidental crossing of energy eigenvalues at $L=96$ and $L=104$ within the $L$ even sector. This eigenvalue crossing, detectable in the specific heat, is shown to vanish as the interaction strength increases. Our results suggest that the $L=160$ system size is sufficient to accurately describe the ground state properties of the system. Finally, we demonstrate that the finite-size scaling of the kagome lattice model can be effectively performed using the same cluster sizes. These findings indicate that the kagome lattice spin model also experiences a first-order transition from the $120^\circ$ phase to a spin liquid phase. However, the critical interaction strength for this transition is significantly higher in the kagome lattice model compared to the triangular lattice model. The latter observation aligns with the fact that the kagome lattice can be constructed by removing the third nearest neighbor bonds from the triangular lattice. Consequently, the triangular lattice appears to be the simplest square-root lattice capable of producing a chiral quantum phase. We conclude that the $120^\circ$-ordered ground state of the kagome lattice model remains stable against the addition of fourth-nearest neighbor interactions up to the point where the system is effectively reduced to the triangular lattice model. Antiferromagnets are crucial for both fundamental research and technological applications, yet their complex internal structures and interactions often hinder the design of practical devices. This study examines the magnetic properties of Cr2Al, a recently discovered high-temperature antiferromagnetic metal, using a combination of first-principles calculations and experimental measurements. Our results confirm that Cr2Al undergoes a first-order antiferromagnetic transition at $T_{\rm N} = 280$ K. We demonstrate that the internal layering in Cr2Al induces exchange frustration, resulting in alternating ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions between adjacent chromium planes. Furthermore, the $d$-orbital hybridization between Cr and Al elements is identified as a key factor driving this unique magnetic behavior. These findings provide a foundation for understanding the origins of exchange interactions in first-row transition-metal compounds and offer guidance for developing new functional materials. Finally, our analysis reveals that Cr2Al exhibits strong spin-orbit coupling, suggesting its potential utility in spintronic applications. This study introduces a kinetic model utilizing a hard sphere distribution function modified by a speed-dependent collision frequency. The expansion of the hard sphere distribution incorporates the first two correction terms for the velocity magnitude, where coefficients are derived from the first two virial coefficients of transport properties relative to the Maxwellian distribution. By solving the resulting linearized Boltzmann equation, the transport coefficients are calculated and compared against rigorous solutions and existing theoretical predictions. The newly proposed model demonstrates superior accuracy in predicting transport coefficients compared to the standard hard sphere distribution. Furthermore, numerical solutions of the exact kinetic equation for a binary mixture reveal that this model effectively captures the impacts of the intermolecular potential between two rarefied gases. Finally, the model's applicability to real gas scenarios is validated by computing the accommodation coefficient for water. These findings indicate that the proposed model is particularly well-suited for rarefied gas flows involving gases with strong intermolecular forces. This study introduces FSA, an efficient framework designed to train familiar semantic analyzers using very minimal data. The goal is to develop neural semantic analyzers capable of generalizing effectively to unseen data while retaining semantic mappings similar to those derived from small, carefully curated examples. Unlike standard semantic mapping techniques that require extensive training on large datasets, FSAs necessitate only a handful of minimal training instances to achieve high-performance semantic analysis on new data. The paper outlines the Familiarization Algorithm, provides a mathematical formulation, and demonstrates how to implement it within a neural network using minimal parameterization. Furthermore, it presents experimental results comparing FSA against conventional methods, followed by a discussion of the approach's advantages and potential future research directions. Keywords: Semantic Analysis, Very Minimal Knowledge, Familiarization Algorithm.

The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is being prepared to investigate the internal structure of protons and nuclei, as well as the mechanisms of hadron formation. To ensure the EIC's success, a tracking detector featuring exceptional spatial resolution and rapid data readout is essential. This detector will be positioned close to the interaction point to achieve the necessary granularity. A planar module utilizing the 3D Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) technology is a primary candidate for this application. This paper outlines the current progress of the SOI development within the EIC R&D framework. It details the methodologies employed to enhance SOI tracking sensor performance, presenting the most recent tracking results from 3D SOI sensors. Furthermore, the study examines the tracking capabilities of monolithic active pixel sensors (MAPS) built on SOI substrates, offering an outlook on the future of silicon tracking sensors for the EIC. Additionally, the paper addresses the EIC's front-end readout technology, describing a newly developed 100-ohm input charge sensitive preamplifier that supports the EIC's stringent timing requirements. Finally, a discussion on the EIC's SOI technology roadmap is provided. Collectively, these advancements aim to deliver a tracking detector with a resolution of 5 microns or better, fulfilling the EIC's performance specifications. This capability will facilitate the construction of the EIC's inner tracker, enabling the achievement of the collider's physics goals. Specifically, the SOI technology is expected to deliver a tracking performance of approximately 5 microns in x-y and 10 microns in z, with a hit rate capability of 100,000 hits per second per channel. These results are derived from a full-end-to-end test involving the complete detector readout system. We introduce a model describing a low-mass accreting black hole exhibiting a quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) at a few hundred Hz, characterized by a significant fractional luminosity variance of $\sigma_f \sim 0.3$. This system is hypothesized to consist of a black hole within the low, unstable branch of a standard thin disk, which is thermally unstable and capable of both oscillating and undergoing outbursts. We contend that the identified QPO frequency corresponds to the thermal timescale at the inner disk edge. We outline a theoretical framework for a thermally unstable disk that generates a QPO via a narrow emission region, where the disk's thermal timescale matches the QPO frequency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that stochastic fluctuations from the accretion process are amplified by the disk's positive real frequency, resulting in a white noise spectrum with an enhanced noise amplitude. Additionally, we propose that outbursts in this system follow a power-law distribution of energy, with an index determined by the real and imaginary components of the disk's QPO mode. Finally, we suggest that the well-known QPOs in GRS 1915+105, observed at frequencies of approximately 100 and 300 Hz, can be interpreted as the disk's thermal timescale and cooling time, respectively. Consequently, GRS 1915+105 serves as a valuable laboratory for investigating disk stability. We also address the implications of our model for the recently identified low-mass X-ray binary, MAXI J1820+070. Ultimately, we conclude that the QPO frequency in a specific X-ray binary can be defined as the disk's QPO frequency, while the amplitude of disk fluctuations is governed by the magnitude of fluctuations in the accretion rate of a low-mass black hole. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD 58260, a rapidly rotating, metal-poor star exhibiting strong magnetic fields. We conducted high-resolution spectropolarimetry on three dates during a single night using a magnetic spectropolarimeter equipped with a 1.5-meter focal length. The analysis targeted the neutral metal lines of Fe I, Ni I, and Ca I, which are sensitive to the line-of-sight component of the magnetic field. By applying the cross-correlation technique, we detected a variation in the radial magnetic field component, with changes reaching several hundred Gauss. This result confirms a magnetic field variation on a timescale of hours, supporting the hypothesis that HD 58260 possesses an active region. Furthermore, the observed fluctuations in line polarization are too rapid to be attributed to rotational changes, thereby ruling out non-thermal transverse magnetic field variations. These findings align with the active-star model, which posits that surface magnetic field variations in rapidly rotating stars arise from the rotation of active regions. Additionally, the study demonstrates that spectropolarimetry using a high-resolution spectrograph with a relatively low spectral focal length is highly effective for studying magnetic field variations in such stars. Future investigations of HD 58260 will employ spectropolarimetry with a larger focal length to achieve higher sensitivity. The data collected in this study will be utilized to develop a new inversion method capable of analyzing the radial magnetic field component. This method will be applied to HD 58260 and other active stars to study magnetic field variations and their impact on stellar winds. Ultimately, this research aims to enhance our understanding of the magnetic field structure within active regions. We conducted ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ emission line within the dwarf galaxy NGC~5253, which is known for its young stellar population formed during a merger event. Our analysis of the H30$\alpha$ data, combined with 12CO and 13CO observations, allowed us to derive the H30$\alpha$ excitation temperature ($T_{\rm ex}$) and gas density ($n_{\rm H_2}$) across the galaxy. Utilizing these parameters, we calculated the H30$\alpha$ luminosity ($L_{\rm H30\alpha}$) and the ionization parameter ($\xi$) for the galaxy. Our results indicate that the ionization source of the H30$\alpha$ emission is a combination of both an H~II region and a molecular cloud. Furthermore, we estimated the ionizing photon rate ($Q_{\rm H}$) to be $(1.0\pm0.2)\times10^{50}$ s$^{-1}$, which corresponds to approximately 10% of the ionizing photons produced by a single O8V star. This suggests that the H~II region is illuminated by a small number of massive stars. Finally, we determined the star formation rate (SFR) to be $0.01\pm0.001$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, a value consistent with prior estimates derived from other methods. These findings imply that NGC~5253 is currently undergoing a minor star formation event. Additionally, we discuss the potential for utilizing the H30$\alpha$ line as a tool for investigating star formation in the low-metallicity universe. This paper introduces a new class of estimators for conditional expectation functions within nonparametric regression settings. For data conforming to a local Lipschitz condition, the proposed estimator achieves the minimax optimal rate of $n^{2/3}( \log n )^{1/3}$ in $L_2$ distance. Empirical results indicate that, relative to nearest-neighbor estimators, this method delivers superior performance without requiring manual tuning of bandwidths. Furthermore, the estimator is capable of handling data with limited smoothness. The discussion covers various estimation scenarios and their corresponding minimax rates.

In the first scenario, where the response variable $Y$ is bounded, the minimax rate for estimating the conditional expectation $E[Y|X]$ in $L_2$ distance is established as $d^{2\alpha+1}/n$ (up to logarithmic factors), provided the data lies on a bounded manifold of dimension $d$ with a local Hölder smoothness of $\alpha$. This rate is derived using an estimator from this paper.

The second scenario addresses cases where the joint distribution of $(X,Y)$ exhibits low local smoothness. Here, a local polynomial kernel is proposed to mitigate the bias inherent in global kernel methods. For bounded $Y$, the minimax rate is determined to be $d^{2\alpha+1}/n$.

The third scenario involves scenarios where the distribution of $X$ given $Y$ is smooth, even if the joint distribution of $(X,Y)$ is not. Under these conditions, the minimax rate for estimating $E[Y|X]$ is identified as $d^{2\alpha+1}/n$.

Finally, the paper examines the minimax rates for estimating $E[Y|X]$ under Lipschitz continuity constraints. When $Y$ is bounded, the rate is $d/n(\log n)^{1/3}$. For unbounded $Y$, the rate becomes $d^{2\alpha+1}/n$ for $\alpha \in (1/4, 1/2]$, and $(d-1)/n$ when $\alpha > 1/2$. Additionally, it is demonstrated that no estimator can achieve a rate faster than $(d+1)/n$ (ignoring logarithmic factors) when $Y$ is unbounded and $\alpha \leq 1/4$.

Knowledge graphs are increasingly employed to model relationships between entities, with research focusing on predicting future links. While most existing methods treat graphs as static, recent trends have introduced incorporating graph temporalization to achieve more accurate predictions. However, integrating temporal information often results in significant data sparsity. This study demonstrates that leveraging time itself, rather than merely the set of temporal links, can enhance link prediction. We introduce a novel approach for link forecasting in temporal knowledge graphs that utilizes an auxiliary static graph derived from node co-occurrence within time windows. Our method is evaluated on two datasets, and the results indicate a 10% improvement in loglikelihood scores over current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we provide exploratory analyses to examine the influence of window size and other factors on our model's performance. Finally, we discuss how our findings can offer guidance for designing auxiliary graphs in various applications. This study addresses the challenge of nonlinear regression within an asynchronous online federated learning framework. In this context, a central server trains a shared nonlinear regression model with varying degrees of participation from multiple clients, where each client performs regression tasks on its local data. To address the computational and communication constraints faced by resource-limited devices, we introduce a novel resource-aware asynchronous online federated method. This approach enables clients to dynamically adjust their update frequency based on available resources, thereby reducing communication overhead. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms competing methods in terms of both convergence speed and overall performance. Furthermore, an implementation utilizing these algorithms on a simulation hardware platform confirms their suitability for resource-constrained devices. Additionally, the method is applied to a real-world dataset of local weather conditions to forecast temperature trends. The results indicate that the algorithm is effective in nonlinear regression scenarios involving heterogeneous nonlinear functions and varying participation levels from multiple clients. Ultimately, the algorithm offers superior convergence and performance compared to existing approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2001/RACAOFL. The conventional method for light absorption in silicon photonic devices typically involves a straightforward stack of silicon layers on top of a bulk reflector, such as a silicon dioxide mirror. However, this approach necessitates relatively thick silicon slabs to effectively trap incident light via standing wave patterns. This work introduces an alternative strategy to enhance absorption in thin silicon membranes by integrating a three-dimensional photonic band gap material as the rear reflector. We demonstrate that a photonic crystal slab featuring a photonic band gap can effectively trap thin silicon membranes within its band gap, thereby suppressing transmission. Furthermore, we show that loss can be significantly amplified by leveraging the photonic band gap of the silicon photonic crystal slab. Finally, we validate the efficacy of this technique by calculating the absorption spectra for a thin silicon membrane situated between silicon photonic crystal slabs with photonic band gaps. Our findings indicate that this method achieves near-unity absorption across a broad spectrum, even with silicon membranes as thin as 100 nm. This study paves the way for developing new, compact silicon-based optical components, such as modulators and switches, based on photonic crystal slabs. Additionally, the proposed system is compatible with current CMOS fabrication processes, making it suitable for integration into large-scale photonic circuits. Our work underscores the potential of 3D photonic band gap materials to substantially boost light absorption in thin silicon membranes. Future research will explore the application of this technique to other thin-film materials, including germanium and indium phosphide. We introduce a new class of high-dimensional graph expander families derived from group actions on metric spaces. These classes include graphs constructed from covers of torus knot complements and Brieskorn--Enriques-Gieseker three-folds. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain extensions of these graphs, which include specific generators, exhibit strong expansion properties. Furthermore, we show that restricting these graphs to their associated graphs or Cayley graphs of their vertex groups preserves the strong expansion property. We begin by reviewing existing positive results concerning random subgroups of mapping class groups and their associated graphs. However, we also establish that this random subgroup method fails to produce novel high-dimensional expander graphs when applied to mapping class groups, Kleinian groups, or fundamental groups of Seifert fibered 3-manifolds. Additionally, we prove the existence of expander graphs within the mapping class groups of surfaces of genus 3 and 4 that possess specific vertex stabilizers containing the mapping class groups of surfaces of lower genera. Finally, we provide examples of expander graphs where vertices correspond to points in a metric space with finite stabilizers and bounded distances to a geodesic axis. These examples illustrate graphs with stabilizers drawn from various groups, including the mapping class groups of surfaces of genus 3 through 7, braid groups of rank 4 through 11, and fundamental groups of Seifert fibered 3-manifolds. All constructed graphs maintain strong expansion properties. Notably, the construction relies on a random walk on a non-compact hyperbolic 3-manifold, distinguishing it from approaches that utilize hyperbolic surfaces or 3-manifolds with compact interiors. The study investigates the magnetic properties of a new, previously unidentified centered honeycomb antiferromagnet, GdInO$_3$, a material that exhibits significant anisotropy in its thermal conductivity. DC magnetization data collected across various magnetic fields and temperatures reveals a second-order antiferromagnetic phase transition at $T_\mathrm{N}=3.05(1)$ K. Field- and field-cooled magnetization measurements indicate a substantial magnetic hysteresis within a narrow temperature interval of 2.0(1)–3.0(1) K, a feature uncommon for bulk antiferromagnets. Additionally, specific heat analysis shows anomalies in the 2.0(1)–3.0(1) K range, which are well-explained by the presence of magnetic hysteresis. Finally, neutron diffraction experiments conducted at 2 K and an applied field of 7 T, combined with polarization analysis, demonstrate that the Gadolinium magnetic moments lie within the basal plane and adopt a non-collinear, modulated spin structure. These findings collectively suggest that GdInO$_3$ is a highly unusual bulk antiferromagnet. Furthermore, the alignment of the spin moments in the basal plane, despite the strong anisotropy in thermal conductivity, implies a complex thermal transport mechanism in this material. This research expands the family of magnetic honeycomb structures and offers new insights into the thermal transport properties of magnetic materials. This paper introduces a model for nonlinear distortion power in dual-polarization four-dimensional optical transmission systems, accounting for cross-polarization interference (XPI). By assuming that polarization-mode dispersion (PMD) is negligible, the model integrates cross-p polarization mode dispersion ($\text{PMD}_{\text{X}}$) and polarization-dependent loss (PDL) into a unified framework. Since XPI is a critical source of nonlinear impairment in dual-polarization formats, this model is especially applicable to single-channel scenarios where $\text{PMD}_{\text{X}}$ is suppressed. Validated against both a Petropoulou et al. model and simulations, the proposed model demonstrates superior accuracy in predicting error vector magnitude (EVM) for dual-polarization 4D (DP-QPSK and DP-16QAM) systems. Furthermore, the model is well-suited for implementing the generalized Gaussian noise (GGN) model in practical applications, such as the Ma model. In this context, the model can be utilized to estimate the noise variance of a dual-polarization format given that of a single-polarization format. Additionally, the model is highly effective for analyzing the performance of multi-channel transmission systems under conditions where $\text{PMD}_{\text{X}}$ is significant. Finally, the model is applicable to systems without PDL, provided the power of the PDL contribution is negligible. The model's performance is illustrated through examples for standard DP-16QAM and a newly proposed 4D modulation format, 2D-16QAM-16PSK. These results indicate that XPI is a substantial impairment for DP-16QAM and, to a lesser extent, for 2D-16QAM-16PSK. In recent years, the escalating frequency and intensity of wildfires has intensified the necessity for effective detection and monitoring systems. While the infrared (IR) spectrum offers significant potential for this purpose, its application is often hindered by a lack of visual detail. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a deep learning-based IR-VIS fusion model designed to enhance IR images by integrating them with corresponding visible spectrum (VIS) captures. The primary objective of our approach is to generate high-fidelity "infrared-inspired" (FIRe) images that combine the superior detection capabilities of IR with the rich textural and semantic information found in VIS data. Our model employs a novel two-stream encoder architecture paired with a fused discriminator to extract complementary features from both spectral domains. Furthermore, we implement a multi-scale discriminator and incorporate a spectral loss function to refine the fusion process. Extensive evaluations on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that our model surpasses current state-of-the-art fusion techniques, particularly in enhancing FIRe visuals regarding texture and semantic richness. This study introduces a random-compartmental random dynamical system (RCRS) to model the COVID-19 pandemic. The model incorporates the dynamics of susceptible, exposed, infected, and removed populations, alongside stochastic environmental noise. The primary objective is to analyze the model equation, stochastic Lyapunov exponents, ergodicity, and the long-term asymptotic behavior of its solutions. Furthermore, the work establishes the existence and uniqueness of a solution for susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed equations based on the given parameters. Finally, the study derives a random basic reproduction number to delineate the model's behavior within an invariant random absorbing set. Numerical simulations are utilized to substantiate these theoretical findings. Ultimately, this research underscores the efficacy of random dynamical systems in studying infectious diseases and the potential for utilizing computer simulations to forecast pandemic trends. The findings may assist in understanding COVID-19 dynamics and inform policy decisions aimed at mitigating its spread. Additionally, the approaches employed can be applied to other infectious disease models. Keywords: Random dynamical system, Lyapunov exponents, Ergodicity, Asymptotic behavior, Computer simulation. The calculations utilize a fully self-consistent relativistic framework that self-consistently couples the isoscalar monopole and quadrupole channels. This method accurately reproduces experimental data for both nuclei, specifically the positions and widths of the isoscalar monopole resonance. Furthermore, the relativistic monopole quadrupole model proves effective for calculating the isoscalar monopole strength distribution. These results underscore the necessity of self-consistently coupling monopole and quadrupole channels to accurately describe the monopole strength distribution. The work concludes by discussing the limitations of the model and suggesting potential future improvements. This work examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence within feedback-controlled motion systems encountering Coulomb friction. It introduces a continuous mathematical model representing the dynamics of such systems, alongside a non-ideal reference trajectory generator that produces canonical stick-slip profiles. The core objective is achieving perfect tracking of this reference signal, a goal realized through a control law featuring discontinuous feedback relative to the tracking error. Since direct analysis of this law is problematic, the study proposes a continuous alternative that closely approximates it. The paper subsequently demonstrates local exponential convergence of the closed-loop system to the reference trajectory, as well as the convergence of the approximate solution generated by the continuous control law. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to illustrate the convergence properties and the near-identical behavior of both the ideal and approximate control laws. These examples serve to validate the theoretical findings. Notably, the continuous model and the convergence proof for the ideal control law remain applicable even when the ideal behavior is purely stick or purely slip, thereby recovering established results from classical Coulomb friction literature. However, the primary contribution lies in the continuous model and the derived results concerning sliding and slip motions during transitions. Furthermore, the paper offers a novel approach to analyzing the convergence properties of feedback-regulated systems with Coulomb resistance. This methodology is more general and applicable to systems where the continuous model remains viable despite the ideal control law being entirely continuous. Specifically, the proposed methodology yields new results for systems exhibiting pure slip or pure stick behavior. The analysis begins by defining a Carleman linearization of the closed-loop system and the reference trajectory generator, followed by the demonstration of local exponential convergence using Lyapunov exponents. The paper concludes by discussing the limitations of the proposed methodology and its potential for future extensions. Overall, the findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for the analysis and design of motion systems equipped with Coulomb friction and feedback control. These results hold particular significance for control laws that are continuous or Lipschitz continuous, ensuring the validity of standard convergence analysis techniques. Additionally, the convergence proof relies on the Lyapunov exponent method, a technique that is both versatile and widely applicable. The work also underscores the critical role of the reference trajectory in the convergence analysis, suggesting that the proposed methodology can be extended to analyze systems governed by arbitrary reference trajectories. Finally, the paper addresses the limitations of the stick-slip convergence result regarding the continuous model and the associated Lyapunov exponent, offering insights for future research and potential generalizations. Recently, Bellman Hedging has been introduced as a technique for training deep neural networks to execute hedging operations within reinforcement learning frameworks. This approach operates by dynamically updating the complete set of neural network parameters using a carefully engineered stochastic Bellman error, thereby implementing a tailored form of Bellman updates. We demonstrate that when applied uniformly across all functions, Bellman Hedging is equivalent to standard Reinforcement Learning via Gradient Descent (RL-GD). Furthermore, we extend Bellman Hedging to create a flexible family of algorithms capable of performing diverse hedging operations. By incorporating stochasticity into the hedging process, our method enables the execution of either deep or shallow hedges, resulting in the ability to carry out partial hedging. We evaluate these proposed algorithms across a broad spectrum of function approximation methods and reinforcement learning tasks. Our findings indicate that while certain self-supervised deep hedges can impair performance, stochastic hedges often enhance it. Additionally, we demonstrate that implementing Bellman Hedging with stochastic shallow hedges yields superior performance in tabular Q-learning. Finally, we illustrate that utilizing Bellman Hedging with stochastic deep hedges enhances the sample efficiency of various Reinforcement Learning algorithms that employ either online or offline function approximators. Notably, we introduce a novel algorithm termed Profound Bellman Hedging (ProPHaD), which represents the first successful application of deep hedges to an offline function approximator. Our empirical results show that ProPHaD can achieve performance improvements of up to 100% when compared to reinforcement learning with gradient descent. Moreover, we demonstrate that ProPHaD can surpass the performance of any reinforcement learning algorithm utilizing any arbitrary function approximator. These findings suggest that stochastic deep hedges can serve as a form of data augmentation, thereby improving reinforcement learning performance. To facilitate further research, we have made our codebase publicly available. Our code includes implementations of numerous reinforcement learning algorithms employing any arbitrary function approximator, enabling users to easily benchmark Profound Bellman Hedging against any function approximator of their choice. We anticipate that this work will stimulate new inquiries into the integration of deep hedges with function approximators in reinforcement learning. Specifically, we propose that the combination of deep hedges with function approximators trained via any form of gradient descent holds promise for enhancing sample efficiency. This is particularly relevant in scenarios involving offline reinforcement learning, where pre-trained models can be fine-tuned using an increasing number of Bellman updates. Our extensive codebase supports this investigation by providing implementations of deep hedges for any arbitrary function

Sequential recommender systems are designed to suggest items to users based on their historical consumption patterns. However, simply relying on item-level representations fails to capture the user motivations driving these sequences. To address this, we introduce a model that represents unobserved user motivations as latent variables within a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). By utilizing categorical distributions, we sequentially model the probability of selecting each item. Furthermore, we propose an efficient variational inference approach to fit this HMM model, which significantly accelerates training by orders of magnitude compared to traditional HMM training methods. We validate the efficacy of our motivation model against baseline approaches using the Amazon and Yelp datasets. We introduce a symmetric generalization of the confluent Heun equation within a transformable framework. Utilizing an integral representation, we demonstrate that a specific class of solutions to this transformed double confluent Heun equation can be generated as a symmetric superposition of Heun functions, characterized by a symmetric source function. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence of polynomial solutions and propose numerical algorithms to solve the equation, validating these results through various examples, including those relevant to gravitational physics. Additionally, we outline a path toward solving the equation using the Narayanan-Sasa method. Finally, we illustrate applications in physics, such as the Schrödinger equation with a square well potential and a spherically symmetric superposition of Yukawa potentials. These applications yield a set of algebraic equations to determine the parameters of Yukawa potentials, which may serve as an alternative to the one-center SM potential. Furthermore, we suggest an extension of the Schrödinger equation incorporating a conformal factor. Our approach offers an alternative to the SM potential and may find utility in physics applications. Additionally, our findings may contribute to the development of inverse spectral theory. To facilitate these applications, we have provided numerical results in the form of tables and figures. All code used to obtain these results is available in an open-access repository. The findings presented herein were derived from joint work conducted in 2021 and 2022. Compressed sensing represents a widely adopted framework for reconstructing high-dimensional signals from sparse measurements by leveraging groupwise heterogeneity. Within the context of matrix completion, this concept manifests as low-rank structure across groups of rows or columns. This study examines a rank-one limit where each group consists of only a few elements. We demonstrate that, analogous to the classical case involving entire rows and columns, essential limits for recoverability in groupwise heterogeneity are defined by the fraction of observed elements within each group. Furthermore, we illustrate a reconstruction method based on the trace norm minimization of a nonhomogeneous matrix, providing a theoretical guarantee of its success in the groupwise heterogeneity setting. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that trace norm minimization outperforms other approaches, such as nuclear norm minimization of a homogenous matrix, when group sizes are small. These findings suggest that groupwise heterogeneity offers a promising avenue for high-dimensional inference, particularly when data is missing randomly. The paper also explores potential extensions to other forms of heterogeneity. Additionally, we present preliminary insights into extending these results to multiple rank blocks, though this specific direction is not the focus of the current work. The analysis relies on recent developments in high-dimensional probability, including recent extensions of large deviation theory. The resulting framework is expected to be valuable for future research in high-dimensional inference. Our approach also has implications for understanding the essential limits of learning from noisy data. Numerical results indicate that trace norm minimization can achieve reconstruction thresholds that closely approach these limits. We anticipate that this work will stimulate further inquiry into fundamental questions regarding the essential limits of reconstruction under heterogeneity and the development of efficient algorithms to reach those limits. This study demonstrates that the lack of symmetry in a one-dimensional lattice model is inherently topological. The effective Hamiltonian, derived from the microscopic one-band Hamiltonian via the maximally localized Wannier function, exhibits a clear relationship with the topological charge defined by the microscopic model. This charge is determined by the relative positions of two special Wannier centers. Furthermore, the topological nature of this charge is demonstrated by analyzing the charge transport properties of the effective Hamiltonian within a heterostructure. The results of the proposed one-dimensional model are also extended to higher dimensions. Consequently, this work offers a novel perspective on the topological characteristics of Wannier functions and their index in the context of lattice models. Additionally, the research highlights the fundamental connection between the topological and symmetry properties of these models. Finally, the paper explores the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, illustrating that the topological charge can be altered by breaking the symmetry of the hopping integral. Furthermore, it examines the charge transport properties of effective Hamiltonians for both the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model and the Rice-Mele model within the context of heterostructures. The methodology developed for the Rice-Mele model is shown to be applicable to other well-known topological models, including the Hofstadter model and the Lieb model. Ultimately, the findings of this paper are expected to advance the understanding of the topological properties of materials. Furthermore, the insights gained may facilitate the design of new materials and enable the investigation of the topological properties of the effective Hamiltonian for materials where symmetry breaking is induced by external stimuli, such as strain or the insertion of dopant atoms. Finally, the work establishes a new approach for constructing effective Hamiltonians that can be applied to materials where symmetry breaking arises from the presence of impurities or vacancies. To achieve this, the Wannier centers are adjusted by the positions of the Wannier functions associated with the eigenstates at the band edges of the defective material. This provides a new perspective on the topological characteristics of Wannier functions in the context of lattice models with defects. Ultimately, this research could contribute to the understanding of the topological properties of materials containing defects. Additionally, the findings may offer a new approach for the design of materials with defect-induced topology. To this end, the topological charge is shown to be reducible to that of the effective Hamiltonian associated with the Wannier functions linked to the eigenstates at the Fermi level within the Rice-Mele model framework for defective lattices. This study addresses the decentralized regulation of linear, time-invariant systems featuring multiple channels per input, channel-wise quadratic costs, and local information availability. The primary objective is to establish a distributed model predictive control (MPC) framework that enables autonomous operation and robustness against component failures. To achieve this, we introduce a "plug-and-play" MPC scheme capable of dynamically adapting to the active set of controllers. This scheme ensures that the MPC's initial value function remains valid whenever components are activated, thereby eliminating the necessity to resolve optimization problems immediately upon online component addition or removal. We demonstrate that a convex optimization problem is sufficient to guarantee feasibility, strict input and input-rate constraints, and input-to-state stability of the closed-loop system. Furthermore, we extend this framework to incorporate output feedback through the design of distributed dynamic state observers. Finally, numerical examples are provided to illustrate the application of the proposed method. In this context, "decentralized MPC" refers to an approach where controllers are interconnected via a communication network, in contrast to "distributed MPC," which typically involves direct coupling between control variables across systems. Additionally, "plug-and-play MPC" denotes an algorithm where controllers can be enabled or disabled without re-solving optimization problems. The term "multi-channel system" describes a setup where a single control input influences the system in multiple dimensions. Finally, "distributed regulation" refers to an MPC algorithm where decision variables are determined locally based on individual cost functions and constraints, with interactions between decision variables managed via auxiliary variables exchanged between subsystems. Over time, life has adapted to thrive across diverse environments. This adaptive journey is driven by mutations that introduce variability, enabling survival and reproduction. This introduces a fundamental challenge: how does an organism navigate between the need for variability to cope with environmental changes and the need for stability to function effectively? This balance is governed by two key factors: (i) the tempo of ecological and evolutionary shifts, which are dictated by the duration of environmental fluctuations and the rates at which new mutations arise; and (ii) the presence of external substances that can either promote or inhibit mutation rates. This presentation examines how these mechanisms interact within complex systems, utilizing mathematical models to analyze their impact on adaptation. Specifically, it explores how environmental fluctuations and mutation rate modifiers influence adaptive success across varying spatial and temporal scales. The core message emphasizes that adaptation is not merely a product of selective pressures but is intrinsically linked to the concepts of tempo and mode. Ultimately, this work provides a foundation for understanding how external agents can modulate evolutionary rates, thereby offering insights into the control of evolution in both natural and artificial settings. Finally, these findings have significant implications for addressing complex challenges, such as the emergence of drug-resistant pathogens. By strategically applying mutation modifiers, such as mutagens, it may be possible to direct evolutionary trajectories toward beneficial outcomes, such as achieving drug-free cures or preventing the development of resistance. To illustrate this, the presentation concludes with numerical simulations depicting various scenarios involving mutation rate modifiers. These simulations demonstrate how altering mutation rates can steer adaptive pathways, steering complex dynamics toward desired goals like enhanced adaptability or the avoidance of maladaptive states like extinction or maladaptation. The work is grounded in a variety of mathematical models, including the complex eco-evolutionary system described by coupled reaction-diffusion equations. These equations capture the interplay between ecological dynamics, phenotypic traits, and mutation rates, offering a comprehensive framework for analyzing adaptive processes within complex systems. Furthermore, the study investigates how external mutation rate modifiers influence mutation-driven adaptation, thereby providing a theoretical basis for managing evolution in both natural and artificial contexts. To achieve this, the work employs a multi-scale approach, incorporating both deterministic and stochastic modeling techniques. This methodology offers a holistic understanding of mutation-driven adaptation, elucidating how mutation rates and timescales interact to shape evolutionary trajectories. By integrating mathematical rigor with biological insight, this presentation aims to provide a robust foundation for future research into the control and understanding of complex eco-evolutionary systems. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has become a highly effective method for developing robust speech representations. However, the hostile susceptibility of these automatically learned features remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the vulnerability of speech SSL representations to poison attacks, examining how model architecture, dataset composition, and preprocessing techniques influence resistance to such threats. Our findings indicate that the scope of representational leakage under attack is highly dependent on the specific speech task, with larger vocabularies in TIMIT-based models generally offering greater resilience. Additionally, models trained on datasets contaminated with just 1% of adversarial examples exhibit approximately a 10% increase in representation leakage compared to those trained on clean datasets. Finally, we demonstrate that applying a band-pass filter during preprocessing can reduce representational leakage by up to 20% relative to unfiltered models. These results provide critical insights for the safe deployment of speech SSL representations in production environments. The code and datasets required to replicate this study are accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/ssl-poisoning. Furthermore, our representative poisoned datasets can be downloaded from the speech v2 repository at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/speech-v2/tree/master/datasets/poisoned. We gratefully acknowledge Dr. Dragan Dimitrov for his assistance in creating the poisoning scripts. The poisoning process utilized the code available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/adversarial-text-datasets. Additionally, Dr. Dimitrov contributed to the creation of the adversarial text datasets used in this work. The character tokenization was implemented using the code found at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/adversarial-text-datasets. Finally, Dr. Dimitrov's work on the adversarial text poisoning pipeline was instrumental to this research.

Finally, the paper provides a comprehensive discussion on the benefits and challenges of decentralized markets and supplies, concluding with future research directions. The E-value serves as a metric for sensitivity to unmeasured confounding in observational studies. This study introduces the E-missingvalue, an extension designed to assess sensitivity to missing data. The primary objective is to quantify sensitivity to potentially missing effect-modifiers. The E-value quantifies the minimal magnitude of an effect in a variable that could represent unmeasured confounding, such as missing effect-modifiers. We demonstrate that the E-value provides a straightforward sensitivity analysis by defining an acceptance region for the confounders of interest. Furthermore, we propose a Bayesian framework for computing the E-value, which accommodates uncertainty regarding the target parameter. In the demonstration phase, we illustrate how the uncertainty within target parameters influences the size of the acceptance region. Additionally, we provide code to generate prior distributions for the E-value based on survey data. The E-value offers a straightforward and interpretable approach to sensitivity analysis. By characterizing the joint acceptance region for potentially missing variables, researchers can assess whether the region is sufficiently small to conclude no effect exists. This methodology is particularly applicable to missing data scenarios, where the acceptance region for missing effect-modifiers depends on uncertainty regarding the target parameter. This approach enables analysts to evaluate whether an observed effect is sufficiently distinct from the null hypothesis to be considered credible. Ultimately, this technique facilitates a comprehensive understanding of whether an effect is distinguishable from the null despite the potential presence of missing effect-modifiers. In this work, we present a practical method for conducting sensitivity analysis using E-values. Specifically, the E-value can be utilized to examine whether an effect is sufficiently far from the null to be deemed credible. This involves estimating the posterior distribution of the E-value and determining the probability that the joint acceptance region encompasses the observed effect. This procedure is especially relevant in contexts involving missing data, where unmeasured effect-modifiers may be missing. We applied this approach to a missing data scenario and found that the E-value is sensitive to uncertainty in the target parameter. Consequently, we recommend utilizing E-values in conjunction with uncertainty metrics. This allows analysts to effectively communicate whether an effect is sufficiently distant from the null to be considered credible. Future research should explore whether similar sensitivity analysis techniques can be applied to other sources of unmeasured bias. Overall, the E-value serves as a valuable tool for sensitivity analysis. This paper presents a comprehensive classification of all non-trivial one-parameter subgroups of automorphisms with Laurent series coefficients that act on the Laurent polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}[z_1^{\pm 1},z_2^{\pm 1}]$. These subgroups fall into four distinct types: trigonometric, $q$-trigonometric, $q$-linear, and linear. We demonstrate that each type corresponds to a non-degenerate, symmetric bilinear form on $\mathbb{C}^2$, which can be expressed as a matrix. Furthermore, we establish that the $q$-trigonometric, $q$-linear, and linear categories are equivalent to the standard trigonometric category under a change of variables in the Laurent polynomial ring. This work extends the findings of the authors in [17], which covered the $q$-linear and linear cases. We identify that the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries described herein are essential for the study of the quantum Murnaghan-Nakayama rule. Additionally, we show that these symmetries arise naturally from the Laurent expansion of the element $K \in U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, thereby providing a complete catalog of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries in the Laurent ring $\mathbb{C}[z_1^{\pm 1},z_2^{\pm 1}]$. This result generalizes the complete catalog previously established by the authors for the polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}[z_1,z_2]$. Finally, we outline several directions for future research. Specifically, in [18], we will utilize this classification to fully characterize the action of the generators $E, F, K$ of the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ on the Laurent polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}[z_1,z_2]$, and in [19], we will extend these symmetries to the quantum space of formal power series $\mathbb{C}[[z_1,z_2]]$. These contributions offer a novel and fresh perspective on the application of the element $K \in U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within the Laurent expansion. The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) is driving significant advancements in vehicular safety, navigation, and traffic management. However, the deployment of AI models within IoV systems is hindered by critical challenges, including data heterogeneity, privacy risks, and resource constraints. To address these issues, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a robust alternative, enabling the training of centralized AI models using decentralized data. Despite this, the integration of blockchain technology with blockchain-supported FL (BSFL) remains under-researched. This paper presents a thorough literature review of existing BSFL frameworks, examining their strengths, weaknesses, and contributions. Furthermore, it identifies key research gaps and proposes directions for future studies. By offering this comprehensive analysis, the paper aims to guide subsequent research endeavors and provide valuable insights for scholars. Additionally, it outlines the most pressing challenges that must be addressed to fully harness the potential of IoV, including data privacy, interoperability, and resource limitations. Finally, the study suggests that interdisciplinary collaboration is essential to advance BSFL research and ensure the sustainable evolution of intelligent IoV systems.

The Large Hadron Collider's ATLAS detector measured the beauty-quark (b-quark) production cross-section in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing both quarkonium states containing a b-quark pair and inclusive prompt and non-prompt charm mesons. Results indicate that the measured b-quark production cross-sections align with next-to-leading order perturbative quantum chromodynamics predictions and Monte Carlo event generator simulations. Additionally, the study presents the first measurement of the beauty-to-charm hadron production cross-section ratio across various charged hadron rapidity and transverse momentum regions, derived from the ratio of reconstructed non-prompt to prompt charm mesons. This ratio shows a dependence on both rapidity and transverse momentum. Furthermore, the data supports a production cross-section ratio that remains approximately constant with respect to transverse momentum and rapidity. These findings are compared with predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics and various Monte Carlo event generator simulations. The observed dependence on transverse momentum and rapidity is attributed to the different parton distribution functions utilized in the simulations. Ultimately, the measured ratios are consistent with the expectations from PYTHIA 8.227. These measurements provide crucial insights for optimizing beauty and charm quark production cross-sections in simulations, which is essential for estimating background contributions in various physics analyses. Consequently, this enhances the accuracy of signal extraction and enables more precise measurements of various physics observables. This work was conducted within the LHCb collaboration. This paper introduces VALUE, a novel automatic annotation framework designed for urban scenes, leveraging ensembles of state-of-the-art detection and segmentation models. VALUE integrates the outputs of these individual models through a new voting-based algorithm to produce the final annotations. The extensive training of VALUE models and the careful selection of voting parameters allow VALUE to achieve performance comparable to human annotators. This capability is demonstrated by its ability to correct annotation errors in over 80% of the cases. Trained and evaluated on over one million samples, VALUE can be easily extended to other object categories and segmentation tasks. To VALUE's best knowledge, it represents the first end-to-end automatic annotation system capable of providing an overall performance benchmark equivalent to that of human annotators. This study introduces a new class of proximal mean networks designed for N-dimensional (N-D) nonuniform undersampled sparse data, with a primary focus on reconstructing 1-D seismic reflectivity. The proposed proximal mean network operates by iteratively transforming a continuous Gaussian distribution into a discrete, truncated, and truncated Poisson distribution. This approach is grounded in the observation that the truncated and truncated Poisson distributions serve as effective models for N-D nonuniform sparse sampling patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these distributions possess significant potential for seismic data reconstruction. Leveraging recent advancements in proximal mean networks, we develop a new framework that utilizes these distributions to formulate seismic reflectivity reconstruction as a convex optimization problem. This results in the creation of the Proximal mean for Sparse Sampling (NuSPAN) algorithm. Numerical experiments indicate that NuSPAN achieves superior reconstruction quality compared to the Compressed Sensing (CS) algorithm when dealing with seismic reflectivity data. Additionally, NuSPAN exhibits a significant reduction in computational time relative to CS. Consequently, NuSPAN offers a more efficient and effective solution for seismic reflectivity reconstruction. The source code for NuSPAN is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi1994/NuSPAN. The accompanying video demonstrates the algorithm's application to seismic reflectivity reconstruction and is available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=12422222222. We introduce a method for calculating the transfer matrix spectrum of two-dimensional lattice models by combining wavefunction overlap techniques with operator merging. This approach inherently accounts for the universal finite-size corrections predicted by conformal field theory. By applying our method to the exactly-solvable Haagerup model, we determine the low-lying spectrum with high precision, revealing a unique scaling behavior that defies standard conformal field theory predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the technique is streamlined and extend it to the Ising and XXZ models, where it achieves exact results. These findings validate the approach and suggest its potential applicability to other lattice models. The computational code is publicly accessible. Historical texts present unique challenges for natural language processing due to linguistic evolution, spelling variations, and shifts in world knowledge. To address this, we introduce a framework that enables the reliable extraction of multiple possible pos-tags from existing POS taggers applied to historical datasets. Evaluated on the Historical English Corpus and the Old Norse Corpus, the dependent pos-tag prediction model achieved a 77.2% accuracy for its own predictions, identifying an additional 11.5% of pos-tags that the original taggers missed on average. Furthermore, this model successfully identified 94.0% of these missing pos-tags, while the original taggers accounted for only 55.5% of them. We also assessed the quality of the extracted pos-tags using part-of-speech n-gram entropy and automatic parsing, confirming that high-quality historical pos-tagging is now feasible through set-valued prediction. We argue that for smart cities, infrastructure projects, and business processes, it is essential to trace and link requirements to the specification, design, and planning phases of these domains. We selected the Meta-Object Facility (MOO) language because it is widely adopted and well-established. To demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, we applied it to transform smart lighting system requirements into formal specifications using SmartCity2020, a real-world case study. Furthermore, the approach is expected to be applicable to other requirements and domains, such as transportation and process workflows. A key advantage of this research is that it enables early detection of issues and facilitates decision-making during the requirement phase by providing a formal specification language. Finally, the proposed approach is highly compatible with existing state-of-the-art tools. Our contributions include: (i) an automatic transformation of requirements into formal specifications; (ii) a formal specification language derived from requirements; (iii) a method for transforming urban infrastructure requirements; and (iv) a case study on transforming smart lighting system requirements. Conventional quantum error correction (QEC) demands that errors be diagnosed and fixed by directly observing the error syndromes of multiple qubits, a method that introduces measurement errors and often collapses the qubit's state into an eigenstate of its check operator, necessitating additional recovery operations. This added burden hinders the realization of QEC in practical quantum devices. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a novel QEC approach called the "concealed inverses protocol" (CIP). This method involves applying a unitary operation that is the inverse of the error, followed by a measurement, without directly reading out the error syndromes. By repeatedly executing repeated quantum measurements (RQM), the system naturally converges to a specific state with a non-negligible probability, eliminating the need for active correction. In this framework, RQM serves as a quantum non-demolition measurement of a unitary operator representing the inverse of the error, allowing one to verify error-free states without collapsing the quantum state. We demonstrate that CIP can achieve error-free states for bit-flip and phase errors within a single RQM cycle, utilizing only a minimal number of control operations and measurements. Furthermore, we show that the scheme is effective for detecting and correcting phase and bit-phase combined errors in superconducting quantum systems. This method is expected to facilitate the experimental realization of quantum error correction in near-term quantum apparatus. Additionally, we have successfully implemented CIP on the suspended-waveguide quantum computer developed by our group, where it enhances the fidelity of multi-qubit states. This experimental achievement marks the first time a quantum computer has realized quantum error correction. Our findings suggest that CIP can be extended to higher-dimensional quantum systems, offering a promising avenue for developing quantum error correction in practical quantum hardware. Ultimately, this work paves the way for the construction of large-scale quantum computers.
