We contend that periodically (or period) is a more suitable term than length for describing the interval between two events, given that the time interval remains perceived as unchanged despite changes in an observer's state of motion. Furthermore, we propose that the term "count" is preferable to "measure" or "measurement" when referring to an integer value derived from comparing an interval to a standard. Consequently, in this work, we argue that "length should never be used again," and that "length measurement" should be replaced by "count," as exemplified by the title of this film.

This work is a revision of our 2008 film of the same name, incorporating refinements based on feedback from various individuals. We are particularly indebted to David Malament, whose insightful comments on an early draft prompted us to re-examine several assumptions. His suggestions led us to revise the argument to address the issue of "simultaneity," which is also reflected in the title of this film. Additionally, Matthew Brown noted that the film fails to demonstrate why "count" is superior to "length," a critique that resulted in further improvements.

The structure of the work is as follows: First, we establish the preference for "count" over "length" by presenting examples of scenarios where the number of length-measuring devices between two events appears invariant, even though the actual lengths vary. Second, we offer arguments supporting the claim that the time interval between two events is best characterized by a fixed count rather than varying lengths. Third, drawing on these arguments, we show that the time interval is "periodically" invariant across all changes in an observer's state of motion, regardless of whether they are inertial or accelerating. This paper proves a Petrenko-type boundedness result regarding the factors of unique values of L-functions corresponding to modular patterns. Furthermore, we provide a specific example that demonstrates the tightness of this bound. Our findings have the potential to refine the bound established by the second author and P. Bykovskii (arXiv:2005.01310) and to strengthen the conclusions of Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3 within Murty and Parnamalai's work (arXiv:2005.01310). Additionally, we offer a novel approach to addressing Corollary 2.2 in the same document (arXiv:2005.01310). To achieve these outcomes, we first establish a bound for the factors of a specific class of functions and subsequently apply this bound to derive our results. Finally, we introduce an example to illustrate that this bound is optimal. Notably, the methodology employed to obtain this bound appears to be distinct from the approach used by the second author and P. Bykovskii (arXiv:2005.01310).

This study investigates the impact of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) on spin transport within armchair graphene nanoribbons. We demonstrate that, in the absence of a magnetic field, spin currents reach their maximum when the spin polarization is oriented perpendicular to the plane of the graphene. Furthermore, by applying a transverse electric field, we show that the plane-perpendicular spin polarization can be efficiently rotated into the out-of-plane direction. These findings indicate that SOC provides a viable mechanism for adjusting spin polarization orientation, an essential feature for developing spintronic devices based on graphene. Additionally, we explore how varying SOC strengths and magnetic field orientations affect the evolution of spin polarization in armchair graphene nanoribbons. Finally, examining SOC in broader nanomaterials could facilitate the design of highly efficient spin-related devices for next-generation spintronics. These conclusions are supported by our theoretical calculations. Our results are anticipated to stimulate further research into the design of highly effective graphene-based spintronic technologies. This study examines the directed flow of identified light charged hadrons from Au+Au and isobar collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 200 GeV. Utilizing relativistic hadron resonance gas (RHGD) model calculations alongside the relativistic Boltzmann equation, we analyze the momentum anisotropies generated by the initial glasma fields, anisotropic side pressure from the quark-gluon plasma, and spectator-induced Coulomb fields. Our findings indicate that the directed flow of light hadrons is primarily governed by the initial glasma field, with significant modifications arising from anisotropic side pressure and spectator Coulomb interactions. Furthermore, we observe a strong system-size dependence on the anisotropic glasma momentum distribution, which results in a distinct directed flow pattern for Au+Au and isobar collisions. These distinctive signatures in the directed flow of luminous hadrons offer a potential means to probe glasma properties and the initial spatial anisotropy within the quark-gluon plasma. Additionally, we predict that the directed flow of Au+Au and isobar hadrons will exhibit similar $p_T$ dependence but differ in magnitude, with RHGD model calculations suggesting a flow ratio of $D_{\textrm{Ni}}/D_{\textrm{Au}}\approx 0.65$ at $p_T=2$ GeV/$c$. These predictions can be experimentally verified using the PHENIX data from Au+Ru+Rh+W collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 200 GeV. Finally, we note that the directed flow of identified hadrons in isobar collisions is highly sensitive to the initial glasma momentum anisotropy, thermal anisotropy, and the equation of state of the quark-gluon plasma. Consequently, future measurements of the directed flow of light hadrons in isobar collisions will provide valuable insights into the initial glasma momentum distribution, thermal anisotropy, and quark chemical potential. This study introduces a new approach to estimating the linear Koefman operator for systems exhibiting chaotic dynamics. By integrating sparse grid techniques with adaptive spectral methods, the proposed Adaptive Spectral Kernel (ASK) algorithm achieves rapid convergence, particularly when combined with systematic sampling. We apply this technique to estimate the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the Perron-Frobenius operator within a chaotic map defined on a compact domain. To assess the method's efficacy across various data scales, we utilize synthetic data generated via the kernel density estimator. Furthermore, the approach is validated using experimental data from the Stanford University TurboLab axial flow compressor surge dataset. For the synthetic case, we employ a singular value truncation method to isolate the system's Koefman modes. In the experimental application, the ASK algorithm effectively identifies the system's underlying dynamics. These findings demonstrate that the ASK algorithm is a highly effective tool for analyzing nonlinear systems, offering superior accuracy and efficiency compared to existing alternatives. The outward complex scaling technique enables the accurate study of atoms and molecules subjected to intense direct current (DC) fields by generating scaled bound states that asymptotically represent physical scattering states. This approach facilitates the modeling of photodetachment and photoionization processes involving low-energy electrons, such as those occurring in autoionization, autoionizing Feshbach resonances, and outer valence electrons. Furthermore, it serves as a vital component for simulating electron attachment, ring electron loss, and various forms of electron over-the-barrier ionization within atoms and molecules under strong DC fields. In these scenarios, electrons are theoretically bound but effectively ionized by the field, resulting in electrons with near-zero kinetic energy. The technique allows for the systematic exploration of low-energy electron emission, including angular distributions, while avoiding singularities and inaccuracies associated with extrapolating from high energies to zero. Additionally, it facilitates the investigation of electron capture, a phenomenon where incident electrons are captured into bound states, a process particularly relevant for anion formation in strong DC fields. This paper reviews the theoretical basis of the method, its implementation, and its applications in atomic and molecular systems exposed to intense DC fields. Furthermore, the study examines the technique's utility in modeling electron emission from nanostructures, such as carbon nanotubes, situated within such fields. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a prominent method for addressing the Schrödinger problem introduced by Geluk, van Handel, and Wang (arXiv:2005.07300). This study examines the localization dynamics of a quantum two-mass system localized by a centrally positioned $\delta$-potential barrier within the framework of the dynamic two-level approximation. By analyzing the localization mass rate as a function of the barrier strength, we determine the optimal localization strength that maximizes this rate. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of anharmonic coupling on the system's spectral properties and select a coupling constant that optimizes the localization mass rate, subject to specific spectral constraints. Finally, we compare our theoretical findings with numerical simulations to validate the accuracy of the dynamic two-level approximation. The resulting models demonstrate high fidelity, successfully reproducing both spectral characteristics and the time evolution of the initial wave function. These results indicate that the proposed approach is highly effective for studying quantum systems with localized states. Additionally, the methodology is broadly applicable to various central potentials and harmonic coupling configurations. This approach is particularly valuable for modeling excitons in semiconductor quantum dots and impurity states in semiconductors, offering a precise and efficient solution to the associated complex quantum mechanical challenges. The selected parameters are based on those of CdSe quantum dots. Ultimately, the findings hold significant potential for applications in quantum information processing and other quantum technologies. To illustrate this, we outline a scheme for quantum state transfer between two quantum dots using $\delta$-potential barriers and bridges as the connecting mechanism. In the bridging scenario, we show that the entire quantum state can be transferred from one dot to another with high efficiency within a specific time interval. Moreover, we demonstrate that $\delta$-potential barriers can serve as effective qubit gates by analyzing their effects on state evolution. In this context, we identify both unidirectional and bidirectional barriers capable of acting as NOT and CNOT gates, respectively, within a defined time range. The parameters for these analyses are derived from those of CdSe quantum dots. These outcomes suggest that the theoretically proposed devices could be realized experimentally in the near future. The models presented in this work may contribute to the advancement of quantum dot-based technologies. To support these findings, we have also included experimental data from CdSe quantum dots. Urban interaction data gathered prior to and throughout the COVID-19 pandemic reveals a marked decline in person-person contacts, a reduction in travel distances, and a contraction in the spatial extent of activity locations. While these changes were relatively uniform across most urban areas before the pandemic, they were significantly more pronounced among lower-income households, thereby intensifying existing income-based disparities in urban mobility. Furthermore, machine learning analysis indicates that pre-pandemic income level was a stronger predictor of the magnitude of the disparity than the city of residence. Consequently, the pandemic's behavioral shifts have amplified the risk that low-income individuals will face greater challenges in accessing essential resources once movement restrictions are lifted. This research underscores the necessity of a holistic approach to analyzing urban systems and the intricate relationship between behavior, behavior change, and urban form. To ensure more equitable urban outcomes, future policy and planning must explicitly address the underlying causes of these behavioral shifts. This study introduces and evaluates two nonlinear field-splitting preconditioners designed for two-phase flow within porous media featuring varying permeability and saturation capacities. The approach relies on applying a suitable preconditioner to a Schur complement derived from eliminating the liquid saturation variable. We derive a practical approximation of this preconditioner by utilizing a local permeability-based mobility ratio and by selecting the anisotropic mean permeability as the domain-scale mobility ratio to construct a coarse-grid block-diagonal preconditioner. These approximations are implemented within the Multipoint Flux Stabilized (MSFPA) framework. Numerical experiments involving vertical flows in a tilted, stratified medium and horizontal flows in a karstic medium demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed preconditioners. The term "nonlinear" refers to the method's ability to linearize nonlinear terms by treating them as piecewise constant. While the strategy shares similarities with existing nonlinear mobility-splitting techniques, it is specifically tailored for the MSFPA method. Consequently, the resulting field-split preconditioner is highly effective for a wide range of permeability contrasts and wettability conditions. However, for highly heterogeneous reservoirs, the current preconditioner may require subdomain-level field splitting to ensure rapid convergence. Future research will explore the development and comparison of various preconditioners based on these approximations. Finally, it is important to note that this work focuses exclusively on two-dimensional cases, and extending these findings to three-dimensional scenarios remains a subject for future investigation. Keywords: MSFPA, multipoint flux stabilization, nonlinear preconditioner, convergence, two-phase flow, porous media.

The feasibility of the ideal fluid warp drive concept was established in our earlier study (ArXiv:1809.00070). In this paper, we extend that concept to include de Sitter spacetime, where an observer perceives themselves as stationary within a "bubble" of ideal fluid. We also examine the implications of a non-zero cosmological constant for this proposal. The resulting warping of spacetime is driven by the issue of dark energy. We derive the necessary equations and define the parameters of the ideal fluid, which must take the form of a non-inertial fluid. Specifically, we obtain solutions expressed via Bessel functions, noting that these solutions do not require the fluid to be sonic. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the required spacetime metric can be achieved through a specific motion of the observer. This motion is governed by the cosmological constant and the equation of state of the ideal fluid. We also address the energy requirements for the cosmic constant solution, showing that the energy needed for this scheme is significantly lower than that of the ideal fluid warp drive proposed in our 2018 paper. Finally, we address the energy conditions associated with both schemes. While the first approach necessitates negative energy, the second may also require it, although the magnitude is substantially reduced compared to the first. Both scenarios rely on the existence of exotic matter. We conclude that the cosmic drive scheme is more viable than the original ideal fluid warp drive proposal. In both cases, the speed of the observer is determined by the equation of state of the ideal fluid and the cosmological constant. We also present the relationship between the observer's speed and the parameters of the ideal fluid. Finally, we show that the speed of the observer can be arbitrarily large, provided the cosmological constant and the equation of state are sufficiently large. However, we also indicate that the speed cannot reach arbitrary magnitudes. Specifically, the speed is limited by the parameters of the ideal fluid and the cosmological constant. Accurate and timely data is essential for managing urban systems and enhancing the quality of life for city dwellers. However, cities often struggle to access, manage, and utilize their data effectively. The GUIDES project aims to develop open-source, scalable, and adaptable solutions to empower these data-driven initiatives. Specifically, the GUIDES Data Engineering & Infrastructure (GUIDES-DEI) work package addresses the foundational technical challenges by creating data engineering and infrastructure components. These components are designed to support downstream GUIDES activities focused on data access, management, and processing. This paper presents the initial findings from GUIDES-DEI, offering a high-level overview of a data infrastructure solution that enables efficient data access and processing. Additionally, we introduce a set of data management tools that facilitate data governance and discovery, as well as data transformation and integration, for both machine and human users. Finally, we describe a data processing solution that provides a framework for machine learning and artificial intelligence workflows, including data preparation, model training, and evaluation. This work represents an early stage of our ongoing research into a modular, multi-purpose data infrastructure for cities, which will be further explored in future publications. By providing these foundational services, we aim to reduce the complexity of data handling for application developers, thereby accelerating the deployment of data-driven solutions in urban environments. The resulting software tools and infrastructure, which embody our research findings, are made available under an open-source license. This paper serves as an introduction to the GUIDES Data Platform, a flexible and modular framework for data engineering and processing. This platform supports various data services and is designed to be extensible for integration with additional services. To support this broader vision, we also provide sample code for implementing city data services, which can be customized for specific use cases. This work demonstrates that a unified, open data infrastructure can significantly lower the barriers to entry for developing intelligent urban systems. We believe that adopting such a comprehensive data infrastructure is essential for the widespread implementation of smart city solutions. Our framework is particularly well-suited for integration into existing urban data platforms and for enabling the development of intelligent city applications. This approach is a critical step toward realizing the full potential of urban data and fostering sustainable urban development. We introduce and implement a laser-driven spin-dephasing protocol to investigate heating rates, non-thermal excitations, and thermalization dynamics within a two-dimensional Bose-Fermi ion mixture. In this setup, a single $^{171}$Yb$^+$ ion, acting as a spin-dephasing probe, is embedded with a degenerate gas of $^{171}$Yb$^+$ ions. The spin-dephasing signal is highly sensitive to the probed ion's motional state, allowing us to characterize its vibrational mode amplitude and the width of its motional wavefunction. By embedding this simple, intuitive protocol into an established experimental system, we demonstrate its robustness and utility for measuring the weak coupling of individual ions to their collective vibrational modes. These measurements can be integrated into quantum information processing tasks to monitor and mitigate decoherence arising from ion-ion interactions. Furthermore, our study of the dephasing process yields a precise measurement of the ion crystal's heating rate. We observe that, consistent with both theoretical predictions and other experimental results, the heating rate is highest at the crystal edges. Our findings offer a direct comparison with heating rates derived from ion-ion qubit gate operations, revealing that the laser pulses utilized for two-qubit gates can induce heating comparable to the crystal's background heating rate. Our results confirm that, following gate pulses, the ions remain within the ground state of the collective vibrational mode, exhibiting only minor thermal excitations. Finally, we compare these heating rate measurements with those obtained from two-qubit gates, thereby advancing our understanding of the heating dynamics in trapped-ion systems. Our work underscores the value of employing multiple, complementary methods to measure heating rates, as this approach provides a more complete picture of the underlying physical processes. These findings are essential for advancing large-scale trapped-ion quantum computing. Furthermore, our study illustrates the potential of spin-dephasing experiments as a diagnostic tool to assess the performance of quantum information processing protocols. By utilizing this tool, we can better understand the physical mechanisms driving crystal heating, which is a critical factor in scaling up trapped-ion quantum computers. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the spatial dependence of heating rates in large ion crystals may necessitate the use of ion subarrays to achieve the large quantum volumes necessary for practical quantum computing. We introduce an efficient method to investigate the light-matter interaction in Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS). This approach combines the density matrix equation with the time-dependent Schrödinger equation to accurately model the quantum mechanics of both chemical bonding and light interaction at the atom-by-atom level. We validate this methodology by simulating TERS signals from a single carbon atom, comparing quantum mechanical results with those derived from semi-empirical tight-binding and density functional theory. Our findings indicate that the derived method is a fast and effective tool for modeling light-matter interactions in the near-field, with direct applicability to TERS. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the technique is scalable to simulate larger systems, such as graphene, where it can capture the impact of strain, defects, and adatoms on the enhancement factor. This establishes a pathway to predict theoretically the contribution of non-tip atoms to the total Raman enhancement in TERS. Finally, our results suggest that the recently observed submolecular resolution in TERS images may stem from spatial variations in the local electronic structure of the tip. However, this investigation is often hindered by the lack of deep observations of faint, non-starburst regions. **Aims.** Our goal is to detect non-thermal emission in the Sardinia Radio Telescope's (SRT) field of view, specifically targeting the diffuse interstellar medium (ISM) of nearby galaxies. **Methods.** We conducted deep observations of the 3C 295 group, the NGC 3077-NGC 4472 pair, and the NGC 3627-NGC 4214 pair using the SRT at 1.4 GHz. **Results.** The 3C 295 group exhibits a diffuse component with a surface brightness of approximately 10 mJy/beam, while the NGC 3627-NGC 4214 pair shows a signal around 1 mJy/beam. The 1.4 GHz band reveals a complex structure in the NGC 4472-NGC 3077 pair, characterized by a diffuse component of about 0.1 mJy/beam. Additionally, we identified a new radio source within NGC 3377. **Conclusions.** These findings provide evidence for the existence of the "Cosmic Web" and suggest that the SRT is capable of detecting the diffuse Galactic-like component in nearby galaxies. Furthermore, the system demonstrates the ability to detect very faint, large-scale structures in the nearby Universe. The new source found in NGC 3377 may indicate a link between old and young stellar populations. Ammonium sulfate serves as a model for molecular crystals, where the entropy change during ferroelectric transitions is well-documented but its origin remains debated. This study demonstrates that the extensive entropy alteration arises from the alteration of entropy associated with molecular orientations. By employing the Monte Carlo method to simulate the molecular crystal within the ferroelectric phase, we calculated the entropy change resulting from orientational disorder. Our findings indicate that this computed entropy alteration is of the same order of magnitude as the experimentally measured total entropy change across the entire ferroelectric transition. Furthermore, we observed that the entropy alteration originates from the loss of information regarding molecular positions and their orientations at the transition point. Consequently, our results confirm that Ammonium sulfate is a suitable molecular crystal for investigating the link between order and information. Finally, we conclude that the entropy change is driven by the increase in the system's information capacity during the transition. These insights are anticipated to advance the understanding of entropy alterations in other functional materials. Notably, the proposed methodology is broadly applicable to the total entropy changes observed in various types of transitions. The quantum-like evolution of a lattice system built upon the complexification of the $E_8$ lattice is examined within the framework of Heisenberg lattice spin algebra. This approach incorporates both quantum entanglement and quantum contextuality. The study derives relevant formulas for the probability amplitudes associated with the final state of a two-qudit system, along with expressions for these probabilities. Additionally, the contextuality of the $E_8$ lattice system's state vector is analyzed through the calculation of the average value of the Clifford algebra element $c_{12345678}$, which corresponds to the 8-vector $e_{\infty}$. This analysis highlights the influence of quantum entanglement and contextuality on the lattice system's evolution. Finally, the paper explores the potential significance of these findings for understanding the structure of the universe's physical laws. Keywords: Quantum lattice, $E_8$, lattice spin algebra, Heisenberg algebra, Clifford algebra, Fierz identity, Pauli matrices, quantum entanglement, quantum contextuality, physical laws of the universe.

This paper examines the strict limit of the $k$-nearest neighbor search problem for time series when using the Fréchet distance as a metric. We demonstrate that for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a sequence of time series datasets where the proportion of queries possessing $k$ close neighbors (based on the $\varepsilon$-discrimination metric) approaches zero as the data generation parameter $\delta$ approaches zero. This finding establishes the strict limit for the classical $k$-nearest neighbor search problem in this context. Furthermore, we extend this result to the estimated $k$-nearest neighbor search problem, where the quality of results is evaluated by the percentage of data points correctly identified as close neighbors. We prove that for this scenario, there exists a specific threshold $\delta_0$ such that for every $\delta > \delta_0$, the number of query points with close neighbors remains zero. Consequently, the strict limits for both the classical and estimated $k$-nearest neighbor search problems are defined by the Fréchet distance's inability to discriminate between time series objects. The paper also explores the relationship between this limitation and the Fréchet distance's invariance under reparameterization. Finally, we outline methods to relax these strict limits, including the adoption of alternative metrics like discrete Fréchet, reducing the query parameter $k$, and increasing the query parameter $\kappa$ in the estimated version. Additionally, we establish strict limits for another problem: the $k$-center clustering problem using the Fréchet distance. Finally, we examine whether combining the Fréchet distance with other metrics can yield effective discriminative similarity measures for time series. The study concludes with several conjectures and open questions. Notably, the proposed approach for discriminative similarity measurement is general and can be applied to various other problems. Measurement errors inevitably arise during the data collection process. To address this, we introduce a novel algorithm designed to mitigate such errors by iteratively unravelling the noisy data generation process. We demonstrate that this method converges to a model that produces a data-generating process closely aligning with the original, noise-free one. The efficacy of our approach is validated through simulations and case studies involving two real-world datasets. First, we apply the method to a binary classification task using the Breast Cancer Wisconsin Diagnostic dataset, successfully lowering error rates by 10%. Second, we evaluate our method on a continuous outcome prediction task using the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset, achieving a 15% reduction in prediction error. Furthermore, we highlight the method's potential for addressing conceptual noise within datasets. Our results indicate that the algorithm performs effectively across various data types, including binary, continuous, and count data. Additionally, we demonstrate that it remains effective in high-dimensional settings and when dealing with non-linear relationships. Finally, we illustrate how the method can be adapted for time series data by applying it to a well-known example from the literature. The interaction between humans and robots encompasses various modes, ranging from autonomous robot operations to human robotics teleoperation. A third mode, shared autonomy, involves collaborating with robots to achieve joint goals, though this concept is not yet widely understood by human users. This paper introduces shared autonomy as a distinct mode of human-machine interaction and demonstrates that it can be effectively conveyed to people through well-crafted metaphors. We present the "co-pilot" metaphor as a metaphor for shared autonomy, showing that this analogy helps make the concept accessible to both children and adults. Additionally, we provide practical recommendations for designing shared autonomy systems to facilitate their explanation via these metaphors. The study includes two studies, one with children and one with adults, which confirm that human users find the co-pilot metaphor intuitive and that it leads to more natural interactions with robots. These findings highlight the potential of metaphors to enhance human-robot interaction and offer a pathway to broaden the demographic scope of shared autonomy applications. Furthermore, these insights can inform the design of future collaborative systems, such as social robots, to improve human-user interactions. Overall, this work underscores the value of drawing parallels between existing standards and new technologies to advance human-robot interaction. By leveraging familiar concepts like the co-pilot metaphor, shared autonomy can be successfully communicated, thereby expanding the range of applications and increasing the number of individuals who can benefit from interacting with robots. The paper concludes by discussing the broader implications of this research for the field of human-robot interaction. Specifically, we explore how metaphors can serve as a mechanism for explaining shared autonomy and how this approach can inform the design of collaborative systems to optimize human-user engagement. The study also examines the potential for expanding the demographics of shared autonomy users and suggests avenues for future research, such as investigating the long-term effects of using the co-pilot metaphor on human-robot interactions. The paper also addresses the ethical implications of using metaphors to explain shared autonomy, including the potential for the co-pilot metaphor to influence human users' perceptions of robots and their trust in them. Finally, the paper calls for further research into the development of more effective metaphors for explaining shared autonomy and the measurement of the impact of these metaphors on human-robot interactions. The work also highlights the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure that the use of metaphors in explaining shared autonomy is both accurate and meaningful. The paper concludes by emphasizing the importance of user-centered design in the development of collaborative systems and the need for ongoing evaluation of the impact of the co-pilot metaphor on human-robot

To enhance the performance of the 2-D complementary array code set (ZCAC), a direct construction method based on multivariable functions is proposed. This approach enables the generation of 2-D ZCACs with arbitrary lengths using a straightforward algorithm. By incorporating prime numbers and performing specific permutations, the method ensures that the resulting 2-D ZCACs maintain zero correlation zone (ZCZ) properties. Furthermore, to significantly enhance 2-D ZCAC performance, an inter-group supplementary code set (IGSAC) is introduced. This new code set maintains the ZCZ property within the 2-D ZCAC groups. Additionally, an inter-group supplementary code set derived from the two-dimensional all-zero vector is developed, offering flexible 2-D ZCZ characteristics. Numerical simulations confirm the validity of the proposed IGSAC. Consequently, the combination of IGSAC and the direct construction method results in the creation of the 2-D supplementary code set (SAC), which exhibits distinct performance compared to 2-D ZCAC. The results indicate that the proposed 2-D SAC offers superior performance in terms of peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) and zero-correlation zone (ZCZ) when applied to 2-D radar pulse compression. Computed Tomography (CT) images are reconstructed from projection data collected across various angles. However, when artifacts stem from physical limitations, such as insufficient photon counts per projection, they appear as noise in the final image. These limitations are common in multi-material scans, where different substances absorb X-rays differently, leading to varying levels of noise. Consequently, different materials manifest with distinct noise variances in the reconstructed images. To address this, we introduce a joint framework capable of simultaneously reconstructing images and modeling their heteroscedastic noise, along with decomposing constituent materials. Our approach leverages the inherent non-convexity of this problem, utilizing an alternating algorithm that iteratively updates the effective potential of each material. This method adapts the sensor noise model for every material, accounting for their unique absorption properties. Furthermore, our technique demonstrates robustness against material identification errors by successfully handling minor mismatches between assumed and actual material types. Finally, we extend the framework to address image uncertainty by providing a mechanism to propagate the variational uncertainty associated with each material. Numerical experiments confirm that, compared to existing methods, our approach achieves superior image reconstruction and more accurate material decomposition. The code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/ahmedhassan1995/PCCT}. The results presented here were developed before the advent of the uncertainty quantification module. The proposed framework holds significant potential for real-world applications, including quality control in manufacturing and medical diagnostics. In quality control, it can reduce costs by enabling the detection of minor material variations in products like plastic components. In medicine, it can identify low-density areas in bone scans that may indicate osteoporosis. Ultimately, our method offers a more comprehensive solution for analyzing multi-material CT scans. Gap surface plasmons are characterized by strong electromagnetic field confinement within nanometer-scale spaces, prompting inquiries into the influence of spatial electron-electron interactions on plasmon resonances. This study examines the stability of gap plasmons by analyzing the optical response of two spheres separated by a small vacuum gap. Theoretically, two critical factors are addressed: the nonlocality of the electron gas, where the density response at a specific point depends on the electric potential across a finite region, and electron spill-over, referring to the finite extent of electron density outside the spherical surfaces. Theoretical predictions regarding resonance shifts and field confinement are validated by comparing them with finite element method simulations of electron densities and electromagnetic fields. Our findings indicate that gap plasmons do not persist in the limit of infinitely large sphere permittivities, $|\epsilon_s| \rightarrow \infty$, because of electron spill-over. Although gap-mode resonance wavelengths scale with the $1/4$ power of the sphere's radius, $R$, the associated field confinement weakens as $R$ increases. Conversely, gap modes exhibit greater robustness when spheres are composed of materials with large but finite permittivities. Furthermore, when gap-mode resonance wavelengths are comparable to those of bulk plasmons, electron spill-over effects become negligible. In this regime, adjusting the sphere permittivity to values slightly below infinity enables effective gap-mode field confinement. Finally, considering a finite electron gas velocity reveals a slight redshift in gap plasmons, with resonance wavelength shifts scaling as $1/R$. This demonstrates that the initial assumptions of electron nonlocality and spill-over effects are mutually compatible. Ultimately, our results confirm that gap plasmons can be sustained by accounting for the interplay between electron spill-over and nonlocality. These insights offer a pathway to achieve tunable, gap-mode resonances, tunable spin-polarized gap modes, and novel electron transport phenomena. Such advancements are essential for advancing nanoscale optical and spintronic technologies. To illustrate these concepts, we also examine a specific system of two spheres connected by a narrow metallic bridge. In this configuration, gap plasmons can be further tuned by adjusting the bridge's material properties. Our findings also highlight the critical role of bridge geometry in determining optical resonances and field distributions. These results may facilitate the creation of new, highly efficient plasmonic devices. Additionally, the proposed electron-based plasmonic systems could serve as a foundation for developing ultra-sensitive chemical and biological sensors. We introduce an interactive machine learning approach for contextually acing NER that leverages term significance metrics. Contextually aware NER (CNER) represents a promising paradigm, utilizing term importance to identify novel entities within a domain's existing knowledge. While significant, this term-based significance signal remains largely underutilized by current interactive machine learning systems. Our method employs Term significance via Random Forests (TSRF) to assign feature weights to the decision tree learner driving the CNER system, thereby enhancing efficiency without sacrificing accuracy. We demonstrate that TSRF effectively boosts performance across a broad spectrum of standard NER tasks, even those lacking extensive annotated data. Furthermore, we illustrate how CNER systems can interactively apply TSRF to query large corpora and reveal novel entities, marking a key step toward achieving practical utility. Our system enables users to input words for evaluation, instantly receives results, and adjusts feature weights to refine performance. We demonstrate that CNER accurately identifies entities significant to the user's domain of interest, even in domains where the system previously had no training data. Additionally, CNER outperforms existing interactive machine learning learners, such as Bandit Average, in both accuracy and runtime. Finally, we show that CNER can discover entities that extend beyond established domain knowledge, including new terms associated with diseases, U.S. states, and U.S. universities. These entities possess high Term significance Random Forest (TSRF) scores and exhibit low false positive rates. Our findings indicate that CNER can identify entities that are 2.5 times more significant than those found by other interactive machine learning methods. These entities are further validated by their presence in news articles and scientific literature. Overall, CNER provides a highly effective tool for the contextually aware discovery of novel entities. It can identify entities relevant to a specific domain using only a small corpus of examples, even if that corpus was not curated by the domain experts themselves. This capability significantly advances the goal of making machine learning more accessible to practitioners. By enabling the easy testing of different feature weightings, our system allows practitioners to rapidly refine and optimize their CNER systems. Practitioners can then interactively query large corpora to discover new entities, gaining a deeper understanding of their domain. Our system achieves this with a 10-fold improvement in runtime compared to other interactive machine learning approaches. Temporal data offers valuable insights into the dynamics of temporal systems and the relationships between events, yet temporal series are frequently displayed passively, restricting the analytical capabilities of end-users. To enhance the analysis of temporal data, we introduce a high-interactivity visualization framework designed for time-series and time-point data with significant longitudinal dimensions. This system manages the rendering of temporal data across multiple devices and the sharing of interactive elements between source and sink devices. By integrating visualization and interaction capabilities with the distributed rendering of temporal data, this framework supports the detailed inspection of temporal data's longitudinal dimension. Furthermore, the interactivity between devices enables collaborative analysis of temporal data, including the sharing of visual encodings and interactive behaviors. We illustrate the application of this framework to temporal data using various examples. Our evaluation demonstrates that the framework facilitates the analysis of temporal data's longitudinal dimension, which is often overlooked in traditional temporal data visualization. Additionally, the framework promotes collaborative analysis of temporal data, thereby improving the overall analysis process. Finally, we outline the framework's limitations and suggest future research directions. Our work demonstrates that the proposed framework effectively supports the analysis of temporal data's longitudinal dimension, a feature not supported by existing temporal visualization frameworks. Furthermore, temporal data analysis can be enhanced by leveraging the interactivity between temporal devices, which our framework enables. However, our framework is limited to time-series and time-point data with a significant longitudinal dimension. Digital health records are essential for delivering high-quality, patient-centered care. While various methods exist for querying and analyzing these records, they are limited to specific views and fail to leverage information across different domains. To address this, we introduce the Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network (D2GNN), a novel framework designed to learn diverse similarity relationships within electronic health records. This approach employs a graph neural network to process diverse embeddings of health records, utilizing a graph attention mechanism to aggregate information from related patients. We demonstrate that D2GNN surpasses baseline models in generating diverse similarity representations, as measured by the DiversityMax metric, and leads to superior performance on clinical tasks. Furthermore, we apply this framework to a clinical scenario involving the prediction of 28-day mortality for patients with sepsis. Experimental results indicate that mortality predictions using our diverse embeddings are at least as accurate as those derived from state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we find that ensembling predictions from multiple runs of D2GNN yields enhanced performance. Finally, we observe that incorporating health knowledge through D2GNN improves clinical utility, resulting in higher AUC scores compared to using purely data-driven embeddings. To our knowledge, this study represents the first application of graph neural networks to the domain of digital health records. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi2019/D2GNN. This study examines the interaction between an electrolyte solution and a polar solvent featuring a charged, soft interface. A self-consistent framework is established to determine the potential distribution within a thin electric double layer, incorporating solvent polarization effects up to third-nearest neighbors. The resulting second-order equation is solved using the finite element method. Numerical results indicate that increasing third-neighbor polarization effects causes the surface potential to approach that of a hard interface, reducing sensitivity to surface compliance. Furthermore, a decrease in dielectric constant amplifies these polarization effects, thereby increasing the significance of the soft interface. These findings offer fresh perspectives on how solvent polarization influences the electric double layer at a charged, soft interface. Additionally, the potential distribution model developed here is applicable to studying soft matter systems where polarization plays a critical role. Finally, this theoretical contribution supports the development of new energy storage technologies, such as supercapacitors, by enabling the design of charged soft interfaces in electrolytes. Specifically, it aids in understanding how interfacial properties impact device performance, facilitating the creation of more efficient solid-state electrolytes and membranes. This paper introduces a collaborative network coding framework designed to minimize energy usage in wireless networks. Within this setup, a subset of nodes is designated as relays to support transmission from a source to a destination. All relays employ binary network coding, assigning '1' or '0' to the output based on the number of received '1' packets versus '0' packets. To enhance energy efficiency, the study jointly optimizes relay selection, power allocation, and power distribution among the selected relays. The study examines magnetic moments, exchange splitting, energy levels, wave functions, orbital and spin magnetic susceptibilities of a single Mn atom adsorbed on Nb(110), as well as the exchange interaction between two adjacent Mn atoms on the same surface. These calculations employ the relativistic initial principles theory. The computed exchange interaction energy is approximately $-0.05$ eV, suggesting that the magnetic coupling between two neighboring Mn atoms on Nb(110) is antiferromagnetic. Furthermore, the magnetic susceptibility of two adjacent Mn atoms on the Nb(110) surface is roughly $10^{5}$ times greater than that of an isolated Mn atom on the same surface. The observed enhancement in magnetic susceptibility for the dimer is attributed to the exchange interaction between the two Mn atoms. Additionally, the magnetic moment of two adjacent Mn atoms on Nb(110) is calculated to be $4.02\,\mu_{B}$, which is $0.2\,\mu_{B}$ smaller than the experimental value. Finally, the energy gap between the spin-up and spin-down states for two adjacent Mn atoms on Nb(110) is determined to be $-0.17$ eV, confirming the stability of the antiferromagnetic configuration. The relative contributions of relativistic effects, spin-orbit coupling, and relativistic mass to the energy gap are $1.0$, $-1.2$, and $1.2$ times the energy spin splitting, respectively. Consequently, the relativistic effect is the primary contributor to the exchange interaction energy. The wave functions for the $3d$ shell of the dimer are predominantly composed of $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$, and $d_{zx}$ orbitals, with the $d_{xy}$ orbital being the most significant. This finding is attributed to the specific crystal field environment of Mn atoms on the Nb(110) surface. Finally, the relativistic initial principles theory proves effective for investigating exchange interactions within magnetic atoms on metal surfaces. The findings may prove valuable for designing new magnetic materials and developing spintronic devices. Additionally, the relativistic character of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states is confirmed. The research was conducted using the computational resources of the High-Performance Computing Center at the University of Science and Technology of China. Non-linear X-ray absorption edge spectroscopy, driven by intense electron beams and femtosecond pulses, has recently enabled the study of electron correlation effects in complex materials. However, interpreting these experimental results remains challenging due to their complex nature and the intricate interplay of multiple physical processes. To address this, we introduce a physically interpretable rate framework that mathematically models the temporal evolution of electron populations, thereby simplifying the analysis of non-linear absorption edge data. This approach is demonstrated using simulated two-photon absorption spectra for copper. Furthermore, this framework can be readily extended to accommodate additional phenomena, such as radiative decay and higher-order non-resonant processes. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a more accessible and comprehensive understanding of non-linear absorption edge effects in materials, facilitating their future application in electronic, spintronics, and photonic technologies. Additionally, the simulation code utilized in this study is publicly accessible via a GitHub repository. Model error represents a fundamental challenge in the dynamical systems community, yet it is also a critical component for creating more natural and effective mathematical models. This survey aims to outline a new organizational framework for interpreting various approaches to mechanistic modeling with intelligence, which we define as "EMMWithMachine." We argue that this perspective will unify diverse methodologies for introducing machine intelligence into dynamical systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that when naturalists embed intelligent mechanisms within their models, the resulting frameworks are deeply tied to machine learning, requiring novel interpretations of established machine learning concepts. Furthermore, we illustrate that this approach clarifies emerging proposals for self-correcting dynamical systems, thereby establishing a unified view of mechanistic models harboring internal machine learning capabilities. Finally, we conclude by discussing open questions regarding EMMWithMachine, including its relationship to standard machine learning, the characterization of its space of possible models, and the associated learning algorithms. We believe this structure will serve as a valuable resource for both mechanistic modelers seeking to integrate intelligence and machine learners exploring applications within dynamical systems. This research investigates the contextual nature of two distinct problems involving set addition under inequality constraints: the order-k preference set union problem (PkSU) and the order-k non-preference set union problem (PkNSU). Both require the union of k disjoint sets, where each set contains only positive integers, subject to the condition that no two resulting elements share the same value. PkSU is a preference ordering issue involving both additive and anti-additive attributes, whereas PkNSU relies solely on additive attributes. We establish that PkSU is NP-hard, while PkNSU admits a polynomial-time optimal solution. Additionally, we introduce a new NP-hard problem, multiobjective order-k preference set union (MPkSU), which addresses scenarios involving multiple attributes. Finally, we examine the practical utility of these two problems through two real-world applications. As computer scientists, we argue that the distinction between preference and non-preference set union is significant and that this paper effectively clarifies that distinction.

Keywords: Set union, Preference ordering, Non-preference, Order-k, Polynomial-time, NP-hard.

The connection between thermodynamic and dynamic properties in supercooled liquids remains a theoretically unresolved issue. This study examines this relationship within a specific class of molecular liquids by employing the glass transition temperatures ($T_g$) of numerous polymer liquids as calibration points. Our findings indicate that the product $T_g\rho c_p^{-1}$—representing the temperature at which the crossover from weak to strong temperature dependence occurs—is constant across all these liquids. This suggests that the thermodynamic framework underlying the relationship between thermodynamic and dynamic properties in supercooled liquids is more universal than previously believed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the recently proposed "fragility index" ($\Phi$) is likely an artifact of specific experimental conditions, such as the molecular weight and cooling protocols used to define $T_g$. Consequently, we propose that $\Phi$ can be substituted with the more universal thermodynamic criterion $\Psi$, defined as the reduced undercooling at which the heat capacity exhibits a power-law divergence. The equivalence between $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ in their respective temperature scales confirms that $\Psi$ serves as a more robust measure of thermodynamic and dynamic characteristics in supercooled liquids. Additionally, we establish a universal correlation between the temperature of the maximum heat capacity and the fragility index, showing that all polymer liquids fall on a single curve when $\Psi$ is used. Finally, we explore the connection between the fragility criterion and the concept of configurational entropy. We argue that the universal correlation between $\Psi$ and fragility arises from the interplay between the entropy of thermal fluctuations and the entropy associated with the landscape of the potential energy surface. This proposed relationship between $\Psi$ and fragility is also validated by simulations of model liquids. Collectively, these results provide a robust framework for interpreting the relationship between thermodynamic and dynamic properties in supercooled liquids. We compute the weights of Kontsevich graphs for curvature graphs (CGs) and Link graphs (LGs) within the context of formal symplectic Poisson structures. Our approach relies on the concept of symplectic fat graphs. As applications, we establish several conjectures proposed by F. Kassel and by J. Bell and D. B. Fuchs, demonstrating that calculating the weights of CGs and LGs in these formal structures is equivalent to calculating the weights of their corresponding symplectic fat graphs (SFGs). Additionally, we examine the properties of SFGs, including their isomorphism classes, weight calculation methods, and an invariant defined as the difference between the number of inner and outer vertices. We verify several conjectures regarding these properties and present an algorithm for determining weights using computer algebra. Furthermore, we evaluate the algorithm's efficiency by providing examples of computed weights for SFGs across various dimensions and inner vertex counts. Finally, we calculate the weights for SFGs with a single inner vertex across different dimensions, presenting an algorithm to express these weights as linear combinations of the weights of connected graphs, thereby reducing the problem to connected cases. We also verify a conjecture stating that the weights of "dumbbell" graphs are positive, and we compute the weights for all SFGs with up to four vertices. Finally, we compute the weights for CGs in two-dimensional formal symplectic Poisson structures up to 12 vertices and for LGs up to 9 vertices, providing an algorithm to express these weights as linear combinations of connected graph weights, thus reducing them to the connected case. We conclude by presenting an algorithm to express the weights of arbitrary symplectic Poisson graph weights as linear combinations of connected graph weights. Finally, we list the weights for structures with graphs containing no loops and exactly one vertex across dimensions 2 through 10. Finally, we verify the conjecture that the weights of "lollipop" graphs are positive. The appendix contains the full list of weights for structures with graphs with up to 12 vertices and 2 curvature points, including a conjecture regarding the signs of these weights. D 104, 026006 (2021)]. We identify a qualitative distinction between entanglement entropy in the ground state and the familiar thermal entropy in the high-temperature regime. This divergence is interpreted as the entanglement entropy arising from integrating out the coupled fields. Furthermore, we explore potential connections to holographic duals. Finally, we present a speculative argument linking our findings to the entanglement entropy of defects in large $N$ gauge theories. These arguments rely on the proposed CFT and a holographic dual involving $q$ hypermultiplets on the worldvolume of $D3$-branes embedded within $N$ $D7$-branes. Additionally, the relationship between entanglement entropy and defects in various limits of the proposed dual offers a promising avenue for future investigation. Our arguments suggest that the defect contribution to entanglement entropy is proportional to $q/N$ in the large $N$ limit. Consequently, the pre-factor of the entanglement entropy for a hypermultiplet in the proposed dual is $2\pi/4\pi=1/2$, which aligns with the entanglement entropy of a defect in the proposed dual. This result also matches the entanglement entropy of a defect in a free $D3$-D7 system. Finally, we demonstrate that the entanglement entropy of a defect in a $D3$-D7 system is proportional to $q/N$ in the large $N$ limit, whereas for a D3-D7-D7 system, it is proportional to $q/N^2$. Furthermore, this observation extends to other research within the Feng and Li corpus. Consequently, it is recommended that subsequent citations clarify this distinction by noting that such works present specific applications of a established technique rather than offering a "comprehensive framework" as previously claimed. Additionally, it is worth highlighting that the valuation of options can be formulated as a free boundary problem in various ways, with the specific approach depending on the available analytical and numerical techniques. In this context, the formulation by Feng and Li represents just one of many possible approaches. Finally, it is crucial to recognize that the term "free boundary problem" originates from partial differential equations, where the boundary signifies the limit of the region where the problem is defined. Given that Asian option pricing involves solving an integro-differential equation rather than a partial differential equation, the term "moving boundary problem" would arguably be more appropriate. We introduce a novel method for determining the average gamma-ray flux ($F_{\rm CGB}$) originating from galaxy clusters, utilizing data from Fermi-LAT observations of 1,000 clusters within the redshift range $0.03 < z < 0.3$. Our results indicate that $F_{\rm CGB}$ is approximately $10^{-10}$ ph cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with a statistical uncertainty of 50%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this diffuse emission is likely produced by cosmic rays (CRs) within clusters. By comparing CR densities derived from Fermi-LAT data with those predicted by numerical simulations, we establish that the CR density in cluster intra-medium (ICM) is roughly $10^{-8}$-$10^{-7}$ of the proton density, with a systematic uncertainty of 50%. Additionally, we show that the gamma-ray flux from clusters is roughly 100 times greater than that from the field, and that this flux remains constant across the observed redshift range. Finally, we discuss the potential significance of this emission in the context of the Fermi-LAT cosmic ray background. We introduce a novel approach for analyzing traditional cosmological collider signals by utilizing a new class of primitives known as "primal features." These features represent the most fundamental building blocks of cosmological collider physics, which stem from massive particles interacting within perturbation theory. While composite signals are typically understood as linear combinations of primal features within a specific parameter space, this paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the complete parameter space. By examining the full range, we elucidate the origins of unusual phenomena and offer a unified perspective on existing signals. Our findings indicate that at high scales, primal power spectra exhibit a step function structure, a characteristic that may be particularly significant for next-generation surveys. Furthermore, we explore the relationships between primal features and identify a new variant of the oscillating feature, termed the "sawtooth feature." Finally, we address the issue of non-physical behavior in primal correlators and propose solutions to resolve it. Overall, this work aims to serve as a complete reference for primitive feature space. Additionally, we provide open-source code for computing the power spectrum and correlators of primal features, which can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenchenWang2017/PrimalFeatures. We anticipate that this code will become a valuable resource for future research. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success across various computer vision tasks, their decision-making processes remain opaque. This study investigates the internal mechanisms of deep CNNs to gain a granular insight into how they process visual data. We propose a novel visual-semantic (Vi-Se) filter attention framework that integrates filter activation and attention strategies. Specifically, our approach dynamically selects relevant filters from network layers that capture critical visual semantics for a specific class, while simultaneously activating only the most pertinent filters within each layer. By combining these two mechanisms, the Vi-Se framework effectively balances computational efficiency with high accuracy. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets reveal that this framework successfully uncovers the internal workings of CNNs, demonstrating that these mechanisms are intrinsically embedded within the networks. Furthermore, the Vi-Se framework achieves state-of-the-art results on the Caltech-UCSD Birds (UCSDB) and Stanford University Database of Cars (SC10) datasets for image classification, while simultaneously providing interpretability. Additionally, we visualize network activations and filters to further elucidate the internal processing mechanisms of CNNs. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the proposed Vi-Se framework offers valuable insights into the workings of deep CNNs, enhancing our understanding of their internal operations. We examine the influence of spin-phonon coupling on the attractive interaction between doped holes within one-dimensional cuprates. Utilizing a model that integrates spin and phonon degrees of freedom, alongside an effective phonon coupling, we identify a specific phonon mode that generates a significant, long-range attractive force between holes. This finding is supported by a perturbative analysis of the phonon-mediated interaction. Our results indicate that phonons can facilitate a long-distance attractive interaction comparable in magnitude to the exchange interaction, implying that phonons play a critical role in the many-body dynamics of these systems. Furthermore, the competition between the exchange interaction and the phonon-induced attraction may help explain the observed variation in the superexchange coupling $J$ across different cuprate families. Finally, our findings suggest that the phonon-induced interaction is essential for comprehending the low-temperature phase diagram of one-dimensional cuprates. Additionally, the phonon effect could be responsible for the recently reported attraction between holes in the $\mathrm{La}_{2}\mathrm{CuO}_{4}$ Mott insulator. Our proposed mechanism offers a fresh perspective on the longstanding debate regarding hole-hole interactions in cuprates. Additionally, the resulting phonon-mediated interaction can be incorporated into existing theoretical models to investigate hole pairing in one-dimensional cuprates. This study introduces a method for reconstructing causal graphs from observational data using linear structural equation models. The approach is evaluated by comparing the recovered graphs against established literature and then applied to rebuild a causal graph from the individual-level data of the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, Heart Disease, Prognosis and the Hispanic Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (MSHE/MPHIA). The resulting graph is analyzed in relation to existing knowledge and subsequently used to generate causal inferences. The inferred relationships align with current literature, and the analysis successfully identifies causal effects that were previously unexplored. The findings highlight the potential of this individual-level structural analysis to deepen our understanding of causal relationships within MPHIA. Furthermore, the results suggest that combining this individual-level approach with population-level methods can yield more comprehensive causal inferences. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the utility of causal graph analysis for advancing knowledge in the use of observational data for causal inference. Magnetic skyrmions are anticipated to function as information carriers in data storage technologies. However, the mechanisms governing their formation and stability remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigate the metamagnetic phase transition and magnetic structure of the spinel Co$_{9}$Zn$_{9}$Mn$_{2}$ under an external magnetic field using neutron diffraction. Our results indicate that a metastable skyrmion lattice emerges during the metamagnetic transition and exhibits an anomalously wide stability range within both temperature and magnetic field parameters. Furthermore, as the system approaches the metastable phase boundary, a field-induced geometric melting of this metastable skyrmion lattice is observed. These findings offer valuable insights into the creation of robust metastable states of magnetic skyrmion lattices for potential use in technology. The material Co$_{9}$Zn$_{9}$Mn$_{2}$ is thus expected to be a promising candidate for scientific research and future device applications. This paper offers a comprehensive review of modeling challenges associated with dynamic influence networks, encompassing both temporal dynamics and high-dimensional dimensions. Initially, we examine the evolution of statistical methods designed to handle temporal data, followed by an analysis of contemporary approaches addressing high-dimensional issues. Subsequently, we identify gaps in existing literature and propose avenues for future research. We conclude by outlining critical questions within this expanding field. Dynamical influence networks are prevalent across various disciplines, including epidemiology, finance, and social media. Although significant methodological advancements have been made, further progress is necessary to address more intricate temporal patterns, such as non-stationarity, and to develop techniques capable of analyzing networks with millions of nodes. This article serves as an introduction to these topics, highlighting both achievements and unresolved issues for the reader. Specifically, it targets researchers and graduate students interested in network science, network epidemiology, network finance, and network social psychology. Furthermore, the text is valuable for practitioners, such as data analysts and epidemiologists, working with high-dimensional dynamic influence networks. Finally, we provide open-source software to facilitate the analysis of such networks. NetworkX is utilized to construct the networks, while Pyro is employed for probabilistic modeling. The Pyro framework enables the construction of large-scale dynamic influence models and supports both probabilistic programming and probabilistic machine learning. By providing open-source tools alongside a review of current methods, we aim to support and inspire further research into high-dimensional dynamic influence networks. The balance problem asks for the $x$-coordinates of a given set that result in a minimal vertical force moment when the set is placed on a horizontal beam. We utilize the concept of the stable point, defined within optimal transport theory, to address this balance problem across both discrete and continuous contexts. Specifically, we employ stable point games, which are defined by a cost function representing the effort required to achieve a stable point. By examining the core of these games, we identify a set of measurements capable of balancing a given system under various conditions. In the continuous case, we apply concepts from convex geometry to demonstrate the existence of a balancing set for any compact set of measures. Furthermore, when the effort cost is convex, the stable point game exhibits superadditivity, allowing us to characterize its large-scale behavior through the balanced support function of a convex body. Finally, we explore the relationship between the core and the Shapley value, showing that a balanced measurement can be derived from the Shapley value if it lies within the core. These findings are supported by both theoretical analysis and numerical examples. Additionally, we highlight an application to the stability of black holes within general relativity. **Keywords:** Balance problem, Black hole stability, Core, Convex geometry, Geometric measure theory, Optimal transport, Shape optimization, Stable point game, Theory of games. **MSC 2020:** 26D15, 52A20, 53C21, 83C57, 91A12, 91A14, 91A12. **Aknowledgments:** The authors acknowledge the insightful comments of Prof. Andr\'as V\'{a}rhegyi regarding the connection between our work and the core of games. Recent progress has revitalized reversible data concealment, with recent approaches utilizing deep generative models like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to achieve this. However, these current methods rely on an idealized assumption that the latent variable follows a standard Gaussian distribution, an expectation that is often invalid in practice. To address this, we propose employing a neural network to learn the prior distribution, thereby enhancing the concealment capacity. Furthermore, we extend our framework to support Bayesian Neural Networks, which explicitly model uncertainty. Experiments on synthetic data demonstrate that VAE-based converters perform suboptimally due to their incorrect assumptions regarding the generative process. In contrast, our approach successfully overcomes these limitations, delivering superior results measured by distortion, expansion, and security metrics. Additionally, the Bayesian VAE-based converter exhibits greater robustness against perturbations in the conditional generative prior. Finally, we validate the method's effectiveness on image-based systems, where it outperforms existing solutions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/bayesian-vae-based-rdc.

We examine the impact of turbulent effects on the spectrum of the mean-field dynamo equation. By utilizing a spectrum of turbulent magnetic viscosity, we develop a complete spectrum of the turbulent $\alpha$-effect and dynamo number. Our findings indicate that turbulent influences, represented by turbulent magnetic viscosity, are critical for determining the magnetic field's growth rate and its ultimate stability. Furthermore, the spectrum of turbulent effects provides fresh perspectives on the interaction among various turbulent mechanisms. This paper introduces the first fully conservative Galerkin solver, tailored for mass and energy, designed to address quasilinear diffusion equations governing plasma turbulence across three spatial dimensions. These equations are fundamental to analyzing momentum and energy transport in magnetized plasmas. The proposed framework is comprehensive and modular, enabling the inclusion of various plasma kinetic models as components. Numerical tests using a six-variable distribution function demonstrate the solver's accuracy and stability. Furthermore, a new application focuses on electron momentum transport within the turbulent scrape-off layer of a tokamak plasma. This case study examines the impact of magnetic field fluctuations on electron momentum transport, revealing that electron radial momentum diffusion is significantly enhanced by such fluctuations. The findings suggest that electron radial diffusion is non-diffusive and exceeds the neoclassical diffusion rate by several orders of magnitude. These results align with recent experimental data on electron radial diffusivity in magnetized plasmas. Ultimately, this research underscores the critical role of plasma turbulence in momentum transport for magnetized plasmas. The developed solver is anticipated to facilitate the analysis of momentum transport in turbulent plasmas, thereby advancing plasma physics research. This study presents a novel Muonium-to-Muonium transition calculator designed to predict the dimuonium-substance interaction cross section. Muonium ($M$), an exotic atom composed of a muon ($\mu^+$) and an electron ($e^-$), is hypothesized to enable high-precision tests of the standard model. Muon ($\mu^+\mu^-$) sources generated at the sub-GeV energy scale are anticipated to facilitate the first $M-M \rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ transitions via interaction with matter. This work details a new Muonium-to-Muonium transition calculator, MuMuPy, which models the sub-threshold production of muonium via the dimuonium-atom interaction cross section. MuMuPy is a Python-based open-source platform that supports a wide range of target materials, including hydrogen, molecular hydrogen, helium, and liquid and solid hydrogen. The sub-threshold production of muonium through dimuonium-hydrogen interactions is calculated to have a cross section of approximately $10^{-16}$ cm$^2$, a value significantly lower than the approximate $10^{-14}$ cm$^2$ required to test the standard model at muon colliders. These findings suggest that the direct observation of $M-M \rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ is unlikely in the near future. Furthermore, the work examines the potential for discovering new physics beyond the standard model through the dimuonium-substance interaction cross section. This analysis indicates that the sub-GeV muon source proposed by the MuMu Collider initiative could enable the first direct observation of $M-M \rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$, thereby opening a new avenue for testing the standard model. Dwarf galaxies are the most abundant galaxy type and serve as the primary stellar component of dark-matter-dominated systems. Their gas components are crucial for understanding their dark matter halos, as this gas is the main reservoir for future star formation. This study examines the interplay between the intergalactic medium (IGM) and dwarf galaxy gas, focusing on the impact of a hot, X-ray-emitting IGM on thermally driven galactic outflows. We demonstrate that in dwarves with low-temperature IGMs, the interplay between the IGM and galactic gas is minimal, whereas in dwarves with high-temperature IGMs, the IGM exerts significant control over galactic outflows. Our findings indicate that the IGM's temperature and density are key factors in regulating gas dynamics within dwarf galaxies. Consequently, the IGM must be considered when investigating the evolution of these galaxies. This research is based on a sample of 100 nearby dark-matter-dominated dwarf galaxies, where we identified 11 hosts with X-ray-emitting IGMs. Our results suggest that the IGM is more prevalent in dwarves with higher stellar masses and lower stellar metallicities. Furthermore, we show that the interplay between the IGM and galactic gas is essential for understanding the galaxy formation and evolution history of these interloper dwarves. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future studies of the IGM and galactic gas in dwarf galaxies. It is demonstrated that if the quasiparticle has a finite lifetime, its spectral weight vanishes identically at high momenta. Consequently, the standard mechanism for quasiparticle formation fails, and the system transitions into a strongly correlated state where the Green's function does not exhibit simple pole behavior. These findings are generalized to include quasiparticles coupled to bosons with arbitrary, momentum-independent interactions. Although the critical momentum scale below which the Green's function retains single-particle characteristics is generally not sharply defined, it is shown to be proportional to the quasiparticle relaxation rate. Finally, the study examines the impact of the local bosonic bath's finite size, revealing that the spectral weight loss occurs over a timescale scaling with the bath size $N$ as $N^{-1/2}$. This implies that an infinite number of bath sites is required to fully suppress the spectral weight of the quasiparticle. These results are derived using the real-time diagrammatic method of equations of motion and are corroborated by numerical matrix product state simulations. The analysis is specifically applied to the Holstein model, although it remains valid for broader systems. Furthermore, the paper addresses the issue of the "unphysical" self-energy component in the diagrammatic approach, showing that it does not affect the spectral weight of the quasiparticle. These insights are particularly valuable for interpreting recent experiments on the Holstein model that report the disappearance of the quasiparticle. Finally, the relevance of these findings to other models is explored, including the Bose-Hubbard model, the generalized Bose-Hubbard model, and the quantum Hall pseudoparticle-boson interaction model.
