Human evaluation has long been a cornerstone of NLP research, yet recent studies on crowdsourced annotation have questioned the reliability of results derived from the Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) platform. This concern is particularly pertinent to summarization tasks, which demand a level of human expertise that may be uncommon among typical MTurk workers. This study presents the most extensive analysis to date, systematically varying specific worker attributes—such as age, prior summarization experience, and demographic factors like gender and race—to identify which worker profiles are best suited for summarization. The ultimate goal is to guide future researchers in recruiting the right worker demographic to enhance the validity of their evaluations. Our findings indicate that workers with NLP or writing backgrounds, who are typically younger, more educated, and less likely to be from the United States, are the most qualified for summarization. We further demonstrate that the distribution of these critical qualifications in our recent Shared Decision Making (SDM) task skewed toward younger workers, potentially compromising the validity of that study's results. Consequently, we offer guidance on the number and demographic type of workers required for such tasks. Finally, we analyze the performance of these qualified workers, revealing that while they are more experienced, they are also more prone to guessing, highlighting the need for workers with specific domain expertise in particular tasks. These insights will assist future researchers in recruiting the appropriate demographic to ensure the validity of their evaluations. Text-video retrieval (TVR) aims to identify a video from a collection given a specific text query. A primary hurdle in this task is the discrepancy between discrete tokens in text and continuous frames in videos. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Token Shift and Choice Transformer (TS2-Net), which adaptively shifts token representations to align with video frame features. TS2-Net comprises three core components: the Token Shift and Choice Transformer (TS2), the Temporal Pyramid Transformer (TPT), and the Textual and Visual Contrastive Learning (TVCL). The TS2 component adaptively aligns tokens with video frames by shifting token features using a novel choice transformer. TPT enhances text-video retrieval by extracting features from multiple temporal segments, thereby better matching text queries with video content. Subsequently, a text tower and a video tower are trained via a text-video contrastive learning strategy to improve overall retrieval performance. Extensive experiments across two large-scale benchmarks demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves state-of-the-art results. The source code will be made available at https://github.com/ChenchenZhou/TS2-Net.

In both scenarios, a new node arrives at each step and establishes a single link to an existing node, selecting $k$ times randomly from all possibilities and attaching with probability $K \in (0,1)$ to the other. We demonstrate that these processes yield different outcomes: the first algorithm generates a class of graphs with a power-law degree distribution, whereas the second produces an exponential degree distribution. Furthermore, we analyze the asymptotic properties of these graph classes regarding various time-dependent metrics, including average path length, diameter, and the probability of connectivity. We also investigate the emergence of a giant weakly connected component and its associated cutoff profile. Finally, we model the formation of a giant directed component as a directed time-dependent percolation problem, providing an analytic solution for the crossover time. Additionally, we provide an analytic description of the cutoff profile for the average path length within this evolving class of graphs. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Our results are particularly relevant for understanding the properties of time-dependent graphs modeling online social networks. Specifically, we apply our findings to analyze a sample of online social networks, revealing that some networks align with our model's predictions while others do not. We conclude by proposing that the uniform attachment mechanism may be more appropriate for online social networks. This paper serves as a foundation for our broader research on time-dependent graphs, which will also address the evolution of network motifs, clustering coefficients, and community structures. Multimedia content, such as videos and audio recordings, is susceptible to significant wireless disturbances when captured using mobile devices. These artifacts, which are difficult to perceive and evaluate, hinder content consumption and present challenges for automatic detection and classification. This study introduces a novel multi-label classification approach designed to efficiently identify and tag wireless interference affecting digital recording media like audio and video. By leveraging unique acoustic and visual fingerprints generated by wireless disturbances, the proposed method utilizes a lightweight convolutional neural network to achieve rapid and accurate classification of recorded material. The efficacy of this approach is validated through a comprehensive experimental analysis of recorded audio and video files. The resulting classification models are highly effective across various recording devices—including smartphones, digital audio recorders, and webcams—as well as across different wireless environments. Furthermore, the method demonstrates robustness in distinguishing recordings subjected to varying levels of wireless disturbance. These findings confirm the method's high accuracy and reliability for subsequent interference analysis and characterization. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a field that has evolved rapidly and has become deeply integrated into our daily lives. However, despite its widespread application, the core concept of AI remains ambiguous. While many AI systems operate effectively, they often lack transparency and are prone to failure. This paper aims to introduce the concept of Enhanced Artificial Intelligence (EAI), which incorporates human intellect into the conventional AI framework. EAI is designed to be more transparent and robust than traditional AI. Furthermore, the study provides examples of EAI-Human to demonstrate its ability to acquire human knowledge and its enhanced transparency and resilience. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of EAI-Human and identifying potential future research directions. Overall, this work seeks to promote the concept of Enhanced Artificial Intelligence. This approach enables the precise tuning of the modulated superfluid state. Furthermore, this modulated superfluid is predicted to exhibit unique low-temperature thermal properties, specifically a suppressed or absent temperature dependence in the chemical potential. Such findings offer a novel method for characterizing the chemical potential in correlated bosonic gases, a capability that extends beyond the conventional features of standard superfluids. A muon collider is a proposed particle accelerator that may serve as a bridge between the collider and accelerator communities, offering a pathway to the Long Range Future of particle physics. However, the collider's muon beam faces significant challenges, including substantial beam-induced background generated by the conversion of decaying muons into electrons and positrons. This background poses two primary issues: it could obscure Higgs and other Standard Model signatures, and it might mask new physics phenomena. Consequently, strategies must be developed to address these problems, such as enhancing detector readout speed and utilizing advanced algorithms for real-time event reconstruction. This paper outlines such mitigation tactics, with a specific focus on the detector aspect. Additionally, it examines methods to leverage the muon collider's unique capabilities to its full potential. The discussion is grounded in the Muon Collider Design Study, a multi-year initiative involving a diverse group of experts from the accelerator and detector communities. The study aims to identify the most critical R&D and other issues that the broader community should address. While this paper does not provide exhaustive details, it offers a comprehensive overview of the tactics currently under consideration. Furthermore, it addresses the necessary accelerator and detector research and development required to implement these mitigation strategies. Finally, the paper explores how to maximize the muon collider's distinct advantages, such as the ability to study the Higgs boson with minimal background and to achieve high energy reach through on-momentum upracing. These opportunities are crucial for the detector community to consider when designing the collider. Overall, the paper serves as a starting point for the detector community to initiate discussions regarding the design of the first muon collider experiment. It is structured into four sections: Section 2 covers the current status of muon collider detector R&D; Section 3 details tactics for mitigating beam-induced noise; Section 4 highlights the detector community's opportunities to capitalize on the collider's unique features; and Section 5 offers concluding remarks. We introduce Spartan, a method that integrates a regularized differentiable convex optimization framework with a non-differentiable concave regularization function to enable end-to-end backpropagation while maintaining interpretability. Spartan functions as a convex regularized concave optimizer, allowing the convergence of the solution to zero-weight regions to be controlled via a transport parameter $\gamma$. By applying concepts from optimal transport, Spartan establishes a lower bound on the concave regularizer, ensuring that the final region of learned functionals remains convex and bounded. This approach facilitates a smooth transition to sparsity, permitting the model to adapt its sparsity level to available computational resources. We demonstrate that Spartan effectively trains sparsely-activated neural networks on MNIST and CIFAR datasets and can be applied to various convex regularizers, such as the $\ell_1$ norm and structured sparsity. Furthermore, we show that Spartan can be applied to both continuous and discrete optimization problems, offering a promising avenue for addressing differentiable intractable problems. Additionally, we present the Deviation Optimizer (DO), which utilizes Spartan to learn a differentiable convex relaxation of a non-differentiable concave optimizer. Experimental results confirm that Spartan can transport optimizers like Grover et al.'s discrete-convex optimizer across a range of problems, including graph coloring, clique detection, and the knapsack problem. The Pauli principle prevents fermions from occupying the same quantum state, a concept that translates into a blockade within the language of bosonic second quantization, where an additional phase factor of $-1$ arises for every fermion in a given state. This emergent Pauli obstruction is expected to significantly alter the behavior of bosons interacting with an ultracold Fermi sea. In this work, we demonstrate this phenomenon in a Bose-Bose mixture by rigorously calculating the momentum distribution of bosons within the MERA framework, a fermionized quantum state of the Bose-Hubbard model. We show that in the deep magnetic trap regime, the momentum distribution of bosons displays a distinct peak at the Fermi momentum, mironing the Fermi edge observed in free gas systems. This effect is absent in mean-field approximations and aligns with recent experimental findings. Furthermore, we analyze the dynamical response of Pauli-obstructed bosons to a quench of the Fermi momentum, revealing a significant reduction in the maximum density reached by bosons. Finally, we explore the connection between this emergent Pauli obstruction and fermionization in balanced two-component Bose gases. Our findings underscore the critical role of quantum obstructions in few-body physics and highlight the utility of machine learning as a versatile tool for investigating such effects. Software testing is frequently perceived as a time-intensive endeavor. This study investigates the "good enough" perspective regarding testing, examining how prolonged engagement with code lacking a robust testing infrastructure—referred to as possessing a high "testing odor"—affects software maintainers' views on the severity of these odors and their motivation to refactor. To validate a novel instrument designed to identify testing odors, we conducted a survey with 18 industry developers who evaluated the detector's accuracy. The participants also shared their general sentiments on refactoring software that is insufficiently tested. Findings from this survey indicate that (i) developers consider testing odors to be serious issues, and (ii) the presence of these odors significantly diminishes their desire to refactor the code. Consequently, the discussion highlights the critical role of refactoring in eliminating testing odors and enhancing the testability of software systems. We introduce KKMCee, a Monte Carlo event generator designed for electron-positron collisions that models the complete Born, real soft, and real photon emission processes for electron-muon and electron-quark annihilation. This tool is especially valuable for simulating Higgs boson and top quark pair production at future lepton colliders. Built upon the multi-photon approximation framework established in our previous work [arXiv:1905.02030 [hep-ph]], the program incorporates corrections up to second order in electromagnetic coupling, ensuring accuracy even at high photon energies. Additionally, it incorporates various corrections to multi-photon amplitudes arising from electron and quark mass effects, as well as from QCD corrections to quark pair production. We validate the software using simulations of the dominant three-jet processes for electron-quark annihilation, comparing our findings with experimental data and other Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, we outline applications of KKMCee to the associated production of a Higgs boson with a top quark pair at lepton colliders. This study introduces the Tiramisu model, a novel framework for estimating inter-beat intervals that surpasses existing methods in accuracy and computational efficiency. We demonstrate that the model's name stems from its layered architecture, which integrates Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and Attention mechanisms. We provide evidence that combining these components yields superior performance compared to utilizing any single component alone. Additionally, we show that integrating both the RNN and Attention components enhances prediction accuracy by effectively modeling both local and global temporal dynamics. Finally, we highlight that the CNN component serves as a lightweight backbone, reducing the model's computational burden. Our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an improvement of approximately 10% in test Mean Squared Error (MSE). This study introduces a stochastic approach to tensor singular value decomposition (STSD) grounded in the alternating least squares (ALS) framework. The proposed algorithm is flexible, accommodating various initialization techniques and enabling users to select an optional pass count for ALS iterations. Additionally, the method supports early termination of computations. Empirical testing indicates that the proposed STSD achieves high accuracy, achieving an error rate of approximately 1% across most cases. Furthermore, the algorithm demonstrates significant computational efficiency, completing tasks in roughly 10% of the time required by the NumPy implementation. Notably, spectral embeddings and the degree matrix consistently demonstrate strong results across most tests. The ground state of $^7$H is characterized as a narrow resonance utilizing the $^3$H + 4n fragmentation channel, with its width defined by the system's lifetime. This study proposes that the excitation energy stemming from the relative motion of the four neutrons follows a Gaussian distribution, thereby establishing a specific width for the $^7$H ground state. Furthermore, properties of the $^7$H state, such as its rms radius and binding energy, are analyzed using the calculated wave function. The findings indicate that the $^7$H ground state exhibits clusterization, behaving as a $^3$H core surrounded by four valence neutrons. Additionally, the wave function is represented by the $^3$H + n + nn + nn + nn fragmentation channel, and the probability of the core being the neutron is estimated. Finally, the $^7$H lifetime is determined to be approximately 10$^{-23}$ s. These results are compared with existing literature, and the implications of the proposed $^7$H ground state wave function are discussed. The study concludes that while the wave function is highly diffuse, the $^7$H ground state remains narrow due to its extremely short lifetime. Consequently, the concept of a "quasi-stable" state is applicable to the $^7$H ground state. These findings may assist in interpreting experimental data regarding $^7$H production cross-sections and are also relevant to the study of neutron-rich nuclei. Specifically, it investigates the existence of singular metrics with constant positive curvature on the standard sphere $S^n_{+}$, subject to singularities at the antipodal poles. In machine learning, the representation of data is essential for learning tasks. This paper investigates the optimal representation of supervised data within the metric space framework. We propose a method to learn the optimal Sinkhorn metric through its potential function, utilizing the gradient of the Sinkhorn divergence as a learning metric. Representations are optimized by minimizing the Sinkhorn divergence between their induced metrics and the Sinkhorn divergence between the Euclidean norm of supervised data and the logarithmic norm of its conditional mean. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that this representation gradient is unique and establishes its relationship with the classical covariance gradient. Empirical results on CIFAR-10 and MNIST datasets confirm the effectiveness of this approach. Notably, when combined with ResNet, our method surpasses current techniques. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi-chen/SinkhornRep.

This study employs a stochastic SIR model to simulate the impact of contact tracing on COVID-19 transmission within London and England. We specifically investigate how the effectiveness of tracing in identifying new cases and preventing infections varies with different levels of testing coverage for traced individuals and the proportion of the population that is traced. Additionally, we analyze the effect of digital tracing applications on these metrics. A key contribution of this work is the investigation into the impact of tracing collaborations between app users and non-users on transmission rates. Our findings indicate that significant reductions in transmission can be achieved in London through active contact tracing, even with low community-wide testing coverage for traced individuals. Specifically, if 80% of the population is traced and tested coverage reaches 20%, transmission in London could drop below the threshold required to achieve herd immunity. However, if only 50% of the population is traced, transmission would need to fall below 5% to reduce the effective reproduction number below 1. Furthermore, we observed that transmission is lower among app users compared to non-users, suggesting that increased testing among app users could further decrease transmission rates. Finally, we demonstrated that tracing collaborations between app users and non-users can substantially lower transmission rates. If 80% of the population is traced with a tested coverage of 20%, transmission could be reduced by approximately 10% through collaborations between traced individuals. If 50% of the population is traced, a tested coverage of 30% is required to achieve a transmission reduction exceeding 10%. These results are based on a transmission rate of 0.3 and a non-digital tracing population size of 1,000,000. The model was implemented using Python and the PySB simulation library. The PySB library offers a platform-independent approach to defining and simulating model equations, while PySBMC enables the parallel and distributed execution of these simulations. Both PySB and PySBMC are open-source projects. The model code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/py-sb/pysb, and the generated simulation results can be explored via Jupyter notebooks at https://py-sb.github.io/notebooks. Utilizing Gaia DR2 data, we present a study of the low-mass open cluster Melotte 72. We determined the cluster's physical parameters, including its center coordinates, angular radius, line-of-sight distance, and total mass. Additionally, we calculated the cluster's distance modulus and reddening values. Finally, we analyzed the cluster's color-magnitude diagram and luminosity function. The derived physical parameters align with values found in prior literature. However, our analysis of the color-magnitude diagram and luminosity function reveals that Melotte 72 exhibits a more extended main sequence than previously reported. We introduce Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning (RCRL), a constrained reinforcement learning framework designed to produce solutions that are both high-performing and easy to comprehend. The core concept involves two agents operating within the same environment: a Solver agent that utilizes standard reinforcement learning to maximize performance, and a Reverse Solver agent that seeks to minimize the understandability of the actions generated by the Solver. Consequently, RCRL aims to locate a solution on the Pareto frontier that optimizes both metrics. Our proof-of-concept implementation applies this framework to two simple simulation environments, where the forward and reverse understandability metrics are determined by the edit distance between solutions and simple scripts. Results indicate that RCRL successfully identifies high-performing, easy-to-understand solutions in these settings. Additionally, we demonstrate how adding constraints to RCRL enables it to find optimal trade-offs within a specific solution space, a capability illustrated through an experiment where constraints enforce collaboration between two agents. Finally, we discuss how RCRL can be extended to address various other spatial understandability problems. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYuan2000/rcrl. Documentations for our python packages, rcrl and rcrl_eval, can be found at https://chenyuan2000.github.io/rcrl and https://chenyuan2000.github.io/rcrl_eval, respectively. GAIA, a mission by the European Space Agency's Science Programme, is designed to create a comprehensive 3D map of our Milky Way galaxy. This mapping encompasses over one billion objects, ranging from the nearest stars to globular clusters and galaxies. The data will be delivered in two stages: the initial release will cover a selection of the most scientifically significant objects with high-precision measurements, while the final release will include the complete dataset. The primary scientific objectives of GAIA are: (i) to generate an unprecedentedly accurate and extensive 3D map of the Galaxy's stellar population and their associated kinematic data; (ii) to precisely determine distances to nearby galaxies and the distance-redshift relation for the Hubble flow; and (iii) to map the positions, distances, and distances-redshifts of supernovae, thereby facilitating a more accurate measurement of cosmological parameters. This paper outlines the GAIA mission and its anticipated data releases. It also details the anticipated data contents, including astrometry, astrophysics, and spectroscopy, along with a summary of the GAIA Data Processing and Validation Consortium (DPVC) activities and the resulting data quality. Furthermore, the paper addresses the GAIA Data Processing and Archiving Consortium (DPAC) data release formats and the services they provide. Finally, it presents a series of GAIA Data Release 1 (DR1) simulations to illustrate the scientific capabilities of the mission. The article concludes with a discussion of the GAIA Data Standard (GADS) and its future evolution. The GAIA consortium and the scientific community are eager to observe the GAIA data and the groundbreaking results it will yield. (2020) introduced a randomized graph sketch that, when applied to a disjoint union of sketches derived from graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$, yields a treewidth-decomposition for the resulting sketch with a sum of bag sizes equal to that of the original sketches. This sketch provides a near-multiplicative approximation of the graph's treewidth. While this technique has enabled the creation of efficient graph algorithms for problems on treewidth or treedepth, the need to multiply the sketch size by the sketch depth has occasionally resulted in running times that are suboptimal. This paper presents a method to compact the vertex sets within the bags of these treewidth-decompositions, thereby achieving asymptotically optimal time complexities for a variety of graph problems. This approach leverages a novel vertex divider, which is a specific instance of a balanced connected vertex separator. We demonstrate that this technique can be integrated with a broad class of vertex dividers, offering a practical and versatile tool for graph algorithms. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of our method with two examples: first, by combining our approach with the work of Fomin et al. (2020), we develop a near-optimal coloring algorithm; second, we introduce a new algorithm that solves a problem on treewidth in a time complexity of $2^{O(\sqrt{k \log k})} n^{O(1)}$, improving upon the previous best complexity of $2^{O(k \log k)} n^{O(1)}$ established by Marx and Saurabh (2017). Both applications utilize a vertex divider with a proven running time, highlighting the utility of our technique for extracting treewidth-decompositions from vertex separators. Additionally, our work offers a practical framework for graph algorithms, as the proposed method is straightforward to implement and can be easily adapted to other vertex divider techniques. Finally, we provide a Python implementation of our approach using the NetworkX library. The source code is publicly accessible on GitHub, enabling other researchers to easily implement, adapt, and extend our work. Grouping algorithms are increasingly utilized to identify communities within complex networks, typically involving the assignment of nodes to groups to either minimize or maximize inter- and intra-group connections. However, existing methods are often restricted to networks with a single link type and positive weights, and they fail to account for the distinction between directly measured and indirectly inferred networks. This study aims to derive necessary conditions for grouping in directed networks featuring multiple link types and positive or heterogeneous weights, while simultaneously proposing an interpretation framework for the resulting groups. We demonstrate that grouping is not always interpretable across all link types or directions, and we establish precise criteria regarding link properties and network interpretations under which grouping offers a clear interpretation. Furthermore, we present an algorithm designed to determine whether a network possesses an interpretable grouping solution. These findings are illustrated using a network of US Supreme Court justices, which integrates court opinions, citations, and temporal co-presence data. Our results indicate that groupings derived from certain link types and directions are interpretable, with nominal networks yielding the most definitive interpretations. Ultimately, this work provides a rigorous interpretation theory for grouped directed networks and clarifies the specific link properties and network interpretations required for meaningful grouping outcomes. Additionally, we offer guidelines for evaluating the interpretability of solutions from popular undirected, weighted grouping algorithms when applied to directed networks. These theoretical contributions are intended to assist researchers in selecting appropriate algorithms, link types, and network interpretations to ensure that group membership assignments remain interpretable. Finally, we outline strategies for combining multiple link types to enhance the interpretability of node groupings. These insights are particularly relevant for applications involving various forms of social media data, such as tweets, retweets, likes, and mentions.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a machine learning method that integrates prior knowledge of physical laws, expressed as partial differential equations (PDEs), into the learning process. By embedding these PDEs into the loss function, PINNs constrain the learned solution to adhere to the specified physical principles. Although this approach offers the benefit of reducing reliance on extensive datasets, the resulting solutions may still violate the target PDEs. This paper introduces a statistical framework to quantify the degree to which PINN solutions satisfy a given PDE, utilizing the residual error from the PDE as a proxy for solution accuracy. This methodology, termed the authorization framework, enables the determination of whether a PINN solution sufficiently approximates the true solution of a PDE initial-value problem. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through two case studies involving non-linear diffusion equations. These examples illustrate how the authorization framework can identify regions where PINNs fail to approximate PDE solutions and how these authorization results can inform adaptive mesh generation. Ultimately, this work provides a mechanism to assess the accuracy of PINN solutions, thereby enhancing their trustworthiness in scientific machine learning applications. Furthermore, it establishes a pathway for developing new authorization techniques for other machine learning methods used in science. Finally, the Python code for these cases is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhamidimarri/physics_informed_neural_networks. Keywords: authorization, physics-informed neural networks, partial differential equations, error estimation, adaptive mesh generation. Linear contextual bandits have been extensively researched, yet most existing literature assumes a homogeneous, shared action set for all users. This uniform setup facilitates standard evaluation using common metrics like regret and is convenient for large-scale testing. However, this approach is ill-suited for real-world scenarios where different users possess distinct action sets. This paper examines the implications of such heterogeneous action sets, noting that they hinder both exploration and inference. To address the challenge of exploration, we introduce a novel exploration bonus that relies solely on local information. For inference, we demonstrate that standard methods often yield incorrect p-values and introduce a new technique to calculate valid p-values that utilizes only user-specific data. We validate our findings through simulations and an empirical analysis of a real-world dataset. Both a theoretical analysis and a lower bound for a specific problem variant support our proposed exploration bonus. Furthermore, we show that the proposed p-value method achieves superior exploration compared to existing approaches that depend on global information. Our theoretical and empirical results indicate that the new exploration bonus results in lower regret than other methods. Finally, we explore how the proposed exploration bonus can be adapted to derive p-values that leverage global information. Empirical findings suggest that combining our p-value approach with global exploration yields even better performance than other methods utilizing global information. We conclude by discussing several open questions regarding exploration and inference in linear bandits with heterogeneous action sets. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are machine learning models specifically designed to process data represented as graphs. Unlike standard neural networks, GNNs retain the structural relationships inherent in graphs while also incorporating node feature information. This characteristic makes them highly effective for graph-based tasks such as node classification and link prediction. However, because GNNs are a form of machine learning, they remain susceptible to data poisoning, where malicious actors manipulate training samples to introduce biases that skew model outputs. This paper introduces a framework designed to investigate data contamination within GNNs. Within this framework, we develop multiple data poisoning strategies utilizing reinforcement learning and present specific algorithms for each. Our approach demonstrates the high efficacy of data contamination, causing models to produce significantly inaccurate predictions for nodes labeled by attackers after training. Additionally, we establish a baseline for detection methods to ensure a fair comparison of our contamination techniques. Finally, we train graph-based models on the Cora and Citeseer datasets to empirically validate the effectiveness of the proposed contamination strategies. Given the nature of reinforcement learning, slight variations in results may occur; however, the overall conclusions remain consistent. This paper demonstrates that every infinite hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ possessing the countable chain condition admits a minimal edge cover $\mathcal{B}$ such that the cardinality of $\mathcal{B}$ does not exceed the supremum of the cardinalities of the hypergraph's edges. Furthermore, for each vertex $v$, there exists a unique set $B(v) \in \mathcal{B}$ satisfying the condition that $v$ is contained in no other edge $B(u)$ for $u \neq v$. The proof relies on a straightforward extension of Kuratowski's maximal by inclusion edge cover theorem. A specific example is provided to illustrate that the second statement regarding minimal edge covers cannot be derived from the theorem by any application of the inclusion postulate. Additionally, the authors explore the relationship between minimal edge covers and retractors within hypergraphs. This work generalizes findings by Sierpiński regarding finite edge covers in infinite graphs. The term "minimal edge cover" is employed rather than "maximal by inclusion edge cover" to align with standard graph theory terminology. However, the authors note that the latter term is more precise, as "minimal" might ambiguously suggest that every edge cover contains a minimal one. Consequently, the authors propose that future literature should prefer the term "maximal by inclusion edge cover" to avoid confusion. By integrating a non-equilibrium statistical mechanical framework with molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the contribution of internal conformational degrees of freedom in soft molecules to the Soret effect. Specifically, we simulate the separation of long n-alkane chains induced by a temperature gradient within a confined space. Our results demonstrate that the Soret coefficient for these long chains is highly sensitive to the freedom of their internal motion; restricting this movement through stronger wall interactions or shorter chains markedly diminishes the magnitude of the Soret coefficient. Furthermore, we establish that the Soret coefficient scales with the temperature derivative of the mean internal energy. These findings align with previous experimental data and computational studies involving polar molecules, underscoring the critical role that internal freedom of motion plays in the thermal diffusion of weakly interacting soft molecules. Additionally, the magnitude of this effect can be tuned by adjusting the system's interaction strength. These insights are anticipated to prove valuable in the rational design of soft molecular mixtures for thermal separation applications. Finally, our methodology is broadly applicable to analyzing thermal diffusion in other systems where internal degrees of freedom are accessible. Human throwing is a complex activity involving multiple movement components, including arm and leg kinetics, trunk rotation, and object release. Research indicates that errors in any single component can disrupt the entire motion. This study examines how an inaccurate point of release affects throwing performance. To simulate incorrect release points, we modified the FauxThrow application, which overlays a dynamic, device-specific model of a throwing motion onto a video using a computer vision system. We recruited 12 participants to record their natural throwing actions using a device-based approach. These motions were then processed by the FauxThrow system to generate simulated incorrect throws. Finally, a new set of 12 participants viewed these simulated motions and completed a novel incorrect point-of-release task using either the original or the modified motions. Our findings demonstrate that participants relied on device-specific visual cues from the generated faux motions to execute the novel task. Additionally, we observed that the further the simulated release point deviated from the original, the more challenging it became for participants to complete the task. This research holds significance for applications involving motion capture, as it highlights the potential impact of false or misleading motions on the capture process. Furthermore, our work has been applied to the safety and security domain to generate deceptive motions that can distract users from critical activities. Although Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has advanced significantly, it frequently fails to maintain accurate grammatical structure, a shortcoming that hinders its utility as a practical tool for multilingual communication. To address this, we introduce a tree-structured decoder that leverages part-of-speech (POS) and dependency links to generate constrained NMT hypotheses aligned with the recipient's parse tree, thereby facilitating error detection and correction. Our method employs a beam search strategy that iteratively refines the beam of top-level subtrees while synchronously decoding lower subtrees. We validate the efficacy of learning syntactic links via self-supervised training on large monolingual corpora and demonstrate the model's effectiveness through extensive experiments on conditional NMT and dependency parsing tasks. We have made our code and models publicly available at https://github.com/MyungJinHan/Top-downTreeDecoding. The experimental results confirm that our approach successfully generates grammatically correct outputs and markedly improves performance in conditional NMT and dependency parsing. Furthermore, our conditional NMT results surpass those of the previous state-of-the-art method. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed model supports multilingual training and inference without necessitating language-specific adjustments. Given these findings, we anticipate that this tree-structured decoding framework will serve as a valuable resource for various language understanding and generation applications. We introduce a randomized procedure to assess expectation values with minimized circuit depth and qubit count. The method relies on sampling expectation values from shallow random Clifford circuits, employing either disordered Pauli or Clifford designs. Specifically, the expected value of a Hermitian observable is approximated by the average over these shallow circuits, weighted according to their probability within the random Clifford design. This weighting function exhibits random behavior, indicating that shallow shades effectively capture the non-equilibrium dynamics characteristic of many-body localized systems. Furthermore, the algorithm demonstrates robust performance across various system sizes and remains efficient for low-density states, such as those found in thermal states. Consequently, it holds significant promise for expectation estimation on near-term noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. Finally, we illustrate the application of this protocol to simulate the time evolution of a many-body localized system, achieving high precision with minimal depth and qubits. This simulation is feasible on existing NISQ hardware, underscoring the protocol's practical utility. Additionally, we investigate the influence of noise on these simulations, revealing that while depolarizing noise impacts the results, it does not entirely obscure the underlying physics. Overall, our protocol is broadly applicable to extract non-redundant information regarding non-reversible dynamics, including those of thermal systems, within an experimentally viable timeframe. This work may also provide a foundation for mitigating noise in near-term quantum simulations. Finally, our findings may contribute to the development of new quantum algorithms utilizing random Clifford circuits. Furthermore, this ensemble can be easily combined with other ensemble strategies to further boost resilience. Meta-learning is designed to enable models to quickly adapt to various tasks using new data. This demonstration highlights how meta-learning can automatically select appropriate illustrations for tasks in a linear regression scenario. We employ a linear-illustration model, which applies a mapping from raw data to tailored illustrations before feeding them into a fully connected neural network. To manage multiple illustration types, we utilize a meta-learning approach utilizing auxiliary classification networks. Our findings indicate that meta-learning can achieve performance comparable to manually configured linear illustrations. Furthermore, the mapping learned by our method yields similar illustrations across similar tasks, even within distinct illustration spaces. This capability significantly aids interpretability, as the learned mappings can be visualized. Overall, our results suggest that meta-learning offers a promising alternative for automatic illustration techniques, fostering a deeper understanding of data within fully supervised learning frameworks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer/illustrations. Sebastian Schaefer's email is sebastian.schaefer@tu-dresden.de.

Low-resource multilingual machine translation (LRMT) is crucial for facilitating communication in languages lacking sufficient training data. However, training end-to-end models from scratch often demands substantial resources. This paper investigates the fragility of models regarding training data quantity by comparing two lightweight LRMT approaches: training directly on limited data versus extracting models from pre-trained multilingual systems. We introduce a method to distill multilingual models into lightweight formats and assess stability across varying data sizes. Results indicate that while extraction yields promising outcomes, particularly for high-resource languages, direct training remains competitive, leading us to conclude that extraction is not always superior for low-resource languages. Furthermore, we identify that unsupervised pre-training and hyperparameter optimization are key factors in enhancing low-resource machine translation performance. The experimental data and code are available at https://github.com/DeepiNus/low-resource-multilingual-machine-translation.

We introduce a method that reduces the dependency on labeled training data for segmenting pulmonary nodules in chest X-rays. Our approach leverages data augmentation and non-linear transformations to generate synthetic pneumonia images. We evaluate several nodule segmentation architectures, including U-Net, Attention U-Net, and DeepLabV3+, individually and in combination. Furthermore, we propose a novel ensemble method that utilizes a weighted average of predictions from these trained networks. Controllable Decoding has become a standard method in Natural Language Processing for managing model behavior through specific prompts. This study investigates the applicability of this approach to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using a regulation task that asks the models to describe images based on a specified emotion. We observe a significant discrepancy between the models' responses and their stated capabilities, indicating poor controllability. Our findings demonstrate an average capability improvement of over 20%, and qualitative results indicate more detailed and regulated image descriptions. This work introduces and evaluates a universal, model-based framework for analyzing and interpreting various metrics of causal damage. The study addresses inquiries such as: Can distinct damage measures be derived from a single general definition? What constitutes the most intuitive formulation for cause-to-effect damage, and how does it align with existing process-level and intervention-level damage concepts? How can damage be analytically characterized using do-calculus? What are the appropriate methods for computing and estimating this formulation? Furthermore, can this approach extend to damage in pure common-effect scenarios, as well as to universal evaluations of disabling, masking, and facilitative effects? The paper provides affirmative responses to these questions, offering comprehensive mathematical and conceptual explanations alongside numerical examples. Additionally, the proposed definition is demonstrated to be robust across both probabilistic and non-probabilistic contexts. Empirical findings indicate that this framework yields consistent and sensible estimates, even when applied to systems with high-dimensional, discrete variables. Finally, the study outlines several promising avenues for future research. Notably, this work represents a significant advancement toward the broader objective of unifying causal damage analysis. By clarifying fundamental questions and establishing a practical foundation for empirical analysis, it paves the way for developing standardized protocols for cause, contribution, and facilitation analyses. Ultimately, this research serves as a critical step toward the larger vision of unifying causal attribution. Specifically, it aids in disentangling the complex relationships among cause, contribution, damage, effect, facilitation, and responsibility. Crucially, this analysis advances the understanding of damage as a distinct and separable construct from its related concepts, thereby supporting the development of a coherent and unified analysis of causal attributes. This understanding is essential for the future development of tools designed to assess human and organizational responsibility. Furthermore, this analysis deepens the comprehension of artificial intelligence systems capable of evaluating damage, including those assessing the impact of their own actions. This contributes significantly to the broader goal of unifying responsibility, damage, and related constructs, which is vital for the future development of AI systems equipped with the ability to judge and assign blame. These advancements are integral to the larger aim of unifying causal attribution. This paper introduces MMLSpark, a new open-source machine learning library that bridges the gap between popular deep learning frameworks and big data processing tools. MMLSpark deep learning modules are designed to be adaptable, expandable, and robust. The team's motivation stemmed from a desire to unify the processing logic across all MMLSpark modules and to create a flexible, high-level interface for popular and easily implementable algorithms. This work serves as an extension of our prior research, which focused on adapting and extending existing MMLSpark modules. We demonstrate that our implementation of deep learning tools is not only adaptable and expandable but also robust, as evidenced by extensive unit and integration testing. Furthermore, we show that our high-level module design is user-friendly and efficient. We anticipate that this research will inspire the deep learning community to embrace our tools for processing and implementing state-of-the-art models. We also hope to encourage the broader big data and machine learning communities to adopt MMLSpark and its deep learning modules to achieve more robust and scalable solutions. Finally, we aim to inspire other research teams to extend the MMLSpark ecosystem by contributing additional tools and algorithms to our open-source project. The source code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/MMLSpark. Voice translation involves converting speech from one language into another language via spoken word audio. We introduce a Coleman-Gurtin type model designed to analyze dynamic boundary restraints, defined by a system of two equations: a boundary balance of power and an evolution equation for the flux. The power distribution is divided into an elastic component, representing the duality between boundary stress and the rate of boundary displacement, and a nonelastic component, which models thermodynamic forces arising from boundary internal variables. This formulation enables the derivation of boundary versions of the balance of energy and the Clausius-Duhem inequality. We provide an asymptotic proof demonstrating the consistency between the boundary equations and the energy- flux-dissipation structure. To ensure well-posedness, we impose a monotonicity condition on the graph of the constitutive map for the nonelastic boundary traction. Specifically, we examine a boundary conductive heat flow constitutive law characterized by a linearly elastic stress and a Fourier constitutive relation for the nonelastic stress. This heat flow process adheres to the energy-dissipation framework, consistent with established results. Furthermore, we establish that the system is well-posed under appropriate initial and boundary conditions. This model serves as a boundary counterpart to the asymptotic analysis of bulk constitutive laws found in \cite{Ciarletta2019}, alongside a simultaneous boundary analysis discussed in \cite{Bazant2013}. Such theoretical foundations are essential for accurately describing dynamic boundary phenomena observed in experiments, such as those involving heat flow in micro and nanodevices \cite{Kane1997}. Additionally, this approach supports the rigorous numerical implementation of boundary constitutive laws within the framework of $\Gamma$-convergence \cite{DalMaso1988}. The paper concludes with numerical simulations illustrating dynamic heat flow on a boundary. These results highlight key differences between the Coleman-Gurtin asymptotic analysis and $\Gamma$-convergence methods, and they demonstrate how the nonlocal character of the nonelastic stress constitutive law influences dynamic heat flow. Furthermore, our numerical findings confirm that the nonelastic stress exhibits a nonlocal dependence on temperature, a property not captured by the analysis in the $\Gamma$-convergence section. This distinction arises because the analysis in that section relies on the linearization of constitutive laws. Accurate and granular probabilistic network load forecasts are essential for managing low-voltage networks in an energy transition characterized by highly variable renewable energy sources and fluctuating demand from decentralized devices. This study introduces a novel probabilistic model for day-ahead high load forecasting at the household level by integrating and extending two techniques: the forecast fusion method proposed by Schmidt et al. and an enhanced version of the forecast hill climbing method by Schmidt and Schlachtberger. This integrated approach learns a multivariate Gaussian distribution from historical data, enabling the calculation of high load probabilities. Results from a day-to-day comparison show that integrating household smart meters significantly improves prediction accuracy, reducing the root mean square error from 1.01 kW to 0.4 kW. Furthermore, this method achieves an 80% reduction in high household loads while increasing the reduction in the household aggregate's peak power by only 1.5%. These findings confirm that probabilistic load prediction can substantially lower peak household loads with only a marginal decrease in the neighborhood's peak power. Overall, this technique serves as a promising solution for mitigating the impacts of the energy transition on neighborhood power grids. Additionally, the proposed method is designed to be computationally efficient, making it suitable for deployment on smart neighborhood controllers. The rapid advancement of machine learning has led to significant algorithmic breakthroughs and successful real-world deployments. However, despite these successes, two primary challenges persist: first, a substantial amount of data is often required; second, domain experts frequently hesitate to adopt these tools due to a perceived lack of transparency and interpretability. This paper introduces a new paradigm for embedding domain knowledge into machine learning, grounded in the management of domain ontologies. We outline a research agenda designed to address current limitations and foster new directions in the field. Specifically, we examine methods for automatically generating hypotheses from learned knowledge, enhancing the interpretability of domain models, and providing frameworks to assess the confidence surrounding these hypotheses. Additionally, we propose strategies for dynamically adapting domain expertise throughout the learning process. We demonstrate the utility of this ontology-driven approach by addressing a specific knowledge discovery challenge in the biomedical sector. Finally, we identify several open research areas, emphasizing self-explainable machine learning and the application of formal methods to validate domain ontologies within this framework. The code and data required to replicate our findings are available at https://github.com/ontolearn/Blueprint. This work was developed within the Ontolearn project, which integrates domain ontologies into machine learning processes. The full article can be found at http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0004370219302101. Our approach offers a novel perspective on embedding domain knowledge, presenting new opportunities for research in this evolving field. We aim to inspire further exploration of this paradigm and its potential to transform how machine learning systems are understood and utilized. Code: https://github.com/ontolearn/Blueprint. Although significant strides have been made in developing AI-based medical image analysis tools for COVID-19, current research often relies on simplified binary classification of whether pneumonia exists, rather than accurately identifying and segmenting the lesions. Furthermore, AI models trained on existing datasets may inadvertently inherit biases regarding patient demographics, such as age and gender. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a weakly guided learning approach for COVID-19 lesion localization and segmentation that bypasses the need for binary labels. Our methodology comprises three core components: a bias-free image acquisition strategy, a weakly guided learning framework, and a robust segmentation technique. We demonstrate that this framework effectively mitigates dataset bias and enhances segmentation precision. Additionally, our approach is versatile and can be applied to other lesion types, including melanoma and lung cancer. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/leeyongchul/COVID-19-lesion-localization-and-segmentation. Our findings indicate that weakly guided learning is superior to traditional weakly supervised methods for non-expert annotation and significantly improves both the accuracy and reliability of lesion segmentation. Furthermore, we show that bias-free image acquisition is essential for training unbiased AI models in medical image analysis. Ultimately, our bias-free framework facilitates the development of more trustworthy AI models for COVID-19 diagnosis. We believe these methodologies will have broad applications in medical image analysis, particularly in the creation of AI-driven decision support systems for clinical practice. We anticipate that our research will contribute to the advancement of AI in medicine. Our work is supported by the following grant: 1R21EB028077-01A1. Accurately localizing and identifying vertebrae in CT images is a critical step for numerous image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT) procedures. This study introduces a novel spine rectification technique combined with anatomically-constrained optimization to achieve vertebral recognition. The proposed method utilizes a new spine centerline estimation algorithm to align the spine with a predefined standard orientation, followed by anatomically-constrained optimization to reconstruct the vertebrae along this centerline. This approach addresses two primary challenges: (1) accurately localizing the superior-inferior position of the vertebrae by leveraging known inter-vertebral distances, and (2) ensuring correct recognition of each vertebra by exploiting the inherent anatomical structure of the spine. The method was evaluated using 100 CT images from 10 patients, where vertebral recognition was assessed by comparing the results against manually labeled ground truth data. The experimental results demonstrate an overall recognition accuracy of 96%. Furthermore, the method's robustness was confirmed by its ability to handle spines with severe deformities. These findings indicate that the proposed technique holds significant potential for application in automated vertebral recognition. This work investigates single electron scattering in the resonant regime under a ultrastrong oscillating light field within a cavity. The field induces vacuum oscillations in the electron, creating a dressed state that behaves as an effective particle with reduced mass. We demonstrate that this effective mass can be reduced to near zero within a specific range of driving fields, causing the electron to scatter at resonant energies determined by the light field frequency. Furthermore, we show that the phenomenon of dynamical stabilization, where the effective tunneling amplitude between the entrance and exit apertures vanishes, significantly suppresses scattering. These findings may have applications in the study of electron dynamics within ultrastrong light fields, such as in cavities or optical lattices. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/ulrikbengtsson/SEEs. See also Bengtsson, J. Phys. B: At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 52, 134001 (2019). Keywords: ultrastrong light field, dynamical stabilization, vacuum oscillations, dressed electron, single electron scattering, relativistic quantum electrodynamics, relativistic electron microscopy. Recent years have seen significant advancements in designing and controlling elastic actuators for legged robots, substantially enhancing their dynamic capabilities. However, existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches for robot control typically treat these actuators as complex, high-dimensional subsystems, which complicates the learning process. This paper introduces a novel RL framework that explicitly incorporates elastic actuator dynamics to achieve superior performance and learning efficiency. By representing the actuator as acting directly on the limb's end-effector, we significantly reduce the effective dimensionality of the control state space. Our method involves training the robot in a simulated physics environment and subsequently transferring the policy to a digital twin for evaluation and minor refinement. We validated this approach on the MIT Cheetah 3 robot, demonstrating that an 8-dimensional policy can effectively control an 80-dimensional system. Experimental results indicate that our policy surpasses previous work in terms of both performance and learning speed. Furthermore, we utilize these 8-dimensional policies to explore new locomotion gaits, successfully discovering a novel movement pattern. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/elastic-actuator-dim-reduction.

This study introduces an independent-variable method (IM) designed to establish lower bounds for energy. The procedure involves constructing a Hamiltonian by utilizing order-parameter fields instead of operators, followed by an energy minimization process. Through rigorous analysis, it is demonstrated that the energy lower bound generated by IM is identical to that produced by the Gibbs-Bogoliubov inequality (GBI) inequality when applied to quantum systems, whether interacting or non-interacting. In both IM and GBI approaches, the same unnormalized field-based Hamiltonian is utilized; however, IM performs direct minimization, whereas GBI employs a variational principle. Notably, while the GBI approach relies on quantum operators, IM depends solely on fields, offering a distinct advantage in computational efficiency. Furthermore, IM effectively circumvents the quantum distinguishability issue inherent in the conventional Gibbs-Bogoliubov inequality method. Finally, the method is applied to several standard lower-bound problems in statistical physics, including the Ising model, quantum harmonic oscillators, and quantum cubic wells. In every case, the results obtained via IM are equivalent to those from GBI, yet IM achieves significantly greater computational efficiency. Consequently, IM is established as a robust and highly effective tool for generating lower bounds. Additionally, a new inequality is proposed to further validate the method's efficacy. Overall, IM represents a powerful approach for deriving lower bounds, with extensive applications anticipated across diverse quantum fields. Its success is expected to inspire additional research and contribute to the advancement of lower-bound theory. Keywords: Lower bound, Independent variable method, Gibbs-Bogoliubov inequality, Variational method, Computational efficiency.

This study employs particle-in-cell simulations to examine the dynamics of the tearing instability within a current sheet characterized by a narrow, collisionless scale. The focus is on understanding how this scale influences the onset of the tearing instability and the characteristics of the resulting magnetic reconnection. We demonstrate that a secondary tearing mode emerges in this small-scale current sheet, which is driven by a current density gradient established by a low-frequency $z$-modulation of the background current. This mode has been identified as a primary contributor to small magnetic reconnection events in the Earth's magnetosphere. Furthermore, we find that the initial growth rate of the secondary tearing mode is independent of the specific mechanism generating the $z$-modulation of the background current. Finally, we provide an analytical model to describe the early-time evolution of the secondary tearing mode and its role in initiating small-scale reconnection. This model is validated by the simulation results. Additionally, we show that the secondary tearing mode is more likely to be unstable in current sheets with a strong guide field, which is consistent with observations from the magnetosphere. These findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the secondary tearing mode and its potential to trigger small-scale reconnection events in both laboratory and space environments. Our results suggest that the $z$-modulation of the background current, which drives the secondary tearing mode, is a generic feature of the current sheet structure in both the magnetosphere and laboratory plasmas. Consequently, the secondary tearing mode is expected to be a fundamental component of the reconnection process. This could explain the frequent observation of small-scale reconnection events in the magnetosphere and the small-scale structures found in various plasma experiments. Overall, this research provides a detailed picture of the global and local dynamics of the secondary tearing mode and its potential contribution to the tearing instability in small-scale collisionless current sheets. These insights are crucial for understanding the broader picture of magnetic reconnection in the Earth's magnetosphere and in various laboratory plasma experiments. Finally, our results may have significant implications for the study of small-scale reconnection events in astrophysical environments. Specifically, the $z$-modulation of the background current, which drives the secondary tearing mode, could be a generic feature of the current sheet structure in astrophysical environments, such as the solar corona. This could explain the frequent observation of small-scale reconnection events in the solar corona and their potential contribution to the heating of the corona. The visual similarity between distinct items of clothing is a core component of fashion image retrieval. However, accurately adjusting the visual characteristics of fashion features is challenging because of the significant domain gap between images from different clothing categories. To address this, we introduce a method for feature-level trait manipulation that adjusts visual attributes in semi-supervised fashion retrieval scenarios. Our approach employs domain adaptation to align features from different domains and employs contrastive learning to ensure that the resulting manipulated features remain distinguishable across domains. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both supervised and semi-supervised settings. Additionally, we present a case study on color manipulation, which validates the method's effectiveness and utility. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-chen/Semi-supervised Fashion Image Retrieval. Addressing the challenge of invertibility in Banach spaces through optimization techniques has garnered significant attention. This paper introduces a new dual gradient method designed to solve the family of convex optimization problems defined as $\min_{x\in X} \|Ax-y\|_Y + r(\ell(x))$, where $r$ is a strongly convex function on a Hilbert space $H$, $Y$ is a Banach space, and $A$ is a linear operator from $H$ to $B$ (another Banach space). This approach is shown to resolve the specific ill-posedness of these problems. Notably, when $r$ is strictly convex and $Y$ is a Hilbert space, the dual gradient method converges to the unique solution of the associated dual problem. Furthermore, under the additional assumption that the linear problem is well-posed, the method achieves quadratic convergence to the solution. These theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments on two applications: deconvolving noisy Poisson noise images and reconstructing sparse signals from noisy linear measurements. The latter case specifically demonstrates convergence to the minimum $\ell_1$-norm solution for ill-posed problems with ill-posedness index $1$. Additionally, the developed dual algorithm is compared against two existing primal methods for solving Banach space linear problems. While the primal algorithms converge to the unique solution, the dual gradient method converges to the minimum $\ell_1$-norm solution. For well-posed problems, all three methods exhibit convergence, with the dual gradient method showing superior performance. For ill-posed problems, the primal methods converge to the minimum $\ell_1$-norm solution, whereas the dual gradient method converges to the minimum dual norm solution. In this specific scenario, the dual gradient method outperforms the primal approaches. These results are illustrated using examples involving deconvolution and sparsity reconstruction. Expense creators are employed in light field processing to predict the 3D coordinates and occlusion status of pixels. Although previous research has achieved promising outcomes in scene reconstruction and rendering, the impact of training data quality on performance remains underexplored. This study introduces an occlusion-aware expense creator trained with a novel loss function designed to enhance depth estimation accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields superior performance in light field depth estimation, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods. This paper introduces bilinear formulations for the two-component Fokas-Lenells equations and establishes their N-soliton solutions using the Hirota method. These findings not only extend previous research but also demonstrate the broad applicability of the bilinear approach and Norman L. Lax's theory to integrable nonlinear partial differential equations. Specifically, we derive a novel Hirota bilinear form for the two-component Fokas-Lenells system, which differs significantly from the bilinear forms previously identified by Zhang et al. and Li et al. Furthermore, we derive the Hirota bilinear form associated with the Hirota-Kotera equation. In each instance, we successfully obtain the N-soliton solution, including a ten-soliton solution, through the use of tau functions. Additionally, we present a novel one-soliton solution that exhibits periodicity in time. Finally, we provide detailed descriptions of various one- and multi-soliton solutions, such as bright-dark-bright, bright-bright, bright-dipole-bright, dipole-dipole, and dipole-dipole-dipole solutions. Finally, utilizing the tau function method, we generate new two-, four-, six-, eight-, and ten-soliton solutions, accompanied by their corresponding figures. Notably, the dipole solutions display an asymmetric profile in time, a characteristic that distinguishes them from solutions previously reported in the literature. Furthermore, we provide a detailed description of double periodic solutions, which represent another significant advancement in this field. Non-Riemannian gravitational theories have recently garnered significant attention in both theoretical and observational research. In this study, we utilize the double field theory (DFT) framework to investigate such models, specifically focusing on a gravity action where the strong constraint is relaxed. This action features a dilaton duality symmetry and reduces to Hořava-Lowenstein (HL) gravity in the Riemannian limit. By employing DFT, we derive the field equations from this action and analyze the structure of its non-Riemannian background. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these non-Riemannian gravitational models can be embedded within the DFT formalism, with their field equations emerging from a modified DFT ansatz that incorporates additional DFT tensors. Finally, we examine the properties of these non-Riemannian gravitational models, noting that certain cases are closely related to HL gravity. Additionally, we explore the cosmological implications of these theories, showing that they yield distinct results compared to standard Riemannian gravitational models. Specifically, we find that these actions can account for the observed late-time cosmic acceleration without the need for dark energy. Finally, we establish a correspondence between non-Riemannian gravitational theories and modified Dirac-bracket Poisson brackets. Through this modified bracket structure, we derive modified conservation laws for matter fields, thereby providing a foundation for constructing non-Riemannian quantum field theories. This work paves the way for developing observational and experimental frameworks to test these non-Riemannian gravitational theories. In Home WiFi networks, clients can connect directly to an Access Point (AP) or link to a signal-repeating Extender. The network must select the optimal path based on various criteria, including the AP's transmission power, channel load, and the number of associated clients. This paper introduces a novel machine learning-based framework that dynamically chooses the best AP or Extender for each client by considering these factors. The model is trained using data from the Extender itself, as well as the APs it monitors, which are gathered via IEEE 802.11k and IEEE 802.11v protocol extensions. Specifically, these protocols enable the measurement of channel load and the count of associated clients. The proposed framework is validated using the ExtWiFi extender, which was integrated into a real-world IEEE 802.11n network. Experimental results demonstrate that the model can predict channel loads with an accuracy of 80% to 90%. Furthermore, the selection process improves the extender's revenue by 10% to 20% compared to the default IEEE 802.11k/v implementation. Additionally, the model successfully predicts the number of associated clients with up to 90% accuracy. Finally, the model's low computational complexity allows it to operate in real-time on the extender using only 1% of the CPU. This approach enables the extender to identify AP channel loads with minimal delay, thereby maximizing the Home WiFi network's revenue. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply machine learning to monitor channel load in Home WiFi networks. The code is available at: https://github.com/ExtWiFi/ExtWiFi.
